- doc. a5-0104/1999 by mr koch, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending directive 94/55/ec on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the transport of dangerous goods by road (com (99) 158 - c5-0004/1999 - 1999/0083 (cod)).
the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the transport of dangerous goods by road, which entered into force on 1 january 1997, contains some transitional provisions which are valid for a limited period of time and are linked to the conclusion of the work of cen, the european committee for standardization. the delays in the work of cen are now causing problems in the application of the directive itself. this applies in particular to the annexes which cannot be adapted to technical and industrial developments. i regret that because we have to act on the fact that others have not done their job. to that extent, i therefore accept the proposal for amending directive 94/55/ec which is under our consideration. failure to act by the european union would require member states to amend their legal provisions in this area for a short period of time, i.e. until the conclusion of the work of cen, which would lead to unnecessary costs and uncertainties. the amendment on the agenda does not therefore entail any change in the existing community harmonization of the transport of dangerous goods. it merely prolongs the transitional rules by postponing the deadlines, removes provisions which have ceased to be relevant and regulates the procedures for (a) ad hoc transport of dangerous goods and (b) the enactment of less stringent national provisions, in particular for the transport of very small quantities of dangerous goods in strictly defined areas. in doing so, the amendment of the directive is fully in line with the spirit of subsidiarity; member states with increased powers. the european commission decides whether member states may adopt specific provisions, the regulatory procedure providing for the support of a committee of experts on the transport of dangerous goods. in june 1999, a council decision redefined the detailed rules for the exercise of implementing powers conferred on the commission. however, the present proposal for a directive amending the directive on the transport of dangerous goods by road dates back to may 1999 and could not therefore take account of the current committee procedure. in two specific cases, the amendments tabled by the committee and unanimously agreed by the committee concern this modified committee procedure. we would like to make sure that this is already stated in the recitals and that the time limit within which the council must take a decision is set at a maximum of three months. the need for greater transparency is also stressed. another proposed amendment would also allow member states where work and transport is regularly carried out at temperatures well below -20°c to impose stricter requirements, particularly as regards tanks, in the particular interest of the northern regions of europe. finally, a final amendment proposal should allow the continued use of tanks and vehicles put into service between 1 january 1997 and the entry into force of this directive if their construction and maintenance meet the requirements. i am aware that this is only a small step towards greater transport safety, but i would ask you to approve this report.

the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with its white paper on the modernisation of european competition rules, the commission has launched an intensive and lively debate among the public, who are very interested in the subject. the reactions of experts and the people concerned range from complete rejection to unreserved support. what is the white paper about? the current system of european competition rules was built up in the early years of the community. under the conditions prevailing at the time, this system, which is based on a centralised notification and authorisation procedure, was fully justified. this procedure has made an essential contribution to the creation of a european culture of competition. however, in the forty years since its inception, the context has changed fundamentally. the community of six has expanded to 15 members and is on the verge of enlargement to 27. the system, however, has remained virtually unchanged. reform is therefore urgently needed. in fact, no one in this debate is questioning it. however, some critics believe that the commission's proposals go too far. the commission wants to abolish the system of notification and authorisation and, in its place, to strengthen the role of national authorities and courts in the application of competition rules. in other words, it is a question of moving from a system of authorization to a system of legal exemption. the principle of prohibition is, however, importantly maintained. i think that when an authority which is accused of a tendency towards bureaucracy and centralism makes a proposal which aims to reduce bureaucracy and centralism, we should at least seriously consider that proposal. the commission considers that the only objective is to tackle agreements between undertakings which restrict competition and abuse of a dominant position on the market. the notification obligation in the case of state aid and mergers remains unchanged. the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has unanimously approved the commission's proposals, minus one vote against and one abstention. however, a final judgment will only be possible after the publication of the commission's legislative proposals. i am also in agreement with the commission's proposals in substance, but there are a number of points which need to be improved or at least clarified. i should like to comment briefly on some of these points. many of those who criticise the white paper argue that decentralisation would threaten the coherence of the application of the law in the community. the national authorities, and in particular the courts, are not yet in a position to play the role which the commission intends to assign to them in the enforcement of the competition rules. first, the national cartel authorities have a proven track record in the application of competition rules over the past few decades. secondly, according to the current case-law, national courts already have the power to apply articles 81 (1), 82 and 86. however, it remains particularly important that the commission assists national authorities and courts through block exemption regulations, guidelines and communications. in addition, cooperation between national authorities and the commission and between national authorities among themselves should be strengthened. as regards the jurisdiction of national courts, we propose in this report that special courts should be set up for proceedings under the law on cartels. this practice is already being used in some member states, with some success. on the business side, there is a fear of a loss of legal certainty. to remedy this, undertakings should retain the possibility, in specific cases, of obtaining prior clarifications from the commission. these are just some of the aspects - albeit essential - which need to be taken into account in the modernisation of european competition rules. however, we are still at the beginning of the process. this discussion will continue until it finally leads to concrete legislative proposals. however, i am convinced that with this white paper we are on the right track. over the past decades, a european culture of competition has developed. the decentralisation proposed by the commission is in line with the principle of subsidiarity, which has since been enshrined in the treaty. this leads to a stronger application of european competition rules at national and regional level and thus provides a broader basis for european competition culture. in conclusion, i would like to say that the reform of competition policy which we are embarking on is a necessity and that in this connection it will be particularly necessary to make it clear that the competition policy of the european union is an essential condition for the success of a social market economy. the commission and parliament must affirm, more than ever before, that competition between companies and the european commission's oversight of it are the citizens' first interests. does not necessarily flow from the source. to avoid abuse, a general framework is essential, for example through the law on cartels. but, for the most part, this only helps to avoid abuse and is not, the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, my contribution to this debate concerns the steel aid code. these are public aids granted in europe in accordance with this code and examined by the commission. in all, 27 cases are reported for 1998. the commission has published its own report on these cases. the ecsc treaty will expire very soon. the question which must be of particular concern to us today is therefore how the aid to the steel industry will be used in the future. parliament welcomes the decisions taken by the european commission as set out in this report, including the decision requiring, in a specific case, the reimbursement of sums allocated and thus applying article 88 of the ecsc treaty. at the same time, the competitiveness of the european steel industry is at the centre of the latest commission communication, which parliament has not yet debated. as in other areas, article 87 (1) of the ec treaty provides for a general prohibition of aid in the iron and steel sector. according to that article, state aid is fundamentally incompatible with the common market, and exceptions are allowed only in well-defined cases. article 88 provides that the commission is to be responsible for the control of state aid. in 1998, the largest case was the equity injection of eur 540 million into preussag in germany. in addition, member states must notify the commission in advance of their plans to grant aid. the current rules for the steel industry were introduced on 18 december 1996. under these rules, aid to the steel industry can be granted only in specific and well-defined cases. these are aid for research and development, aid for environmental protection, social aid to encourage the closure of steelworks and aid to finance the permanent closure of noncompetitive undertakings. in addition, there is a derogating regulation for greece, which is capped at eur 50 million. however, it is clear that the implementation of the steel aid code has raised problems in recent years which have not been fully discussed in the report. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the aid is not used to finance the production of steel products. we cannot decide to weaken the guidelines contained in this code. no one wants europe to be the scene of a frantic race for subsidies. the commission therefore concluded that the measures in force were in line with the met/it guidelines. parliament therefore considered that, in view of the unequal treatment of the steel industry, it was essential to reform the steel aid code and asked the commission to submit a new regulation to the council. it is known that the council has so far refused to adopt such a regulation. this is partly because it is thought that when the code expires, we will be able to do as we please again, free of the heavy controls of the european commission. we therefore ask that, after the expiry of the treaty, aid to the steel industry be regulated by a council regulation in accordance with article 94, because this is the only way to guarantee the necessary binding nature and clarity. this is the only way to implement the formal prohibition of all aid not covered by the code. a council regulation is a directly applicable act, which regional governments must also comply with. in future too, distortions of competition and market imbalances must be avoided. the commission's practice of approving a number of aid schemes for steel undertakings which it considered did not fall within the categories mentioned in the code is also to be criticised, even though the court of justice has approved this unequal treatment for certain decisions. we ask that in the report for 1999, which is still to be drawn up, the commission highlights in detail the active role it plays in the preparation of restructuring plans and in the authorization of derogations and thus allows an adequate assessment of the overall context to be made on this basis. the committee on economic and monetary affairs adopted the draft report unanimously, with two abstentions, and i ask the house to give its full support to the draft which we have put before you.

programme, the presidency considers it important to explore, in the light of the principles of title vi of the treaty, the appropriate forms for better informing the european parliament on the progress and conclusion of these negotiations in the framework of the united nations convention. the court of justice network has seen important developments, including the start of operation of the telecommunications system for the european judicial network at the end of 1999. in addition, a number of actions were carried out within the framework of the multidisciplinary group in implementation of the 1997 action plan. but it must be stressed that the adoption of the strategy for the new millennium must take place as soon as possible in order to give impetus and continuity to the work developed under the previous action plan. as regards judicial cooperation, important progress has been made in the area of criminal protection of the euro and the european parliament is being consulted on a framework decision of fundamental strategic importance. we believe that the credibility of the criminal protection of the euro requires that we avoid a multiplicity of instruments and that we must therefore make a joint effort to be able to approve in march a single instrument which deals with all the matters to be dealt with, both those concerning initiatives already presented by france and those whose necessary adoption is emphasized by the commission. in this area, measures concerning the mutual recognition of judicial decisions should be put into effect. we believe that it is possible, with the work already undertaken, at least in the area of seizure of property, to adopt measures enabling mutual recognition of decisions. finally, as regards europol, whose activities began precisely in 1999 and which led the council to adopt a set of instruments known to parliament to make its operation viable, there is of course still a substantive question concerning democratic control and judicial control, questions which naturally take on a different dimension with the political option adopted in tampere to deepen europol's powers and, above all, its operational dimension. the french presidency has left us with an important working document which envisages different scenarios for addressing and resolving the questions of democratic control and judicial control of europol. the portuguese presidency will shortly be presenting a working document on the eurojust network, because, of course, it is not necessary for europol's judicial control to be carried out with the help of eurojust, and it cannot be ruled out at the moment that this could be an option. it is therefore essential that the council's debate on the development of europol and eurojust take place simultaneously so that the conclusions are drawn simultaneously. i believe that it is within this framework, and within the dialogue that the council and parliament will necessarily have to establish on the evolution of europol and eurojust, that we can find an institutionally acceptable solution for the liaison between the council and parliament as regards europol. we know the positions of parliament and we know that parliament knows the positions of the council's legal services. i believe that this question will find a definitive solution in the context of the resolution of the question of the democratic control of europol; a solution that mobilizes and strengthens institutional cooperation between everyone. commission - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen of the council, first of all, without wishing to enter into a competition of emotions with the ministers, i must say that i am not moved but disturbed by the fact that for the first time two of my personal friends are representing the presidency. i hope that this will not alter the separation of powers which is essential to the proper functioning of our union. secondly, i would like to thank mrs anna terrón for raising the question which gives rise to the first annual debate of this parliament on the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice; i would also like to thank all the members who have actively participated in the preparation of this annual debate in the various committees, as well as the representatives of national parliaments and civil society. on the occasion of this first speech, i would like to share with parliament the commission's view of the most significant events of 1999. i believe i can say with conviction, but also with satisfaction, that 1999 was a year of turning points and consolidation for the union in the area of freedom, security and justice. it has already been said here that the treaty of amsterdam entered into force in may and this parliament has said that the most profound innovation of this treaty was the recognition of the need to create an area of freedom, security and justice. it is both a major qualitative leap and a logical and indispensable step in the development of the union, after the completion of the internal market, the introduction of the single currency and the launching of a common foreign and security policy. this project, which is much more than a project of the institutions, is a project of the citizens of our common union. this is why all citizens residing in the territory of the union must be guaranteed genuine freedom of movement, recognising that this freedom only makes sense if it is achieved in a safe context, firmly anchored in an efficient judicial system to which everyone can have access under simple and equal conditions, in which citizens can actually have confidence. the union's commitment to achieving an area of freedom, security and justice was confirmed in tampere. i would like to emphasize the strong political message sent by the european council, reaffirming the importance which the heads of state and government of the union attach to a fundamental project, and the number of political guidelines and priorities which will make it possible for this area to become a reality, according to a progressive strategy, with a five-year perspective and above all, a balanced area in its three components: freedom, security and justice. 1999 was also marked by the german presidency's initiative to draw up a charter of fundamental rights for the union. in the current phase of development of the european union, i believe that the fundamental rights currently in force at union level should be brought together in a charter, so as to make them more visible and accessible to all citizens. as i have said on several occasions, i am in favour of, and the commission is in favour of, the drawing up of a charter which reflects as broadly as possible, in a dynamic process, the common constitutional traditions of the member states and the general principles of community law, which are not limited to the simple statement of a common minimum denominator. as the commission's representative, i will ensure that the charter and the actions that follow from it are the affirmation of a union based on the set of fundamental rights which are an integral part of europe's common heritage. only in this way can we help to restore legitimacy to the project of an enlarged union, based on respect for rights and freedoms, the guarantee of the safety of persons and property and effective judicial protection, in the eyes of all european citizens. in other words, a union rooted in the political values which justify modern democracies. i am not forgetting that 1999 was also the year in which the 1999-2004 european parliament took office, the new commission took office and a commissioner with sole responsibility for justice and home affairs took office. beyond these events, i would like to remind parliament of some of the points that were approved in 1999. in the field of immigration, borders and asylum, the commission presented the proposal for a regulation on the creation of the eurodac database, the proposal for a directive on the conditions for admitting third-country nationals to the member states of the union for the purpose of family reunification, as part of a specific policy on the integration of persons legally residing in the territory of the union. we have submitted a communication on common asylum procedures and a recommendation for a decision authorising the commission to negotiate an agreement with iceland and norway to extend to these two countries the rules applicable to the member states of the european union under the dublin convention. the commission has actively contributed to the work of the high level group on immigration and asylum. finally, in december, the commission put forward a proposal for the creation of the european refugee fund. in the field of judicial cooperation, the commission has tabled proposals for regulations to bring certain conventions into line with community law: one on judicial cooperation and the enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters (brussels i), another on jurisdiction, recognition and enforcement of judgments in matrimonial matters (brussels ii) and another on the service of judicial and extrajudicial documents in civil and commercial matters. in 1999, we also presented a communication on victims of crime in the union, initiating a reflection on the subject which was born in tampere and calling for the development of minimum standards on the protection of victims of crime, especially on their access to justice and their rights to compensation for the damage suffered, including legal costs. i would also mention the presentation of the draft decision on the fight against fraud and counterfeiting of non-cash means of payment. in the area of the union's legislative framework for the fight against financial crime, the commission has presented a draft revision of the money laundering directive. in 1999 we witnessed the inauguration of europol. after what has been said here by the portuguese presidency, with the new cycle in the fields of justice and home affairs, the beginning of the reflection on the implementation of the new competences conferred on europol by the treaty of amsterdam, we sincerely hope that it will be possible to discuss in the same way with the commission as regards the question of democratic control and the link between europol and the relevant judicial bodies, in particular eurojust. in 1999, the commission presented its contribution to a european action plan on drugs, which forms the basis of the strategy adopted by the european council in helsinki. this non-exhaustive list of actions enables me to reaffirm today before the council presidency and the members of this house, with great conviction, that while 1999 was the year in which the union's action in this fundamental area was consolidated, it was also the beginning of a new phase in accelerating the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice. the year 2000 will undoubtedly be the year of truth for the european institutions and the way in which they will be able to meet the citizens' demands for a guarantee of freedom of movement, with respect for rights and a guarantee of security and stability, through adequate judicial protection. this means that the year 2000 will be a test year for the council, parliament and the commission as to whether they have the political will to take amsterdam seriously and to contribute to the foundations of an enlarged political union for the next decade. as i have said, the commission is aware of its share of responsibility. in this context, it finalised a first draft proposal for an evaluation panel, a scoreboard, so that all the institutions and other parties concerned can assess progress in implementing the necessary measures and in respecting the deadlines set by the amsterdam treaty, the vienna action plan and the tampere european council conclusions. this evaluation panel will not only be an instrument for legislative programming, but also and above all an instrument for strengthening the transparency and accountability of all the european institutions towards the citizens. because it is for the citizens that we are creating the space of freedom, security and justice. the progress achieved will not be due to the commission, the council or even the european parliament, but to the association of the european institutions and the member states themselves, insofar as, as has been said here, certain tasks of the scoreboard will be entrusted to the member states under the principle of subsidiarity. in the next few weeks, i will be making a tour of the capitals to seek the views of the ministers of justice and home affairs. i intend to discuss this draft scoreboard with the european parliament and civil society. we intend to present the final version to the justice and home affairs council, under the portuguese presidency, after the consultations i have just mentioned. i intend to make this scoreboard a tool for policy and strategic guidance for all the institutions, but also a tool for public scrutiny. i therefore recognize - and i believe this is a challenge we all face - the need to develop a communication strategy which enables the general public to perceive the real added value of the union in everyday life, in these so essential areas of citizenship, respect for the law and, in fact, democracy itself. beyond the scoreboard, i would like to say that the commission intends to present the following initiatives during the year 2000, and i would like to stress here that i welcome the fact that the portuguese presidency considers the development of this area as one of the priorities of its work programme. i hope that it will be possible, with the portuguese presidency, to work clearly in the spirit of interinstitutional cooperation, which is also the political message of tampere, and that this spirit of interinstitutional cooperation will be followed by subsequent presidencies. as regards immigration and the right of asylum, the commission intends to submit proposals for the elaboration of a community instrument on the temporary protection of refugees; to start analysing the criteria and conditions for improving the implementation of the dublin convention and the possible amendment of its legal basis, in accordance with the treaty of amsterdam; continue the debate on the basis of the communication already made on the rules leading to a common asylum process across the union; the commission will also present proposals for legislation providing for the granting of residence permits to victims of trafficking in human beings who cooperate with the judiciary against trafficking networks. i also intend to contribute to clarifying the role of action plans in the area of work of the high level group on immigration and asylum law, and to make progress in adapting community agreements in the area of readmission, through the inclusion of model clauses. as regards a central issue for the free movement of persons, such as crossing the external borders of the member states, i shall be presenting in the coming days a proposal for a regulation which renews the list of third countries whose nationals must be in possession of a visa when crossing the external borders. in the area of judicial cooperation, in addition to an initiative on the law applicable to non-contractual obligations, i sincerely hope that it will be possible to submit to the council a draft of minimum rules guaranteeing throughout the union an adequate level of legal assistance in cross-border cases. i also intend to continue to consider the development of specific common procedural rules for the simplification and acceleration of crossborder judicial proceedings concerning small cases in the commercial and consumer court, maintenance cases and uncontested cases. following the tampere and helsinki conclusions, the commission will present its contribution to the definition of a union strategy for the prevention and fight against organised crime. we will organise and support actions such as, in particular, the debate on the need to develop a legislative programme for the implementation of the principle of mutual recognition of judicial decisions in criminal matters. the commission also intends to present specific measures in the field of crime prevention in order to develop the exchange of best practice in this field, especially as regards the prevention of urban and juvenile delinquency, and to present a legal basis for the programme financed by the community to this end. the commission will also contribute to the presidency's efforts to clarify the legal framework and the framework for administrative, police and judicial cooperation in the fight against money laundering in a highly inter-pillar perspective. the commission will respect the responsibility assumed in tampere and will present proposals for the approval of common definitions, charges and sanctions in the context of trafficking in human beings, the economic exploitation of migrants, the sexual exploitation of women and children, with particular attention to combating the use of new means of communication and, in particular, the internet for the dissemination of child pornography material. we are also preparing a communication by launching a debate on how to ensure a safer information and knowledge society and how to combat cybercrime. the year 2000 also marks the beginning of the implementation of the european strategy against drugs 2000-04. in this context, the commission, in collaboration with the portuguese presidency and the european parliament, will give its full support to the interinstitutional conference on drugs to be held in february. as regards schengen, without going into the council's area of competence and, in particular, the integration of the schengen acquis into the community framework, i would like to stress, as regards the question of the reintroduction of border controls, that the commission once again reiterates its willingness to examine the question of better monitoring of the application of article 2 (2) of the schengen convention, with a view to making it more imperative. the recent reintroduction of certain internal border controls leads me to conclude that it is necessary to carry out a detailed analysis of the conditions for the adoption of a legislative instrument based on article 62 of the treaty. as was stressed in tampere and in the run-up to the feira european council in june 2000, we will have to sum up the implications of the new external dimension of home affairs and justice with a view to adopting inter-pillar political strategies which strengthen the coherence of the union's internal and external policy in this area and which contribute to the union's assertion in the world. i would stress in the meantime that all these actions will of course have to take account of the principles agreed at the helsinki european council with regard to the candidate countries so that they cooperate and are involved as quickly as possible in this project of creating an area of freedom, security and justice. it should also be remembered that the jha negotiations will begin in 2000 with the first group of candidate countries and i believe that we will be able to make substantial progress in the preparation of the negotiating files on the second group admitted to membership in helsinki. finally, i would like to reiterate that the commission intends to take a leading position in the presentation of proposals to follow up the implementation of the amsterdam treaty. i hope that the commission and the council will reach an agreement on the sharing of responsibilities in the exercise of the right of initiative and in the conduct of the legislative process. as i said in parliament, the task ahead is enormous and ambitious, the commission must have the human resources to meet this challenge and hopes to be able to count on the support of parliament and, why not, of the council to guarantee these resources and objectives, so that the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice becomes a reality in the union as soon as possible. we can all therefore contribute, in a spirit of interinstitutional cooperation, to the implementation of this project, which is undoubtedly the 'crown jewel' of the amsterdam treaty.

- the next item is the report (a5-0102/1999) by mr turmes, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the establishment of performance requirements for ballasts for fluorescent lighting (com (99) 296 - c5-0010/1999 - 1999/0127 (cod)).
commission. - (es) mr president, i should first like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr turmes, on his excellent report and to thank all the speakers and the house for the great support they have shown for this proposal which, in the commission's view, can make a significant contribution to increasing energy efficiency and which sets the objective of saving 20% of the electricity consumed by the tertiary sector. all this is necessary to significantly improve the efficiency of the end use of electricity, thereby contributing to meeting our kyoto commitments. the proposal takes a conservative approach to improving efficiency without imposing an unbearable burden on ballast manufacturers. i would like to say to you, ladies and gentlemen, that, as has already been pointed out by some speakers, before we put this proposal into practice, we consulted and discussed it with the sector concerned. ladies and gentlemen, we are starting with a proposal comprising different scales. the first stage, which will be effective one year after the adoption of the directive, will involve the phasing out of low-efficiency ballasts. from there, a second tier of higher standards will gradually reduce the number of conventional ballasts and make the use of high-efficiency, high-efficiency ballasts mandatory. i must say - in order for you to realise the change that this will entail - that at present conventional ballasts account for approximately two thirds of total current sales, which means that this second stage will have very significant effects and undeniable repercussions on the industry, which is why we are proposing a four-year transitional period. as regards the proposed amendments, i am pleased to announce, ladies and gentlemen, that the commission can accept all those tabled by the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, with the exception of amendments nos 1, 17, 19 and 20 concerning the introduction of the third level of efficiency automatically. the commission agrees that a dynamic approach is needed, which is why the proposal envisages a possible third phase. however, we believe that it will be difficult to define this third phase in all its aspects today. in our view, it is better to assess the technical and economic situation at the time of the entry into force of the second level and determine, in consultation with the parties concerned at that time, whether we are completing this third stage, as we are doing, what technical definitions and requirements should be imposed and by what timeframe they can be implemented. consequently, the commission can also accept the second part of amendment no 23, but not the first part. the commission can also accept part of amendment no 1, but in a different form. we also agree with amendment no 12, which aims to ensure effective enforcement by the member states. the amendments to clarify that all ballasts marketed as independent components or incorporated into lighting are covered by the proposal, namely amendments nos 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 21 and 22, as i have said, are all acceptable to the commission. amendment no 2 is also accepted as the commission agrees with the exclusion of the types of ballast mentioned. the same applies to amendments nos 15 and 16, which extend the transitional period to 18 months. finally, the commission accepts amendment no 8 on the promotion of performance standards in international fora. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have summarized the commission's position on the report. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr turmes, again on his excellent work and i hope that the council will be able to adopt a common position to resolve this problem quickly. (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to thank our colleague, mr palacio vallelersundi, for his initiative in putting an oral question. what is it ? in summary, the theme is the following: contradiction between consumer protection and e-commerce. in other words, how can we effectively protect consumers in the european union without harming the development of e-commerce? the discussion is currently focused on the question of the principle of jurisdiction and therefore the applicable law in cross-border e-commerce disputes. in the event of a dispute, must the consumer assert his rights in the country in which he resides or in which the supplier of goods or services is established? which law applies? i do not wish to list the pros and cons of this today. they're well-known enough. the commission held a hearing on this in november. today i would simply like to draw your attention to the fact that in my opinion the discussion on consumer protection on the one hand and e-commerce on the other is too narrow, too succinct. this discussion is also in contradiction with the strategy formulated by the commission itself in its communication on a strategy for the internal market. the commission's communication explicitly states that balanced solutions must be found where the interests of consumers and those of the economic sector diverge. the european union must give a realistic chance to the development of electronic commerce in the european union. however, a balanced solution to this conflict between consumer protection and electronic commerce will only be possible if the discussion is not limited to the question of jurisdiction and applicable law, but is very broad. the idea of effective consumer protection must be based on the practical aim of ensuring that consumers are brought to justice quickly, without going bankrupt or wasting too much time in administrative procedures. is this really the case if the consumer can bring a complaint in his country of residence on the basis of national law? a judgment in the consumer's country of residence is even worse for the consumer, because he has to have his judgment enforced in another member state. it is usually long, tedious and expensive. for effective consumer protection, alternatives to cumbersome and costly legal proceedings must be evaluated, irrespective of the court and law involved. an extrajudicial settlement of disputes, possibly combined with other harmonizations, is in my view the magic word. the directorate-general has already studied the subject of out-of-court settlement of disputes in the field of cross-border financial services in depth. it held a hearing on this matter last october. i suggest that the ideas and conclusions of the commission working document which formed the basis of this hearing and the communication on the results of the hearing expected for the middle of the year should also be considered for electronic commerce. in my view, the approach of the e-commerce directive must be politically privileged and therefore not be countered by the regulation contained in the brussels/lugano convention and the rome ii convention. i therefore propose that the procedure be continued either by postponing the amendment until all the outstanding legal issues in this area have been settled or by maintaining the status quo of the balance of interests between suppliers and consumers in the event of amendment of the brussels/lugano convention.

(de) mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, commissioner, i agree with my fellow rapporteur, mr dimitrakopoulos, that the agenda agreed in helsinki is not enough to overcome the challenges of enlargement to 13 new states. in our view, a mini-reform would be a missed opportunity which would also threaten the stability of the european union. the european parliament could not and should not accept that too broad an extension and a lack of depth would thus endanger the european union. we would like to remind governments once again that parliament must give its consent before a new member can join the union. parliament will certainly also take this decision on enlargement in the light of the results of this intergovernmental conference. on 18 november 1999 we set out the main points of our agenda for the intergovernmental conference in the year 2000. i shall confine myself to mentioning some of the points: provisions for enhanced cooperation between these 20 or 25 member states; the integration of security and defence policy into the community framework; the incorporation of the charter of fundamental rights into the new treaty; the constitutionalisation of the union by dividing the treaties into one fundamental part and another; the reform of article 48 so that, in future amendments to the treaties, parliament is effectively and fairly involved in the negotiations and - which i also want to mention - a statute for european parties so that, in the next european elections, the debates really concern european issues and not national domestic policies. finally, the strengthening of the institutions and, in order to balance european monetary integration with the single currency which we have already decided on, the creation of economic, social and employment policy instruments. in addition to a broader agenda, we also want a better method for drawing up this new european treaty. in the interests of the citizens, it is necessary to ensure greater transparency in the political process at the intergovernmental conference. that is why we are calling for a broad involvement of parliament at all levels. the union has a twofold legitimacy: it is a union of states but also a union of peoples. it is time that this was reflected in the method of drawing up a new treaty. representatives of the european parliament must therefore be genuinely involved in the preparatory group, both at ministerial level and in the european council meetings devoted to the intergovernmental conference. the governments decided to open this intergovernmental conference on 14 february. the conditions will now be met for the conference to open. i am not going to hide from you that many of our colleagues would have preferred to wait until we had a report on the rotation of capitals undertaken by the portuguese presidency in order to see if things were moving, if there was a positive dynamic for the extension of the agenda. but we have confidence in the portuguese presidency and in the commitment it has made in this house to propose, at the lisbon summit in march, the inclusion of other items on the agenda. we ask the governments to follow the proposal of the portuguese presidency. it is therefore a matter of trusting prejudice and we hope that we will not be disappointed to give our opinion now without knowing exactly what new dynamics are at work and what items will be added to the agenda. our advice to you is a clear message to governments not to miss the last opportunity to carry out ambitious eu reform before enlargement and to increase acceptance of this next european treaty by greater transparency and the guarantee of full involvement of parliament. i also thank the portuguese presidency and commissioner barnier for their cooperation. i ask the house to support our view broadly.

private and public investment in the production and use of energy from renewable sources. since the current programme expired at the end of last year and the council did not accept the amendments is astonishing. i must also say, however, that the finnish presidency of the council has been relatively able to act as long as the member states have been standing in the way of the necessary increase in these resources. the commission's original proposal of eur 81.1 million was unilaterally and unjustifiably reduced by the council to eur 74 million. the parliament could therefore logically only ask for the original appropriation to be restored. apart from the financial allocation of the programme, a number of other points of dispute also existed between the council and parliament. the essential requirements we had formulated were agreed with the council in the conciliation procedure, as is the case with the opening of the altener programme to the associated pursue a reasonable programme on the substance. that is why we have finally agreed to the compromise, even though we are not entirely satisfied with it. we have agreed to increase the resources to 77 million. if this is not a fully satisfactory result, it is nevertheless acceptable. we have agreed to this compromise so as not to jeopardize the continuation of this programme. however, unless member states make more efforts, it does not appear possible to achieve the community target of producing 15% of primary energy demand from renewable energy sources by 2010. this ensures the continuation of an important community environmental and economic policy programme which contributes to the limitation of co2 emissions, the increase in the share of renewable energy in the energy balance, the reduction of our dependence on energy imports, security of supply and local and regional cohesion and development. but of course, this is not enough. the member states have also made enormous efforts to do so. on 9 december the conciliation committee approved the final text of the programme, thus paving the way for the future promotion of studies and actions in this field aimed at exploiting the potential of renewable energies. furthermore, the continuation of the alterner programme ensures that pilot actions for the creation and development of infrastructure, knowledge transfer and targeted actions to facilitate the penetration of renewable energies can be encouraged and carried out. this is particularly feasible in the field of geothermal energy, wind energy, for smaller hydroelectric power stations, for the passive and active use of solar energy in buildings and for the use of biomass. in considering these areas, we can see how necessary and important it is to continue to provide a reasonable framework of support at european level in the field of alternative energy sources. i would like to thank the commission and the commissioner responsible for this matter, mrs de palacio, in particular, for supporting parliament's position. the european parliament has managed to reach a reasonable compromise and to change the council's common position. i would be grateful if my colleagues would approve the conciliation committee's outcome.

the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, every year in europe nine million cars end up in the mill or in the landfill. in addition to being unable to drive, these nine million cars have the distinctive feature of being traded and transported across borders, not only within the community but also across the union's external borders. it is therefore right, in substance, that the european union should establish community rules for the recycling and treatment of these nine million vehicles each year. we believe that the directive shows some weaknesses which this house would like to remedy in order to produce a directive which would then actually be a future directive. that is why there are so many amendments. i personally think that the scope of this directive is beyond its purpose. i do not think it is necessary to include vintage vehicles in this directive. i also do not think that motorcycles should be part of this directive because the motorcycle world is so imbued with a culture of recycling that we do not need a european directive in this area. i am not pushing for high recycling rates for special purpose vehicles either. i would like to see special purpose vehicles such as ambulances have high rates of reuse. that is my main concern in this area. i think it is right that the directive requires a certificate on the way cars are handled in europe. in this respect, we can leave things as they are as proposed by the commission. member countries ensure that there are suitable storage places for drying vehicles, which for example treat 32 million litres of waste oils, extract brake fluids, etc. an important part of this directive is what do we do with used parts? what we do with the crushed products. in this connection, it should not be forgotten that while the percentage is an important element of recycling, reuse, and what else, it is not the only one. because i would ask you not to forget that, as far as the mobility of a vehicle is concerned, 80% of the constraints imposed on the environment result from driving, 1% from recovery and 19% from the construction of the vehicle. percentages are therefore not the only parameter for environmental sustainability but one of many. i naturally think that we need serious objectives. but percentages should not be an end in themselves; we need to understand that it's important to have a global view of the environmental impact of cars. i would much rather that, from a car that weighs 1,400 kilos today and travels an average of 200,000 kilometres, we should end up in the future with a car that weighs only 1,000 kilos and also travels 200,000 kilometres. we would actually be transporting 400 kilos times 200,000 kilometers less. this is the first real environmental progress because it leads to a big reduction in co2 emissions, and if i understand the kyoto protocol correctly, this is the essential element. therefore, we believe that vehicles which in the future are significantly and verifiably derived from lightweight construction methods will produce less co2 and should be given a special preference in terms of percentage of incineration. whether or not these lightweight vehicles - many people are also talking about the three-litre car - are given a special preference should not be decided by each member state but by you, madam commissioner. we think that is the case. let me say a few words about costs. some say that all the costs should be borne by the manufacturers; that would be fair and very favorable to the consumer. this is highly doubtful, because the producers will pass all these costs on to the consumers and will take over a recycling monopoly allocated to the state. i can only warn you not to approve of this. the amendments propose that the costs be shared in half between the manufacturer and the buyer of a new car. from such a pool, from such a system, whatever else you may think of it, we could, as of 2006, take over all existing vehicles at no cost to the last owner. that is also an explicit wish of my group. our proposal for cost-sharing has the very decisive advantage of not turning into a candidate for the court of justice as soon as we have adopted this directive. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's energy policy is not distorted by the effects of the single market. that is why i propose a cost-sharing between the first owner and the manufacturer. i come now to the banning of materials - we naturally need to ban certain materials. cars contain dangerous components that eventually need to be banned. to do this, we need a pressure instrument. the commission has put forward some proposals which were too strict and we have developed alternatives to this. there are - (de) mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, if you look at the leaflets that have been distributed in recent weeks, you might think that we are discussing the ultimate ecological disaster or the death of the automobile industry in europe. neither of these hypotheses is correct. we must objectively see that the directive before us is a good directive. it is an ecological advance for europe and we can be proud of it if we incorporate it into legislation and implement it. there is one point, however, on which our views differ. this may be a minor point in view of the scale of the directive, but it is the subject of controversy. it concerns the question of the costs of recycling. we are fundamentally different from the discussion that took place last year in the council. the fact that the procedure was free of charge for the last owner and the question of financing had been put in the same bag and the free of charge had been called into question. in february last year we decided in this house - and we social democrats are committed to this decision - that there should be no doubt about the fact that this is free. but who pays for the treatment that the vehicles have to undergo? it seems clear to us that for new vehicles it must be the manufacturer, because in doing so he is required to design and manufacture recyclable vehicles. but what about the vehicles that are on the road? for example, if the british firm rover were responsible for all end-of-life vehicles, it would have to take care of 5.8 million vehicles in the european union and would have to set aside eur 250 million immediately to cover recycling costs, while a korean manufacturer that builds similar cars would have to put peanuts in reserve - as a representative of deutsche bank once said. these are distortions of competition which have nothing to do with environmental protection and which only affect the investment capacity and jobs of those who make cars in europe. we therefore propose, in order to guarantee the principle of free distribution, to set up a fund for end-of-life vehicles which will pay for the costs of recycling these vehicles. i can understand some colleagues from countries where we have not produced cars saying that manufacturers must bear the full cost and mocking the problem of distortions of competition caused by the reservation of these funds. but i ask these colleagues to stand in solidarity with the two million people who build cars in europe and make a living from them, so that these jobs can be maintained in the future. i am in favour of strict environmental requirements: you know this from the car-oil programme and the debate on the exhaust gas thresholds. but i think they should be the same for everyone.

commission - (it) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, a five-year programme is a very large undertaking, so i preferred to have the full text of my speech distributed to you, which is available in four languages. in order to respect the time allotted to me, i shall confine myself to recalling the main lines of my programme, a programme from the beginning of this parliament, from the beginning of the century, when it is legitimate to look at europe from a wider perspective, a europe beset by a paradox. let us not forget that europe has enjoyed a period of peace, security and freedom in its 50 years of existence and that a united europe has also helped to bring us unprecedented prosperity. we are now on the verge of a strong recovery which, if we are wise in our policies, seems to have a very long-term prospect. this recovery is the logical consequence of our efforts, it is not the result of chance but of the consolidation of public finances in european countries which have brought inflation under control thanks to a policy focused on cost control and on increasing productivity in a europe which has begun a vigorous restructuring of its industries, its banks, its administrations, even if there is still a long way to go in this respect. despite all this, there is disappointment and concern in europe because of the slow decline in unemployment, the technological backwardness which seems to be getting worse and worse and which, above all, is beginning to be accompanied by a serious backwardness in the scientific field, and because the european institutions seem distant, because they do not seem to be up to the challenge, starting with the commission. the crisis in the commission was indeed a crucial moment in the relations between europe and its citizens, and the low turnout in the european elections was a worrying sign of this. however, the feeling of insecurity, of unpreparedness for a world that is changing, a world that is changing completely, a world where globalization is finally changing our benchmarks, is even deeper. this is not a new phenomenon: europe has already been confronted with a similar upheaval, with an explosion of its markets, with a change of its benchmarks, with a different perception of the world. i'm thinking here of the 16th century, after the discovery of america, when everything changed. some countries, such as france and spain, have risen to the challenge by giving birth to large nation states; other countries, such as italy, have not taken up this challenge and have lost the lead they had taken in many areas since the first part of the millennium: science, technology, economic progress, defence structures and military organisation, thought and literature. today europe faces an identical challenge and we know that history will not forgive us more today than it did in the past. in the face of major upheavals, to prevent our national states from disappearing as a result of globalisation, which is shaping dimensions and conditions unprecedented in our history, we need an economically strong europe. globalisation requires unity, because every day brings new agreements at the global level and every day we learn that changes have also taken place in europe. but what we need most is a europe that is politically strong. in recent years, the single market and the euro have been the focal point of our action, the driving force of european life. today, the new frontiers of european integration are political: the common foreign and security policy, justice and internal security and - then - the crucial question of the fundamental political values on which our coexistence is based. that is why the commission has approved the strategic plan 2000-2005, a plan which has been sent directly to the european parliament and which you are already aware of and which i will not go into in detail in my speech. some may find it too synthetic, but no political structure produces detailed five-year plans. it is the european union, not the soviet union. our plan sets out the main points of reference, the main lines of action: first, the development of new forms of government for europe; second, the expansion and enlargement of the area of peace, freedom and security; third, the development of the european union's external relations. thirdly, the launching of a new phase of economic development; fourthly, protection and improvement of the quality of life. these are our broad guidelines for the next five years. as regards the first - the new forms of government for europe - you already know that the commission has committed itself to presenting a white paper and not a complete legislative text because, faced with the major problems which are changing the structure of our way of life, the commission is first preparing the discussion. then she talks about the content with you and that is how a political document, a legislative document, is finally born. this way of acting to involve all the european institutions and citizens is transparent and effective. this white paper is a response to the challenges of enlargement. it requires us to re-examine the functioning of all our institutions, to re-examine our policies - all our policies - and above all to re-examine what we will have to continue to do at union level when we have twenty-five or thirty member states, and what will be more appropriate to do at national, regional and local government level. but enlargement is not the only reason for this new thinking. as i said, the globalisation of the economy and politics itself is also driving us to do so. we must govern europe in a way that is more effective, closer to the citizens, promoting participation by all, starting first of all with the great problem of women's participation. one of the main differences in the comparison made during this period between europe and the united states is not so much the mobility of workers or the problem of venture capital, but rather the participation of women in economic life, a much higher participation in the united states than in our country. this is an area where europe has always been at the forefront and we must carry out a profound, open reflection, and all the institutions - commission, parliament, council - will have to think about their own role, their own policies. we shall therefore immediately get back to work on this white paper, although we shall have to wait for the outcome of the intergovernmental conference to complete it. it will therefore not be presented before spring 2001. it will not be a philosophical book but a practical one, rich in specific proposals. we - the commission - are the first to know that we must completely overhaul our organization. we will therefore do two things: we will work, and we are already working, to push for internal reform, and we will thoroughly review our policies. i have asked all the commissioners - and we will repeat this request in an even more analytical way - to identify all the activities that can be abandoned. the commission must determine what its core activities are, what it should focus on, and delegate non-core activities so as to generate new resources and to report more correctly and achieve greater cooperation with countries, regions and local communities. we will therefore release other resources, but there will come a time - i fear, and i say this in front of you - when the resources we are already releasing will no longer be sufficient to enable us to meet our new responsibilities. i am thinking of enlargement, the new justice and home affairs sector, health and environmental problems. when we have spent all our resources, i will not hesitate to come to you and ask for more, but i say from today that we will not accept new tasks if the financial means to undertake them do not follow because there would be no coherence between the tasks to be carried out and the resources available. as regards internal reform, you know the commitment my commission has made on this point from day one. i know full well that we will not be able to achieve any political objective if this deep and complete internal reform is not achieved, if the commission does not show itself to be more effective in all sectors, starting with the one where we have accumulated the most backlog, that of external aid. providing rapid assistance where it is needed saves lives; providing help late can sometimes be worse than not providing it at all. when i speak of external aid, i am thinking first of all of the balkans, where we are seeing some encouraging signs of the commitment of our officials on the ground, an extraordinary commitment given the organizational problems encountered. i am also thinking of the efforts made by mr kouchner, the stability pact which we support energetically and with absolute dedication, but also the new elements, for example in croatia, where the situation has changed in a few weeks. the european institutions immediately opened the door to dialogue with that country, they welcomed these changes, knowing full well that the problems of bosnia and especially serbia can only be solved if democracy is established in serbia. this is the new element we must help spread in the balkans. we must be more efficient in this area, we must restore traffic on the danube. there is no point in giving aid to romania and bulgaria and preventing these two countries from using their main resource. we have to decontaminate the river. to this end, the commissioner responsible for the environment will present in the coming days specific plans to control this serious problem. we have done a lot in the balkans: our new european agency for reconstruction in kosovo, the task force for the balkans, a new regulation to speed up procedures. but we must do more. we must liberalize trade in the region and trade between the region and the european union. we must help to establish infrastructural links that break down centuries of isolation. we must intensify our efforts to build a democratic and pluralist society in these countries, with institutions, public structures, police forces and civil society organisations, but above all we must encourage these countries to cooperate in a unified regional perspective, both politically and economically. if we do not, we will be failing in our duty. the marshall plan was not only effective because of the importance of its resources, but it was even more effective because it forced us europeans to work together to develop a new perspective, to give a new horizon to our politics and our economy. that is what we must do for the balkans. europe must prove - from the balkans to the rest of the world - its capacity to expand the area of security, peace and freedom, its capacity to act on the international stage. it is clear that once again we are returning to enlargement, which must be carried out while extending this area of security, peace and freedom. we have made many promises in this area, but i believe that we will be able to keep our promises, even if the road ahead is very difficult. the enlargement which will accompany us throughout our five-year term and even beyond - i am thinking of the aspirations of the applicant countries - must be carried out in safety and in the objectivity of the criteria, but also by reassuring public opinion in the countries concerned and, even more so, public opinion in our own countries. the enlargement will be marked by friendship, serenity, openness, but also by severity. i repeat: we must reassure public opinion in the applicant countries, but above all in our own countries. our responsibilities counsel. - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the presidency of the council of the european union, i would like to share with you some information concerning the resumption of negotiations in cyprus and the recent developments on this issue. everyone will agree that what happened in helsinki at the end of last year, as well as the new atmosphere prevailing in particular in the framework of relations between the european union and turkey, is a background at community level which influences the framework of relations between the two cypriot communities. i would like to point out that at the beginning of december last year, after a break of several years, negotiations between the communities of the north and south of the island of cyprus resumed in new york. the talks were indirect, mediated by the un special representative, mr álvaro de souto. another round of negotiations took place in january this year, starting on 31 january, and a third round is due to start on 23 may in new york. it is possible that these talks, although this is a possibility which is by no means confirmed, could take place directly and continuously, with work extending until september this year. there are essentially four aspects to this discussion: the security issues, the issues of government structure, the issues of territorial adjustment and the issues of refugees and compensation arising from the situation created after the partition of the island. it was agreed, however, to introduce other issues, for which the representative of the northern part of the island, mr rauf denktash, proposed three new topics: the question of sovereignty, the question of confidence-building measures and the question of lifting the embargo on products from the north of the island. the discussions we have had so far are essentially based on two developments: the possibility of structuring a direct information channel between the european union and the north of the island, without this necessarily implying recognition of this part of the island as a legal entity at international level, in order to facilitate the adoption of a community acquis with a view to eventual accession of the whole island, if the overall problem of the partition of the island were to be solved in the meantime. the second development which seems important to us is the statement by the un secretary-general at the end of the first day of talks that if a comprehensive solution to the situation is to be found, it will involve recognition of the specific features of the north of the island. this is the position taken by the secretary-general of the united nations, and it is a point which will of course be taken into account in our future analysis. the third round of negotiations raises certain expectations, given the scenarios being prepared involving representatives of the united states and the united kingdom, particularly in the areas of security and the constitutional structure, which should be presented in this round through the representative of the un secretary-general. this will take place in the context of the post-election period in the north of the island, which is scheduled for 18 april. the portuguese presidency of the european union has also decided, as previous presidencies have done, to appoint a representative to be responsible for contacts with the various parties concerned by this issue. the representative has already contacted all the parties concerned and is following the work of the various cycles in close liaison with the representative of the un secretary-general. we intend in particular to ensure the presence of the european union on this issue, especially since cyprus is a candidate for accession whose negotiation process is quite advanced, which naturally raises certain expectations and which explains why the european union has a certain importance in this context. the orientation we have taken in this discussion and our participation in it has been essentially to take advantage of a certain climate of easing of tensions. this climate was born of the conviction, which we all seem to share, that it is necessary to continue negotiating and that the continuation of the negotiations and their maintaining pace are also in themselves a building block of hope for the conclusion of a final solution. there is another important point, which i mentioned at the beginning of my statement, and that is the commitment of turkey to help prepare the north of the island for accession. we believe that we must not only read the conclusions of the european council in helsinki carefully and with caution, but also follow up on the turkish authorities' possible willingness to help to find a solution to this question. i went to ankara and had the opportunity to discuss this matter with prime minister bülent ecevit. despite the fact that we are aware of the difficulties and the specific sensitivity, as well as the very idiosyncrasy of the turkish approach to this issue, i believe that there is a window of opportunity that cannot be overlooked. this window requires a combination of factors, one of which is the dynamic of relations between turkey and the european union, and we must not hide this fact. this is a crucial element for the future of this issue. we also believe that it is important - again in the light of the way in which the european union is involved in the matter - to encourage the exchange of information between the commission and the northern cypriots, without this implying any formal recognition, but that must be clear. however, we consider, and i think this is the commission's reading, that the whole process of approximation at the level of the assessment of the acquis at the basis of the overall process of integration of the island into the european union in the context of future accession, presupposes the involvement, as soon as possible, of the communities of the north of the island and also the possibility for the european union, in its effort to assess the conditions of accession, to have access to elements enabling it to consolidate its own accession project. it is also necessary for the council to encourage - and this parliament could also do so, in my view - the involvement of the commission in this effort. i think we must send a message of confidence to the commission as to its role in this. finally, i think we must continue to work actively with the united nations, given the skillful, intelligent and capable way in which the secretary-general and the united nations structure have conducted this discussion and, in particular, their attempt to contribute to the harmonization of positions between the parties. that is also the intention of the presidency. as i said at the beginning, the conclusions of the european summit in helsinki last december clearly had an impact on the evolution of the positions of the various parties to the process. the nicosia government expressed satisfaction with the conclusions of helsinki, which open up the possibility of accession to the european union without first resolving the question of partitioning the island. i cannot help but notice that these same authorities are concerned about the pressure they might be under to resolve the issues raised by this partition, issues which of course suggest some concessions. this concerns the observed evolution of population displacement and the possibility of a rearrangement of the displacement of these same populations in the case of a different solution for the island. the turkish cypriots are also concerned - and this should not be hidden - that turkey's application for membership of the european union will lead to a certain softening of ankara's position on this issue. apart from the fact that these are common fears of the two communities in the context of this rapprochement, i believe that these aspects may lead to a negative interpretation of the situation by the authorities on both sides, but they may also be a reason for hope for a definitive solution. this final solution will obviously require one of the most important elements of present relations in the region, namely the extremely positive development of relations between athens and ankara and the essential role played by both the greek foreign minister, mr george papandreou, and the turkish foreign minister, mr ismail cem. we believe that in this context the conditions are right for things to develop in a favourable way. we, the presidency of the council, will be following this development closely and will be working with the secretary-general and his personal representative. we will inform the community institutions of what we can do and what can be done in terms of articulation, not only on the political level but also on what the commission can achieve in its capacity as manager of the accession process. in particular, we will communicate the flexibility which has been shown by both sides in this matter.
commission. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, today's debate deals with a subject which is essential from two points of view. this is partly the question of funding for cyprus and malta, financial protocol which expired at the end of 1999. we need these instruments to be able to meet our financial commitments under the pre-accession strategy for cyprus and malta. i thank parliament for supporting the commission's efforts to get the draft regulation through as quickly as possible. the committee on foreign affairs and the committee on budgets have tabled a number of amendments. envelope as such, how much do we really want to spend? the commission will propose a budget of €95 million. the council also agreed on this amount. i know that parliament wants more and i can understand the reasons for that. believe me, as a competent member of the commission, i would have liked more money too. but the situation is such that a higher amount would not be consensual at the moment. in the final analysis, the budgetary authority must set the final envelope. the second important point is the question of transferring funds to heading 7 of the budget. it is a purely technical matter; in fact, it's a very political issue. i myself have said here on another occasion that i thought the idea was appropriate. i think i can say that the commission is in principle prepared to follow this idea, although it has not yet taken a formal decision. the decision on this cannot be taken with this regulation, however, and will only be possible in the context of the planned revision of the financial perspective. the regulation provides for technical and financial assistance for the period 2000-04 to the two candidate countries to implement the acquis communautaire, to participate in community programmes and certain community agencies, and to improve the capacity of their administrations and courts. of the total amount of €95 million, €57 million
