the resolution of the political problem. we have also always agreed - and i think this is a really good thing - that the negotiations to solve the political problem should take place under the auspices of the united nations and that the solution must continue to be a bicommunal and bi-zonal federation. the integration of a united cyprus remains the objective of the european union. the european council in helsinki reiterated that a settlement of the political conflict would facilitate cyprus's accession to the european union. however, as the presidency has just explained, the council added that this was not a sine qua non condition for the conclusion of the negotiations. should the cyprus question not yet have been politically resolved at the time of the conclusion of the accession negotiations, the council will decide on the accession of cyprus to the union taking into account all relevant factors. that is the political situation today. the decision of the helsinki european council on the future organisation of relations between the european union and turkey has created a very important momentum. i would like to emphasize that in this case several political processes are taking place simultaneously and are closely interlinked. the eu-turkey relations are mentioned. the council also discussed developments in greek-turkish relations and the peace process in cyprus. we have already spoken of the window of opportunity that opens up after helsinki because of the greek-turkish détente. so what can we do to use this window of opportunity with regard to the cyprus problem? i think we need to take a smart, measured approach. if we approach this matter too decisively, we will create unrealistic expectations. i am, on the contrary, in favour of a smart, tailor-made and gradual approach. the first thing we can and want to do is to strengthen dialogue and communication between the two cypriot communities. this is an idea that our greek and turkish partners support. we therefore want to revive the so-called bi-communal activities, especially those of the young. we also want to inform the turkish cypriot community better about the objectives of the union. i am firmly convinced that a better understanding of the treaty, a better understanding of what the european union is and wants to be, can help to overcome fears and prejudices. i will go to cyprus in the middle of march. my aim will be to help convince both communities of the benefits of a new collaboration. we have again provided funds for this in the new financial regulation. these funds are not insignificant. i think it is very important that we call on both sides to cast out the demons of the past and gradually establish a new form of cooperation and, finally, cohabitation. the un discussions took place in new york in december and in geneva in early february. they will begin the third round in may; maybe it will be decisive ? the negotiations must continue until a solution is found or, at any rate, until sufficient progress has been made on the major issues which the presidency has just raised. what is the commission's role in this respect? it is interesting to note that all those involved in this process consider the role of the european union to be crucial. everyone involved in the process is looking for contact and looking to collaborate with us. all participants are aware that the peace process and the transposition of our common acquis are inseparable and must not be in opposition. i must say that i also highly value the cooperation in this matter with the un secretary-general and his special envoy and i can say that this cooperation is carried out in confidence and without any misgivings. it is therefore legitimate to conclude that the settlement of the cyprus question has taken on a more rapid dynamic since helsinki. i won't go any further at this time. the union's decision to start and continue the accession negotiations without delay, also as a catalyst for the solution of the political problem, seems to me to be the right approach. in any case, i see no other alternative that makes any sense and i can only say that the commission will, until the end of the accession negotiations, continue to influence the solution of the political problem and to use the accession negotiations themselves as an important instrument for resolving the conflict.

counsel. - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have listened carefully to what has been said here and especially to some of the more emotional statements on the cyprus question, particularly in defence of what is now the legality in cyprus, which the european union recognizes by recognizing precisely what the relevant resolutions of the united nations security council are on the subject. reading that led him to decide, in luxembourg at the end of 1997, to begin the process of accession of the republic of cyprus to the european union. i would like you to understand that, apart from the more or less emotional decision-making on these kinds of issues, the day-to-day business of international negotiations normally forces governments - when i say governments i mean all governments - to have a slightly more flexible reading. we need more emotional stances to maintain the scenario in which all these issues are projected on the human level. but we must also bear in mind that it is through the rationality of political positions and the flexibility of negotiation that solutions can be found to overcome the great differences which are ultimately at the root of some of the great tragedies of history. regardless of who is to blame - we are not here to list the culprits, the relevant un resolutions are clear - i believe that we must take advantage of the opportunities offered by the new situation without emotion and with greater rationality. the european council in helsinki had the courage to take certain decisions and i believe that various parts of these decisions are already taking due account of these opportunities insofar as they can, as i said at the beginning of my opening speech, constitute a window of opportunity. it is not by exploiting tensions in this the un secretary-general that we must continue. the european union's position on this matter is unequivocal, ladies and gentlemen, and i do not think it is worthwhile to engage in second readings of possible phrases which might be found in the council's speech or in another position statement. we are not playing political correctness in this parliament, we are playing for what is right on the intentions.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would, however, like to make the clarifications that have been requested. firstly, as regards headings 4 and 7, it is very simple: in berlin, for the large package of agenda 2000, a special heading was created, the famous heading 7, for the candidate countries of central and eastern europe, and only for these countries. malta, cyprus and turkey were not yet planned. our colleague mr schroedter called this a lack of consistency. perhaps you should ask the president of the council at the time, who is not far from you, madam, how we came to this so-called lack of coherence. i was a little bit involved too. i do not think so, but the reason for this decision was that a special instrument was wanted for the central and eastern european countries, which do not have the same conditions as cyprus and malta in the accession process. i said that i understood the arguments put forward here and that the commission would try to take these wishes into account, but as it is agenda 2000 and the financial perspective that is at issue, we cannot act without amending the financial perspective. this has obviously not been possible so far. to be clear, if we move this from heading 4 to heading 7 it will have no impact on the overall balance of the budget. if we do that, then heading 7 would increase in proportion to the decrease in heading 4. it is impossible to add it to heading 7 while leaving heading 4 unchanged. parliament cannot spend money it does not have, unless it has a press in the cellar to print euro banknotes! as regards the cyprus peace process and the link with the accession negotiations, i would like to say again that the accession negotiations have always been directly related to this. the commission and the council have always endeavoured to involve the two cypriot communities in joint projects. as you know, this has not succeeded so far and i am asked if there are any premises. i am convinced that the present context has improved in order to achieve such agreements. i don't have any commitments at the moment. i also don't wait for them until we've started the direct discussions. they'll be here later. the context has changed because the decisions taken at helsinki have made many things possible and, above all, because the participants have completely changed their political strategy. i have always thought that the old position that cyprus would only join once the political conflict was settled was weak in that it did not convincingly stimulate the turkish cypriot community to really get involved, because in the face of this strategy the turkish cypriot community had nothing to do but to sit back and wait. the question of cyprus's membership would not have been raised. the turkish community now has to seriously consider the risk that cyprus will actually join the european union, with the resulting increased prospects of welfare and security for the greek community, while the turkish community, already much less prosperous, will continue to be alienated. i am therefore firmly convinced that the - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, comitology is a concept that most people are completely unaware of and few know what it actually means. it brings to mind secret societies and conspiracies, which was also the case in the past. however, this term refers to nothing more than the definition of the detailed rules for the exercise of the implementing powers conferred on the commission. the detailed rules for these implementing powers consist of a limited number of comitology procedures. until the treaty of amsterdam, there were about 20 variants of these comitological procedures, which did not contribute to the clarity of the application of the legislation or to transparency for citizens. on the contrary, the european parliament itself was not informed for a long time. the first significant step in the fight for greater transparency in this jungle of committees was for the european parliament to be at least informed of everything the commission intended to decide in these various committees. this progress was recorded in 1988 in the plumb/delors exchange of letters. a further step towards transparency was taken with the modus vivendi of 20 september 1994, whereby the european parliament was given not only a right to information but also a certain possibility of intervention. parliament was also given scrutiny. the amsterdam treaty has considerably improved the situation, since it has made it possible, as parliament had long called for, to reduce drastically the number of comitology procedures. the procedures are now three in number, namely the administrative procedure, the regulatory procedure and the consultation procedure. the information and monitoring rights which parliament has enjoyed in the past must now be clearly redefined, in accordance with the treaty of amsterdam, by an interinstitutional agreement. our rapporteur, mrs frassoni, has done a thorough job and has highlighted the issues that need to be clarified in the context of this interinstitutional agreement and the internal administrative procedures in parliament that may need to be changed. the main problem is still the time factor. when parliament is informed, it must, as a rule, take a position within a very short period of four weeks, if it so wishes. as soon as questions involving the health and safety of citizens are raised within the european union, the commission, as the guardian of the treaties and the only institution with the right of initiative, must be able to react very quickly, sometimes within a few days or even hours. however, the european parliament's right to information and, where appropriate, to react must be preserved. in the light of these difficulties, our rapporteur proposes very useful solutions which my group can only support. i have one last request. in paragraph 2 of the german version of the draft resolution, a passage was mistranslated. i would urge clarification on this matter, and also from those responsible for printing afterwards. instead of "must be reintroduced", i thought "must be maintained". this is not so clearly stated in the german text. i would therefore ask that this be checked. i would also like to thank our rapporteur. it is a difficult subject and i hope that the way we have approached it will now allow us to make better use of it.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, although this morning we are not paying much attention to mr di pietro's report, it is one of the most important reports on which the committee on civil liberties and internal affairs has had to deliberate in recent years. it is one of the most important reports because it deals with a very sensitive point in the political future of europe. we are creating a vast area of economic freedom in the context of ever-accelerating economic integration in europe. but it is mainly where a wide area of economic freedom appears that illegal economic activities are also likely to develop freely. we are therefore in a situation where we have an economic area in which unlimited crime is not excluded. however, the fight against this crime, both in terms of cooperation between police authorities and in terms of mutual legal assistance, remains primarily an interstate matter - unlike economic legislation which is now part of community law. the di pietro report particularly emphasizes the fact that the requirements of the fight against crime must be organized in the smallest detail in agreements between states. if you ask people in the judicial or prosecutorial professions how long the current proceedings for the execution of letters rogatory for serious and manifest crimes of a crossborder nature take, you will come to the following conclusion: we can certainly assume that some technical and organisational improvements will be made as a result of the convention under discussion and for which mr di pietro has drawn up a report, but the fact remains that we are only at the beginning of the road leading to a faster, more efficient and freer cooperation of judges within the european union. my group also believes that there is still a long way to go before we achieve what we so badly need, namely a european public prosecutor's office which cooperates with a european police force in clearly defined areas of competence and, compared the environmental consequences of this disaster, at least in terms of damage to the environment, to those of chernobyl. the populations of three countries - romania, hungary and yugoslavia - are affected. the tisza, hungary's second largest river, perhaps the country's most beautiful and cherished river, is the most affected. as with all other disasters, the long-term consequences are the that we must do everything in our power to help to deal with this disaster as quickly as possible. that is certainly the view of my colleague, commissioner wallström, who i know would have liked to government and the international commission for the protection of the danube river to obtain more information on the accident as a matter of urgency. the romanians have asked unef and the bcah in access to the sites is guaranteed for nationals of both countries, which is obviously crucial. it is obviously essential to have a clear picture of the extent of the damage as soon as possible so that has mobilised some €20 million over the past seven years to support the protection of the danube basin. as part of the preaccession aid for the region, it may be possible to redirect some of the aid we are providing through ispa and the phare programme to deal with the most damaging consequences of this accident, as long as the polluter pays principle is fully respected. in the longer term, we power to prevent such terrible accidents from ruining its future.

commission. - i would like to thank mr cox and his group for the way in which some members have shown a strong commitment and a keen interest in the details of the reform which can sometimes be quite tedious but which is always worthwhile, as has been said. the communication of september is unprecedented. this will not just be one of the reviews that the commission has undertaken periodically but a thorough and thorough review of the directorates-general and the commission for which we have established a mechanism for reviewing the requests that are addressed to us and the means at our disposal to respond to them. it may therefore be - that is certainly an objective - but also to 'hold them accountable' - that term is appalling but we all know what it means. by developing our organisation in this way, i am confident that we can achieve or even surpass the success and increased staff motivation that has resulted from similar developments in several administrations in both the public and private sectors over the last decade or so. i think that the end of the centralised system will certainly not lead to a relaxation of the efficiency of financial control but will increase its efficiency and its links with operational tasks. financial control will be fully guaranteed both because of the way we are going to introduce the changes and because we will introduce a completely professional and independent internal audit service. as i said earlier, we are aiming for total security of the money and a good value for money. we also take an interest in valuing the people who work for us. changes in financial management and control will greatly improve the possibilities for achieving all this.

commission - i also thank mrs theato, at the risk of repeating myself, for the considerable attention she has given to these matters and for having helped to bring about, if i may say so, many of the changes that are now taking place. i hope she's proud of the child she shares in the kinship. first of all, i am not sure that i have understood the interpretation correctly, but i do not think it would be possible for someone as expert as mrs theato to speak of abolishing independent financial control. the financial regulation does grant a degree of independence to the present financial controllers. however, due to the mix of the roles of financial management and control, and of audit under current conditions, it is very difficult to think of this as an uncompromising role, however important the integrity of the person who actually has to fill it. so the changes we want to make - as i said, in line with the very strong and very clear recommendations of the committee of independent experts - are not in any way negative. consistency, uniformity and universal standards of good quality in a decentralised financial control system are guaranteed by a range of measures. one is to ensure high quality training, and the other is to ensure that no single directorate-general can take responsibility for financial control unless and until the audit department is absolutely convinced of the soundness of the system. another measure is the establishment of a central financial service, as the honourable members will see from the white paper, to ensure that these standards are put in place and monitored. and then there is the theoretical and practical approach to an effective and independent internal audit service. in a parliamentary reply of this kind, i will not go into all the details, but i am sure that on examination mrs theato will be able to see that the details of the white paper give us strong guarantees. it will also be shown that we have taken account of representation in this house, and especially in the committee on budgetary control, which is significant in the use of ex ante visas in the directorates-general. the ex ante system may be used if it is considered by a directorate-general to be an important and effective means of improving financial control. naturally, there are several requirements within the commission which depend on the number and nature of financial transactions carried out by each directorate-general. the white paper takes this into account too, but when such a system is desired or clearly necessary, it must certainly be possible to use it. the last point is the transition. i share mrs theato's reservations about the so-called "soft law". we have had this discussion before and she knows that i distinguish between different forms of codes which can have a very positive effect and which can eventually be transformed into what we might call 'strict legal norm'. but in this case, there is no room in my view for the 'soft legal rule', and that is why, in the transitional period, there will be full adherence to the current financial regulation until that law is changed by a proper democratic process in this house and in the council. the white paper gives us a full guarantee of this and it contains provisions to do so. in addition, however, and this is very important because this is a transitional period, there will be training, advice, support, guarantees and the new head of audit unit will take full office on 1 may. with all these and a number of other guarantees, i think we can be as confident as possible that the system will be totally safe even during the transition period. i must make two further remarks because this is a key issue at the heart of the reform. my first observation is that citizens feel - for reasons i understand very well - that this transition involves risks of irresponsibility or inertia. irresponsibility because some think there won't be enough control and discipline. i really do not agree with that simply because of the standards for commission officials, the responsibility of directors-general and the safeguards we have built into the system. inertia would only result from anxiety and we do everything we can in terms of support and training to reduce the risk of this happening. finally, the present system - as the committee of independent experts has emphatically stated - is now unsustainable. the court of auditors has declared it fiction. there will have to be change anyway, and change implies a period of transition because it is not possible to invent a system, whatever it is, that can get us from one system to another in a weekend. for the time being, since this is quite possible with all the advice at our disposal and all the design capacity we possess, i am sure that we have put in place, or will put in place, on the basis of our proposals, a system which will guarantee the union, its taxpayers and this house total security.

the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there are still so many of you in this chamber shortly before midnight. in the internal market, companies are not only operating across borders, they also have more and more assets and establishments in several countries. however, the internal market is not only a place for winners; there are also losers. unfortunate but probably unavoidable. the problems resulting from bankruptcy, from insolvency, are far from being solved. for example, what effect does the opening of insolvency proceedings in one member state have on assets in another member state? what about the right of disposition of the defaulting debtor? can he move his assets after the opening of the insolvency proceedings, practice some kind of forum shopping? there is no international legal agreement worthy of the name, nor is there a european solution. a convention was drawn up in 1995 but has not yet entered into force. with this regulation, these problems are solved in a comprehensive, definitive and, above all, directly binding way by means of a european legal standard. in my view, this regulation can be described as a masterstroke and an important step towards a uniform, coherent european law on the conflict of laws in insolvency cases. the competent court and the applicable law are defined by the state in which the debtor is domiciled. the opening of insolvency proceedings, the listing of all assets - including foreign assets and the participation of foreign creditors - the conduct of the proceedings and their conclusion are in principle carried out in accordance with this lex concursus. the opening of the procedure has immediate effects throughout europe, but subsequent decisions also have direct repercussions without any specific recognition being required in the other member states. the regulation is based on the principle of universality and uniformity of procedure. in principle, insolvency proceedings should cover all the assets of the insolvent debtor and involve - and satisfy fairly - all creditors, both domestic and foreign; in short, to have a cross-border impact. however, due to legal differences between member states, for example in the case of guarantees or employment contracts, this principle of universality cannot be strictly respected. this would be an intolerable violation of the rights of third parties. for this reason, compliance with the national law in force is provided for in specific attachments which are provided for certain important legal situations. this applies in particular to real rights, immovable property, registered rights, legal institutions such as the reservation of ownership, the possibilities of compensation, the rights of cancellation of creditors, and also - which is not insignificant - employment contracts. although these particular links are imperative, the regulation also authorizes, where a subsidiary exists in another country, the opening of one or more other insolvency proceedings in respect of that establishment, proceedings conducted as ancillary, secondary - and so-called territorial - proceedings, the effect of which is nevertheless limited to the territory of the country concerned. in my view, and in the opinion of the report and the legal affairs committee, there are some reservations in this respect. the principle of universality, which is ideally integrated into the logic of the internal market and the creation of a uniform european legal area, is violated in a way that is not, as in the case of the particular links mentioned above, practically imperative. in any event, and this is very important, this applies to secondary proceedings which must be initiated after the opening of the main proceedings. the opening of insolvency proceedings in the country of the main establishment already has the effect of bringing about the insolvency in the country of the secondary establishment. that is why my report proposes that, in cases where a main procedure has already been initiated, another, secondary procedure may be authorized only after the consent of the principal. this would place a new and important emphasis on achieving a coherent and uniform european legal development. the committee on economic and social affairs and other opinions also oppose the multiplicity of procedures. they create additional complications and demarcation problems. the proposal is not so much due to the substance of the case as to the constraints involved in seeking a compromise. i think that parliament should put a different emphasis on this and i would therefore ask those who have tabled amendments to reconsider this point. other proposals concern clarifications, for example, on safeguarding the independence of legal persons and other matters. in conclusion, i would like to thank finland and germany for the laudable initiative of submitting the proposal. the regulation sets out a concise, definitive and binding set of rules on insolvency law in a single european legal standard without prejudice to national insolvency law. this is an advance which, in my view, can be exemplary. i therefore call on the council to adopt this regulation as soon as possible and to take account of parliament's proposals.

(laughter) the agenda calls for the recommendation for second reading (a5-0043/2000) by mr bouwman, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a european parliament and council directive on port reception facilities for ship-generated waste and cargo residues (11195/1/1999 - c5-0251/1999 - 1998/0249 (cod)).
(de) mr president, madam vice-president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by saying that we had a good debate on both readings. i should like to thank the rapporteur, mr bouwman, very much for taking up the matter and explaining it so well. we agree with the council on three points. first, each european port must have adequate port reception facilities for ship-generated waste if it does not already have such facilities. so these facilities must exist. secondly, all ships, regardless of flag, must deposit their waste. thirdly, the costs must be borne by the vessel. we agree on these points. we want to achieve together a system which will prevent economic incentives from leading to the dumping of waste at sea. first of all, we want to protect the flora and fauna. secondly, there are many coastlines which are popular with tourists and where jobs must also be created. that means we want to have an effective system. where we differ from the council, apart from minor details - we want to exclude museum ships from bureaucratic requirements and we are a little more strict on large fishing vessels and pleasure boats. the really decisive difference is the way in which the storage costs are charged to the ship. mr bouwman has already presented the situation. two experiments were carried out. the first concerns the baltic sea, and it is not the work of a particular country, but of the whole baltic sea region. it shows that when a large part of the costs of landfilling are covered by general port charges, there is no incentive to discharge waste at sea. as the deposit has already been paid, it is equally important to make it in the port. the other system is the pure polluter pays principle. the ship that discharges the waste must bear additional costs. this second system has proved ineffective, because why is the mediterranean so polluted? why is the north sea so polluted? because the polluter pays principle doesn't work without proper controls! that is why the committee has affirmed to a large majority - not a large majority, the representatives of the minority opinion will speak now - as has the whole of parliament at first reading, without any controversy, that the best system is a system without specific charges. it provides an economic reason for ships not to dump waste at sea but to deposit it in appropriate port reception facilities. that's the deciding question. we are prepared to reach an agreement with the council. but so far the council has refused to engage in any serious conciliation with us. i therefore call on this house to support our proposal to have a significant proportion of the costs, up to 90%, covered by general port charges. we have the opportunity to reach agreement with the council in the conciliation procedure, whether it be on 75% or any other figure. i would also ask the commission to be careful which side it chooses. i think that in the interests of environmental protection and a sustainable and thriving tourism industry in many countries of our community, it is better to have an effective system. so support our system without specific fees. perhaps then we will be able to reach a reasonable compromise with the council in the conciliation procedure.

far as accidents involving heavy goods vehicles are concerned, we are unfortunately seeing an increasing trend in the number of deaths and injuries. the causes are often technical defects. we cannot accept that. in a year, a heavy truck travels about 90,000 miles. compared to a private car, this is an order of magnitude unimaginable. such use requires maximum technical safety in the interests of road safety, environmental protection and, let us not forget, fair competition. the poor state of technical maintenance of a fleet of heavy goods vehicles should certainly not constitute a competitive advantage and, conversely, the carrier who maintains his vehicles in an optimum technical condition should not be penalized. the european population is clearly not in a position to do without control. sanctions should be available in case of doubt. the council then said, perhaps not the correct wording, that the sanctions were directed against the member states. no, the sanctions must be directed against the hauliers, against the owners of heavy goods vehicles and against the drivers. that is why, as has been discussed in committee, i am now tabled an amendment to amendment no 2, which abandons the concept of 'harmonisation'. i am not saying that we should not be concerned about the fact that the council is not in a position to take a decision on the matter. however, and the council must know this, it is obvious that the member states will have to agree within the council at some point on such checks and on the penalties involved. it would be absurd, for example, if offences were punishable by almost a prison sentence in finland but only a small fine in a southern country, or vice versa. it doesn't make any sense. it's not european either. i would therefore like to repeat the point on procedure: amendment no 3 replaces amendment no 2 adopted by the committee. it should therefore be voted on first tomorrow. if you could convey this to the presidency leading the vote tomorrow, i would be very grateful. this would avoid any procedural problems. so first, let's vote on amendment 3. it would then replace amendment no 2. this has been discussed in committee, and we could then very quickly have this regulation without going through a laborious conciliation procedure for a solution which is sound in principle.

- (de) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the charter of fundamental rights is politically very urgent and necessary. as integration progressed, a growing gap in the protection of fundamental rights was revealed. this is because the states have transferred more and more sovereign rights and competences to the union, but the protection of the fundamental rights of people living in the union has remained confined to the national framework. finally, this shortcoming in the protection of fundamental rights must be addressed. the charter of fundamental rights is also a great opportunity for europe. firstly, because after many years, we are finally taking up a project that has long been demanded by many committed citizens, by non-governmental organizations, by various political forces and also by this house. secondly, it is an opportunity because it can give a positive identity impulse to european integration, on the one hand by strengthening democracy and, on the other hand, because by fixing the rights of people living in the union, we can finally make this europe visible and understandable to every individual. i think it's extraordinarily important. we have all seen, on many occasions, how great the incomprehension and rejection of this imaginary and distant brussels was. we are constantly being asked what europe really is. what 's the point ? what can i take away from this on a very personal level? if we want citizens to say that this europe is also their project, the charter of fundamental rights can help to do that. what does this charter have to bring if we are to really take advantage of this opportunity? i would like to make five points. firstly, the standards of this charter of fundamental rights cannot be lower than the fundamental rights existing in our countries or those laid down in the european convention on human rights. at the same time, it must be able to cope with the 21st century, taking account of the most modern developments in our societies. secondly, it must of course concern all the policies of the union, both community law and the second and third pillars, and thus oblige all the bodies and institutions to guarantee fundamental rights in the context of their decisions and the formulation and implementation of their policies. thirdly, and on this point i can only agree with my colleague from the green group/european free alliance, the charter of fundamental rights must set out the rights of all people living in the union and not create first-class and second-class rights for first-class and second-class citizens. fourthly, i agree with the report's demand that the charter of fundamental rights be legally binding and an integral part of the eu treaty. in this respect, i believe that the council should reconsider and revise its position. if the charter were not a part of the treaty and therefore not invoked by every individual, people would rightly express disappointment and incomprehension and say that nothing else would have happened in brussels but the drafting of one more document. fifthly, it is particularly important for our group that fundamental social rights should not be ignored or taken lightly. i would like to support very strongly what mrs van den burg said on this point. the right to work, the right to housing, the right to health, the right to form trade unions and the right to strike are inalienable. we are concerned about this, especially after we have seen that almost all the proposals to this effect have been rejected in committee. we will be resolutely committed to the consolidation of social rights. we also hope that, in the vote in plenary tomorrow, this parliament will send a clear political signal on this matter. in conclusion, i would like to add this: we cannot hold an extraordinary summit in lisbon and declare that full employment should be our political objective and at the same time refuse to include fundamental social rights in the charter. i think that, politically, this contradiction is not tenable.

the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, you said that this is already the second reading of the directive on the award of the eco-label. the european eco-label is a spin-off of the internal market. it is designed to mark products and services which have a high degree of ecological friendliness, in order to respond in a way to the ever-increasing cross-border trade in goods. on the one hand, it has the function of ensuring that consumers are informed across borders. on the other hand, it is a question of developing awareness in industry and among citizens, of recognising and creating ecological relationships. this is of great importance for everyday purchases. i believe that the merits of a european label adapted to the internal market require very little discussion. however, the distance between a good idea and its proper implementation is often a long one. this is also the case with the eco-label. unfortunately, the label is particularly attractive today because it is almost unknown in most countries. i think only a small minority have ever heard of it. therefore, the totally inadequate preparation of the label has received the utmost attention in my report. what are the weaknesses in the ecolabel regulation that have led to the unsatisfactory situation we are in today? i think one of the main problems is the cost structure. the verification procedures that companies have to undergo to obtain the label are lengthy and costly. we therefore demand that the establishment of the verification criteria be accompanied by a rigorous minimisation of prices. this should not, of course, be interpreted as a qualitative weakening of the verification criteria. in addition to the costs of the verification procedures, the fees to be paid to the european eco-label scheme are also important. on this point, we also foresee cost reductions for smes, companies in developing countries and companies concerned by other areas of european and international environmental protection legislation. examples of this are emas and iso 14001. in addition to a reduction in costs for certain companies, the report provides for a maximum fee. in doing so, we follow the example of almost all national schemes, which also provide for such coverage. this approach aims to make the labelling system attractive to large producers of consumer goods and service providers. this is not a gift to the big multinationals, as has been criticised in part - i want to be absolutely clear on this point - but an important step towards the label finally gaining influence. we must also realise that the european label will not gain ground without some initial funding. i think we should take responsibility for this contribution. another important point in the report is the regulation governing the relationship between the national eco-label and the european label. at first reading we had still called for the national labels to be phased out in favour of the eco-label. our change of opinion is not without foundation. in some countries, national labels are well established and are recognised in society. this is the case, for example, in scandinavia with the nordic swan and in germany with the blue whale. in my view, it would be foolish and contrary to the spirit of subsidiarity to want to abandon a national label which has proved its worth in favour of a european label which has not yet been established. our approach has to be different. we must ensure that the coexistence of national and european labels is coordinated. in this respect, the work plan provided for in the common position - which we have completed in a few areas to which i think you will also give your assent - is of great importance. the ecolabel regulation provides a bridge between economic and ecological interests. some of us want to impose strict environmental criteria on it, while others are more concerned with the marketing aspect of the label. the two groups are, however, united in one: they want the eco-label to succeed. i believe that the regulation as voted today will have been a good compromise between the interests of all the parties concerned. i am convinced that the constructive proposals of our assembly will also be heard by the council and will ensure a greater success of the european eco-label.

president of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, human rights are individual rights which have been enshrined in national constitutions and international law conventions as rights or norms which are superior to those of the states and are inalienable. they include individual and political freedoms as well as basic social and economic rights. the idea of human rights is one of the grandest ideas ever advanced by mankind and was born in the last century as a result of the experiences of the concentration camps and the gulag. it addresses what makes man a human being and makes him aware of his dignity, his uniqueness, his freedom and his equality with all other men. the spread of this idea of man shows the power of its radiation; attention to the human being and human dignity are at the heart of all human rights policy. fifty years after the universal declaration of human rights, ambition and reality still diverge widely. while more people have never lived in democratic systems and awareness of human rights has grown, their implementation and respect in the world as a whole remains largely inadequate. respect for human rights is particularly important, not only for moral reasons but also for political reasons. political prisoners, the violation of the most basic rights of women, child soldiers, too many poor people living below the minimum required, economic exclusion, environmental destruction leading to the suppression of the livelihood of many people, massacres of civilians in armed conflicts are just some examples. it's a vicious cycle. in the end, economic success cannot be achieved without respect for human rights and the guarantees of a constitutional rule of law. where human rights are not respected, there is the threat not only of discontent but also of economic and social decline. and when the development spiral is downward, so are human rights. the maintenance of human rights is essential for conflict prevention and peacebuilding. those who trample on human rights are laying the foundations for the conflicts of tomorrow. governments that are subject to democratic accountability are generally better at looking after the welfare of their people. in this respect, the promotion of democracy is the supreme requirement, as are the principles of tolerance and pluralism which are linked to it, but a pluralism which is not devoid of values but which is, on the contrary, oriented towards human rights. in this matter it is immaterial whether people are oppressed in the name of a race or a class. there is no political motivation for the oppression of human beings, whether it comes from right-wing or left-wing extremism. in the context of globalisation, there is no longer a domestic affair. the general recognition of the globalisation of human rights must therefore be strengthened. human rights are indivisible. the universality of human rights shows that in political and social matters, their realization has become the benchmark of progress and of civil society and culture. as a global player, the european union must, through a strengthened human rights policy, take human rights into greater account both internally and externally. it must assert itself as a community of values. it must act in a preventive manner in the field of foreign and security policy and in the field of development policy and react by means of sanctions, for example by suspending aid. to this extent, a global human rights policy is increasingly a central mission of foreign policy. but a more responsible human rights policy must begin within the union. the democrats who turn to human rights, who want to support and implement fundamental rights in their constitutions, must show in the political struggle that they are prepared to oppose extremes of left and right so that there can be no violation of human rights for any reason whatsoever, and in this regard i think we must make it clear to all parties that for us human rights cannot be used to justify any particular political system: it is a matter of individual human rights, human dignity, and it is therefore unacceptable, whatever the political motivations, to violate human rights in any way or at any stage of development. so this means that the democrats must come together and reach a fundamental consensus against all forms of extremism, not only from the right but also from the left. mr president, i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. we were able to visit some of the flooded areas, including the village of chaquelan where more than 28,000 people had already found refuge. we have seen firsthand the consequences of the floods that have ravaged the region, and also the immediate impact of some of our aid. from the beginning of the crisis, the commission has endeavoured to assess the consequences of the bad weather in mozambique in a global perspective. our focus has been on the following areas of intervention: emergency relief, resettlement, reconstruction, macroeconomic stability and long-term development. as regards rescue, search and recovery operations, the problem is that the commission does not have the instruments designed for such operations, unlike the member states which have the logistical capacity to carry out such operations. as regards emergency first aid and resettlement, the commission has approved two echo decisions for a total of eur 2.7 million for mozambique and we are preparing a third decision for eur 5.5 million. these decisions cover food aid, drinking water supplies and sanitation equipment, essential first aid items, as well as small-scale reconstruction of basic health care infrastructure and measures against the threatening cholera epidemic. in addition, eur 1,4 million under the budget line for food security was made directly available to the mozambican government and the commission delegation. the commission is planning to finance the supply of seeds and tools to farmers to encourage them to resume sowing once the floodwaters have receded. in addition to the action it is already financing in botswana, the commission is currently carrying out an assessment of humanitarian needs in zimbabwe, zambia and madagascar. as regards the reconstruction phase, i announced during my visit that a first additional tranche of eur 21 million would be released from the development budget, of which eur 5 to 10 million would come from the budget line for cofinancing ngos and the balance from the reallocation of edf appropriations. the commission stresses the need to strengthen coordination with the government on participation in the overall reconstruction plan. a group of representatives of the main donors meet weekly in maputo with government representatives at ministerial level. the eu presidency and the commission delegation participate in this group. the commission intends to take part in the preparation of the international donor conference which is likely to take place at the end of april. the allocation of its financial assistance for reconstruction will be in close coordination with eu member states and other donors. finally, on macroeconomic stability and long-term development, the commission is working with the government and the world bank on proposals to contribute to economic stability in mozambique. additional resources of up to eur 15 million could be made available for this purpose. in order to maintain the pace of growth in recent years in mozambique, the levels of cooperation achieved before the disaster will be maintained and even strengthened, which is expected to generate an estimated €150 million in expenditure for this year, compared to €100 million last year. in the context of the community, we are expected to contribute up to eur 1 billion to the debt relief of the acp countries, including mozambique as a retroactive case. it will therefore be eligible for debt relief under the enhanced hipc initiative this year. as regards coordination with other donors and international aid agencies, the government of mozambique, together with the united nations office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs, provides the main platform for the coordination of rescue and relief operations, as indicated in their joint appeals. the external donors must not question this local control over the coordination process, at least as long as it is functioning reasonably well, as confirmed by the information from the un organizations present in maputo. obstacles have arisen in the response to this terrible disaster. in view of the scale and suddenness of the floods in mozambique, the commission, the member states and other donors wondered whether the aid could not have been delivered more quickly, as some speakers also pointed out during the debate. i now begin to see better how we could overcome such obstacles to bring the community's humanitarian aid even more rapidly and effectively than it is today. it should not be forgotten, however, that this was a real disaster, with many surprises, and that it was not easy for the member states to mobilize and deploy such delicate and inconvenient equipment as helicopters, for example, very quickly. it's not an easy task. in conclusion, i would like to draw your attention to the figure for international aid. the total amount of aid released for this disaster now stands at some €109 million, of which more than €91 million comes from the commission and the eu member states. it was said during the debate that europe's reaction is, relatively speaking, a sign of its real willingness to do something. our contribution, in financial terms, is far from negligible. however, it is not the only way, and we will continue to look for other, more effective and faster ways of responding to such situations. and excellent motion for a resolution. i am glad that parliament can support the proposed integrated and inter-pillar approach, which - i quote - 'may' produce positive results. i understand that parliament takes a cautious approach to these action plans and the commission would like to follow suit. on the one hand, the commission is pleased to note that, in general terms, the council's approach to the development of these action plans is in line with that advocated by the commission in its 1994 communication on immigration, which received broad support in this parliament. on the other hand, it is important to be aware that these action plans are only on paper at the moment. the implementation of these plans will require, as several members of this house have pointed out, a very different combination of policies: political cooperation, human rights, the rule of law and democracy, trade, social and development policies and economic aid will have to be coordinated with measures to better manage the flow of migration from these countries and regions. clearly, this is not an easy task. let me emphasize and endorse a number of the important points in your draft resolution. partnership with the third countries concerned will always be a key element in the success of such a policy to promote co-development. i would therefore support your view that we should enter into a political dialogue on the implementation of the action plan on the basis of an agreed basis of mutual benefit, both for the member states of the european union and for third countries. we that non-governmental organizations will play in the implementation of these action plans. we are fully aware that the immigration problems will not be solved next month. we must bear in mind these very serious limitations when the european council receives the first evaluation of these action plans in december this year. i fully share your observation that the european union should adopt a long-term structural policy to tackle the causes of immigration and therefore i agree that the timelines set out in the action plans are rather optimistic. however, the action plans can be seen as a first step in the creation of an external eu policy on immigration and therefore they must be given a chance. i also agree with you that hosting in the region does not exempt member states from their obligations towards asylum seekers under the geneva convention. it is extremely important, when implementing these action plans, to maintain a balance between the various measures, so that efforts are not focused exclusively on short-term defence actions. the commission stresses that it will play an active role in maintaining this balance. implementation will require close cooperation between the council and its competent bodies, the commission and the member states, in accordance with their respective responsibilities as defined in the treaty. the important role which the member states must play was recognised at the justice and home affairs council on monday 27 march. the presidency invited the member states to translate their political commitments into real activities, an invitation which the commission supported. of course, the commission is prepared to play the active role that is expected of it, particularly in areas such as development aid and economic aid, human rights, good governance and institution building. the commission currently lacks the financial means to play a similar role in other measures. i therefore welcome your proposal to allocate additional appropriations to cover cooperation with third countries in the fields of justice and home affairs, with particular reference to immigration. these budget lines should, above all, not only provide humanitarian aid, including the improvement of basic living conditions, as we are already doing through the echo programme, but also propose initiatives aimed at economic development, improving respect for human rights, improving the independence of the judiciary, and equal opportunities for men and women in third countries. they should also provide assistance to those countries to establish legal and practical mechanisms to deal with asylum seekers and refugees. mr president, i would like to conclude by saying that you consider that the action plans pay too little attention to internal affairs. however, i understand that the primary purpose of these action plans is to contribute to the development of an external policy of the union on immigration. i would like to assure you, however, that the commission will take up its own responsibilities in developing a common internal policy of the european union on immigration and asylum, as envisaged in the tampere conclusions. the performance chart adopted by the justice and home affairs council on monday and sent to parliament earlier already contains a detailed analysis of our intentions. in the autumn of this year we will have a further opportunity to debate the priorities of a comprehensive immigration policy when the commission presents to the council and parliament a revision of the 1994 communication to take account of new dynamics, new social, political and economic realities of the world in which we live, in immigration policy.

the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, child sex tourism is not a national or european problem but a global one which has only become more relevant and widespread in recent years. this motion for a and its member states must use all available means to protect the most vulnerable members of our society, namely children. the motion for a resolution therefore contains two crucial requirements. must still be possible to prosecute the perpetrators in their country of origin. secondly, the principle of extraterritoriality must be taken into account. we need harmonized national legislation at european level to criminalise child sex tourism, regardless of where it is carried out. europe must assume its responsibilities towards its citizens, including those beyond european borders. these requirements can be summed up very briefly: the right of children to be protected is not diminished because their country of origin denies them the necessary protection. nor can we turn a blind eye to what is happening within the european union. we all know about child abuse in our own countries. the council and the commission have indeed confirmed the principle of extraterritoriality, but the texts do allow for the imposition of double penalty in exceptional cases. this means that in exceptional cases it may still be possible for child abusing 'sex tourists' to go unpunished if the country where the abuse is committed does not criminalize such abuse. the european parliament clearly rejects this exceptional regulation. member states must vigorously combat anything that promotes or minimizes the seriousness of child sex tourism. in order to provide a fundamental guarantee for the protection of children, respect for the rights of the child must be enshrined in the european council adopted on 17 january 1995 a resolution on the legal interception of telecommunications. the resolution, published in the official journal, lists the specifications of member states authorising them to carry out lawful interception of telecommunications with regard to network operators and service providers. this list enables each member state to adapt its national legislation in order to identify and overcome the difficulties encountered in introducing technical specifications for interception in modern telecommunications systems. in november 1995, the 15 member states and norway established a code of conduct incorporating the list of specifications provided for in the resolution. in this connection i should like to say that the governments of the united states of after four years of negotiations, the draft convention on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters is about to be concluded. at its meeting on 27 march the justice and home affairs council examined the most important outstanding issues, including those relating to the interception of telecommunications. i am very pleased to announce that at this meeting we have reached full political agreement on the arrangements for interception. it is therefore to be hoped that the act establishing the convention will be adopted at the justice and home affairs council in may. measures to ensure data protection under the europol convention were also envisaged. in this respect, it should be noted that europol does not have investigative powers or develop operational activities. in fact, europol is responsible for analysing data provided by member states or third parties and cannot collect such data directly. in order to give the european parliament a more complete picture of the matter, let me give you some further clarifications. it is the responsibility of each member state to send the data to europol. consequently, any controls concerning data protection are carried out in the member state of origin, in accordance with the council of europe convention of january 1981 and the recommendation adopted by the committee of ministers of the council of europe in september 1987. the general rules on the protection of data transmitted to europol by the member states are thus respected. it is in this context that the convention states that the question of whether data have been properly collected in the member states must be answered at the level of each of them. it is therefore the responsibility of each member state to correct, delete or amend data transmitted to europol where it is found that such data are incorrect or infringe the rules laid down in this regard. it should be stressed that europol itself is not in a position to determine whether the data transmitted by a member state has been appropriately collected. each national supervisory authority has a key role to play in this respect. a few words on the data protection rules in the schengen information system. this system provides for an authority responsible for the protection of personal data. this common supervisory authority is composed of the supervisory authorities of the various member states and ensures that the principles of the system on data protection are respected, in particular as regards their content and use. the interests of citizens are thus fully protected in accordance with the instruments ratified by the member states. finally, a final word on data protection under the third pillar. the member states and the commission intend to examine the question of the extent to which data protection should be provided for in a horizontal perspective for the whole of the third pillar. in this debate, certain aspects will be given serious consideration. we will therefore consider whether it would not be appropriate to create a common supervisory authority for all the instruments relating to the third pillar, or whether it would not be appropriate to create a common secretariat for these authorities. the portuguese presidency also intends to submit to the council, in due course, initial reflections on the desirability of developing general principles governing data protection, which would be applicable to all the instruments of the third pillar. these ideas are still in the embryonic stage and are only the subject of initial study. in any event, i would like to say that the portuguese presidency, in full respect of the community's operating mechanisms, will inform the european parliament in due course of the further development of this work. that, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, is the council's position on the work that is being done or has already been done in the field of legal interception of telecommunications. in conclusion, i would like to say that i fully understand the political concerns behind this initiative by the european parliament. the presidency wishes to stress that it is prepared to follow closely the progress of the european parliament's work in this area, because it considers that it is entirely justified not to compromise when the principles of freedom, democracy, respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms of citizens are at stake.
the commission has taken note of the recent debate with concern. we received a letter yesterday from mrs fontaine to mr prodi asking the commission to focus its statement on certain issues. i'll try to treat most of these. the european union is founded on respect for human rights and the rule of law. the european convention for the protection of human rights recognises the right to privacy as one of these rights. all the member states of the european union are signatories to the convention. the specific competences conferred on the community are defined by the treaty. the commission can only act within the limits of the powers conferred on it by the treaty. it is clear that the community has competence in the field of data protection and in research and technological development. under the so-called third pillar, the union has competence in law enforcement and the fight against crime. national security matters are the exclusive responsibility of the member states. the lisbon summit last week set ambitious targets to make europe the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world. harnessing the full potential of information technology and the internet is the key to achieving these objectives. electronic communications are playing an increasingly important role in the daily lives of european citizens. having an infrastructure for electronic communications to function smoothly has become crucial for our economies. building trust in electronic communications among citizens and businesses is a prerequisite for achieving the lisbon objectives. one of the key tools for this purpose is encryption, which ensures the confidentiality of electronic communications. encryption means transforming data into a form that is unreadable to anyone without the decryption key. when the european parliament considered the problem of telecommunications interception in 1998, it stressed in its resolution the importance of encryption. european research efforts and a relative opening of markets have created conditions which have enabled european companies to develop world-class expertise and high-quality encryption products. it is interesting to note that the us government has recently taken steps to ease its controls on exports of encryption products. at present, intra-community trade is regulated by what is known as dual-use regulation. in terms of foreign trade, the wassenaar arrangement imposes controls on exports of powerful encryption products. the purpose of export control is to try to prevent the unwanted spread of these products to certain countries and to criminal organizations. the commission recognises the need to balance the availability of encryption products with public security and crime prevention concerns. the lisbon european council called on the council and parliament to adopt the dual-use export control regime as soon as possible - before the end of the year. the commission hopes that the revision of the dual-use regulation can be completed during the portuguese presidency. in addition, the share of the fifth framework programme budget allocated to research on technologies for enhancing security and confidence has been increased. the commission considers that strengthening the security of internet communications through encryption is a priority. the introduction of such products is complex. software whose source code is not open leaves the user in uncertainty. the possibility that a means of circumvention is integrated into the encryption cannot be excluded. on the other hand, the effective use of encryption requires a secure decryption management system. as regards its own communications infrastructure, the commission is currently considering the adoption of more powerful european encryption products for its electronic communications. i now turn to the question of data protection. the directive of 24 october 1995 on data protection states that member states must protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons, and in particular the right to privacy, when processing personal data. in addition, member states are required to establish a supervisory authority to monitor the application of the provisions of this directive. the data protection directive is supplemented by the directive on data protection and privacy in the telecommunications sector. this directive also concerns legal persons and requires providers of public telecommunications services to guarantee the security and confidentiality of communications. these two directives exclude from their scope activities which are not within the community's competence. article 1 of the data protection directive in the telecommunications sector states that 'this directive shall not apply to activities which are not covered by community law, such as those referred to in titles v and vi of the treaty on european union, and in any event to activities concerning public security, defence, state security (including the economic prosperity of the state in the case of activities related to state security) or state activities covered by criminal law'. as you know, titles v and vi of the maastricht treaty concern the common foreign and security policy and justice and home affairs. the provisions of the directive reflect those of article 8 of the convention for the protection of human rights. in adopting these directives, the council and parliament have tried to strike a balance between the right to privacy and the legitimate needs of law enforcement and public security. but at the same time, activities outside the community's competence were to be excluded from this regulation. the commission was not fully satisfied with the transposition of the data protection directives. as regards the general data protection directive, the commission has initiated infringement proceedings against six member states. as regards the directive on data protection in the telecommunications sector, the commission has also initiated infringement proceedings against six member states. as regards the activities under the third pillar, which the president of the council discussed with mr prodi today, a number of actions in the field of law enforcement and the fight against crime are under way; these actions include the issue of lawful interception of telecommunications for the purpose of criminal investigation. as has been said, the activities of the intelligence services of the member states in the spying on transmissions fall outside the scope of community law. the commission was asked whether it could confirm the existence of the activities described in mr campbell's report. because of the nature of espionage, those who are not involved cannot confirm or deny its existence. however, it is clear that the technical possibilities for intercepting electronic communications exist. and it is impossible to say that the available technologies are not being used. following the recent allegations made in the public debate, the commission requested clarifications from the member state mentioned in this context. we have received a letter from the permanent representative of the united kingdom to the european union stating that the british secret services work within a legal framework set by the uk parliament and which explicitly states the purposes for which interception may be authorised, namely national security, safeguarding the nation's economic prosperity and the prevention and detection of serious crime. the letter also stressed that the human rights committee considered that the system provided for in the british legislation was in conformity with the european convention for the protection of human rights. the uk legislation also provides for a special parliamentary monitoring committee. the commission also requested clarifications from the us government. we received a letter yesterday from the us state department stating that the us secret service does not engage in industrial espionage activities. the letter also states that the u.s. government and intelligence agencies do not accept assignments on behalf of private companies and do not collect proprietary, commercial, technical or financial information on behalf of private companies. madam president, i repeat that the commission attaches the utmost importance to respect for human rights and the rule of law. in the event of infringement of community law, the commission shall not fail to fulfil its obligations under the treaty.

commission - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have come here today to make a statement on european patent no ep 69 53 51 issued by the european patent office to the university of edinburgh on 8 december 1999. the granting of this patent has raised some concern in parliament and in organisations such as greenpeace about the true scope of this patent. i would like to say on behalf of the commission that the commission shares these concerns. it seems clear to all concerned that this patent should not have been granted as it stands. the european patent office has issued a press release to this effect. i know that some of you today feel that the european patent office has at best not told the whole truth or at worst has seriously misled the public. the joint motion before you today contains such reproaches. i would remind you that the european patent office is not a community body; it was set up and operates under an international agreement to which all the member states of the european union and four other countries have acceded, but not the community itself. therefore, i am not in a position to give you official information on the actions of the european patent office in this particular case. however, as i am familiar with the european patent office, which i recently visited in munich, i would be personally very surprised if this unfortunate circumstance had its origin in anything other than an error in the patent granting procedure. regardless of the cause of the problem, it is clear, as i have just mentioned, that this patent should not have been granted in its present form. the question is therefore what the commission intends to do about it. that's what i'm here to answer today. the motion calls on parliament and the other institutions of the european union to formally oppose the patent within nine months, during which time it is possible to file an opposition in accordance with the rules governing the grant of european patents. opposition to this patent has already been registered. however, if the european patent office follows its usual rules on opposition, it is likely that a patent amendment will not occur before december 2000 and may even have to wait longer than that. such a delay in correcting what is admitted to be a mistake is clearly unacceptable. i have therefore written to the european patent office in munich to ask that all possibilities for a speedier solution to this problem be examined. i am pleased to inform you that the european patent office has agreed, in view of the particular nature of this case, to appoint immediately an opposition board, which, as soon as it is set up, will prepare a first communication giving a preliminary opinion. however, the european patent office stated that such a preliminary opinion would be expressed without prejudice to the final settlement of this dispute. but the office assures me that the proceedings will reach conclusions quickly, with due regard for the rights of the parties to be heard. mr president, i am sure that the members of this house will appreciate, as i do, the willingness of the european patent office to respond to some of the concerns expressed by this parliament, which is a direct result of the approach taken by the commission. i am pleased, mr president, to hand you copies of my letter to the european patent office and of the latter's reply to the commission. naturally, i will inform you as soon as possible of the conclusions which the commission's legal service will reach after having carefully studied the reply of the european patent office to the letter i recently sent to it. in conclusion, therefore, let me repeat that the commission, like everyone else, regrets that this patent has been granted in its present form. we have started an action - in full cooperation with the european patent office - which i believe will lead to a rapid resolution of this unfortunate incident.
