and this was a key point - the principle of equal treatment of the public and private sectors has now been accepted. as regards interest rates, the council proposed 6% and the parliament 8%. in the conciliation procedure, the figure of 7% was agreed. all in all, this is a reasonable solution and, i repeat, it is a solution which helps above all small and mediumsized enterprises in the union. i myself was surprised to read that late payment is one of the main causes of insolvency in europe. some 450 000 jobs are lost each year in the eu. we often give a lot more money for a lot fewer jobs. in this case, we get the desired effect, so to speak, for free - i think parliament should let the outside know that it has done a lot to secure jobs. in conclusion, let me make one more remark about the commission. late payment is also a breach of contract when the commission is responsible for it! it is true that this is not part of this directive, but experience has shown me that small and mediumsized enterprises, as well as large enterprises, often complain to us during our visits that the commission is fulfilling its own payment obligations, which it has contracted to promote research or in other fields, much too late. i hope that the commission will be guided by the spirit of this directive to make its own payments on time, because in this case too - i repeat - it is a breach of contract. i would like to thank once again all those who have taken part in this work and we hope that parliament will approve this compromise when it is voted on tomorrow.

- (de) mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, if economic and social cohesion is rightly considered to be the heart of european policy, we can safely say that the structural funds are the catalyst. today we are talking about the functioning of a political instrument which we have in the meantime replaced with a new and - we believe - better programme, with agenda 2000. parliament can and must, however, still evaluate the structural funds by means of annual or activity reports and draw the necessary political conclusions from them, even if these seem to be outdated by the course of events. in his report on the commission's 10th annual report on the structural funds for 1998, mr turco does both of these things very well. the report has been substantially enriched by the many amendments. i shall not repeat here the verifiable criticisms. mr turco and other colleagues have also mentioned them. i would like to reiterate one requirement, however, namely that the commission should present in its next activity report a separate chapter on the measures it has taken in response to the criticisms expressed by parliament in previous years. the 11th annual report should therefore also contain a progress report. because of the short time available, i shall only focus on four problems and approaches which we believe will be of use in the future. firstly, the year 1998 covered by the report was characterised by the fact that the total allocation of funds for the programming period was made possible only by last-minute measures. experience shows that we need specific strategies for the initial and final phases of programming periods, as well as a flexibility mechanism for crisis situations such as those encountered in 1997-98. secondly, the principle of additionality is one of the pillars of our structural policy. i won't question it. but between desire and reality, there is a margin. for example, it is often the case that, for objective 1 regions, there is only a limited scope for a structural policy of its own, to which the european structural policy is then added. this is often because all the financial means politically available must already be used for co-financing, which is right. for the principle of additionality, this means - to give an image - that i get a european suit to wear on top of a regional tie that i can afford myself. this problem will become even more acute with the forthcoming enlargement. i think we need to redefine additionality. this could be in the direction of european added value, as is already the case with the research framework programmes and the interreg community initiative. thirdly, we believe that the principle of partnership with local and regional sectoral associations and with the social partners is a step in the right direction and must be strengthened. we need not only more local initiatives and pacts, but also regional debate on the region's priorities. our structural policy will thus contribute to regionalisation. it reacts and creates regional structures. fourthly, controls and evaluations are the essence of a structural policy whose noble objective is to become superfluous as soon as possible. even if the regions differ greatly from one another in terms of structure, we must continue to look for common methods and indicators of evaluation. only then will we be able to make a horizontal comparison between member states of the strategies and projects carried out in certain sectors of activity. the previous speaker raised the problem. in this policy area too, benchmarking must be made possible as soon as possible.

commission - ladies and gentlemen, i should like to express my great interest in mr turco's report and congratulate him on the precision and competence of his work. i would also like to say to him that, beyond the observations, criticisms and proposals, this reading is extremely useful for the future as i am the new commissioner for regional policy, who has been in office for a few months. i would like to devote my speech to answering each of you as precisely as possible on the most important points and, first of all, on the implementation of the funds in 1998. your rapporteur, mr turco, expressed some satisfaction with the overall implementation of the funds in 1998, where 100% of the available appropriations for the year were committed and 100% paid. beyond this observation - which is the fruit of the work of my predecessor, mrs wulf-mathies, and of my colleagues who were also her colleagues, and i think it was right to mention it - beyond this observation, i can also tell you and confirm that at the end of 1999, which is also the last year of the 1994-1999 programming period, 99% of the appropriations had been committed and 75% paid: results that are still insufficient, of course, but which nevertheless mark progress in the direction you want. it is true, however, that the situation of the community initiatives is somewhat different and this is due to the particular characteristics of their implementation. there is the innovative aspect of most programmes, a new approach based on partnership and the difficulty of implementing transnational programmes, both by national and regional authorities. nevertheless, ladies and gentlemen, a very clear improvement was noted in 1998, confirmed in 1999, particularly as a result of the exercise of reallocation of resources between the various initiatives, as requested by the european parliament. at the end of 1999, 95% of the appropriations for the period had been committed under the community initiatives and 57% paid. as regards implementation, mr esclopé, since you have mentioned the disparity in implementation between the various member states, i think it is not wrong to say that part of the explanation you are looking for is that programmes and projects differ from country to country or region to region. we know that the countries and regions that are proposing projects are very different, i repeat. and so, i want to explain some of the observation you make by the differences between these programs and these projects. finally, if we compare the implementation of the commitments with the financial perspective agreed at edinburgh, i see a near-match with you. however, ladies and gentlemen, i have heard the criticisms or the comments that we can do better. mrs schroedter or mr markov have noted differences which are still unbearable. i would point out, however, that it is possible to demonstrate the effectiveness of the structural funds, since disparities between the member states have been reduced. however, you are right and i am myself concerned by this observation, the differences between the regions - mrs sudre has mentioned the extremely clear and eloquent figures - prove that there is still not enough efficiency or concentration in the allocation of these structural funds. there are still unjustified, intolerable differences between regions, between the group of the poorest regions and the group of the richest regions. i would also like to say that i am extremely attentive to the fact that this social divide, as it has been called, this economic divide between the group of the richest regions and the group of the poorest regions, is not yet aggravated by a new divide linked to the new economy - i have in mind, moreover, some extremely worrying figures on this subject - which i could call the digital divide, that is to say the democratic access of the most remote, the poorest and the most disadvantaged citizens to the new technologies and the opportunities offered by these new technologies. the second point is monitoring, evaluation and control. in your resolution, mr turco, you acknowledge the importance of monitoring, evaluating and controlling the interventions of the funds. on the subject of monitoring and evaluation, there has been, quite frankly, significant progress, and i would like to mention three of them. first, the development of a harmonized methodology. secondly, the interim evaluations were completed during 1998 and resulted in some very substantial financial adjustments to the programmes. thirdly, and finally, the carrying out of thematic and horizontal evaluations, particularly on the themes of small and mediumsized enterprises, equal opportunities and partnership. these evaluations are gradually bearing fruit, particularly, as i see it, in the case of the new programmes for the period 2000-06. there is still progress to be made in this area, but it is clear that the culture of evaluation now seems to me to be more present in all the commission departments and also in all the programme managers. i was able to see this at the beginning of june last year when i organized for the first time a seminar bringing together the member states and the managers of the programmes, the managing authorities of all the regions and countries. i had invited the chairman of your committee, mr hatzidakis, and mrs theato, chairman of the committee on budgetary control, to participate in this seminar. it showed, i say frankly, that the culture of evaluation, which is a modern and necessary culture, is progressing. as regards control, the commission broadly shares your assessment of the complexity of the current structural funds system. however, improvements have been made since 1997, particularly in the context of the sem 2000 initiative, and i thank mr bradbourn for mentioning them. the rules for the eligibility of expenditure for cofinancing are now laid down in an implementing regulation for the new period. the standards to be met by the member states in the field of financial control will also be the subject of a regulation. the guidelines for the application of net financial corrections are also being translated into an implementing regulation for this new period. i would also like to remind you that the regulations for the new period - which mr musotto has just said are inadequate, i have noted this - provide for a simplification of the monitoring systems for assistance. the new rules also make the member state directly responsible for the controls carried out on programmes carried out on its territory. the commission, as you know, ladies and gentlemen, is responsible for ensuring that the control systems are sufficiently robust and reliable. all of this is naturally complex. i have even heard calls recently for less brussels bureaucracy, less complications. i'm going to think, lucidly and objectively, of all the ways that i can make things less complicated. i shall do so in particular as part of our joint reflection on what the new regional policy 2006-2013 will be. in the meantime, i am bound by a general rule, which you know well from berlin and which i must apply. i must therefore find, with my services, the best possible synthesis and balance between, on the one hand, the wish expressed by some of you earlier, for greater decentralization, for greater confidence in the member states and the regions, and, on the other hand, your demand for rigor, which the court of auditors also asks me to do, in order to be able to answer to the taxpaying citizens. what i can say about this, and in particular to mrs hedkvist petersen, who spoke to me about it the other day when i was in her area, is that i will look for the best synthesis. but try to understand me: i am caught between your concern for more decentralization and the need to give fair accounts to the european parliament, to public opinion and to the court of auditors. your rapporteur rightly points out that the number of on-the-spot checks carried out by the commission in 1998 was not sufficient. in fact, mr turco, despite the importance which the commission attaches to the sound financial management of programmes and to reliable control, i must say that the resources at my disposal have not enabled us to carry out as many control tasks as we would have liked. finally, i would point out that negotiations are under way on a framework agreement between our two institutions, which is partly in line with mr bradbourn's request. the framework agreement is now finally completed with regard to the transmission of documents to parliament and it is on this basis that the commission will forward to your parliament all the documents it wishes. many of you, mrs attwool, mr maccormick, have raised the question of additionality. i would like to point out that the new rules seem to me to improve considerably the possibilities for checking for objective 2, which, as you know, posed major statistical problems in the previous period. the commission had also proposed a link between the verification of this additionality and the allocation powers to subnational bodies, as you write: autonomous communities, regions and länder. i am obliged to respect the general regulation on the structural funds, at least as it stands until 2006. partnership is a principle which the commission wants to make as comprehensive as possible. progress was already made in 1998, in particular with the introduction in 1997 of the territorial employment pacts, which involve the regional and local partners, as well as the social partners. but the commission goes much further with the new 2000-2006 regulation. the partnership is now being extended to new actors who were not really involved or very rarely involved until now, and i want them to be involved now. the economic and social partners, associations, certain non-governmental organisations, particularly in the field of the environment and equal opportunities. the new rules also extend the partnership to all stages of programming, from the drawing up of plans by the member states to the evaluation of programmes. fourthly, complementarity with other community policies. mrs flesch, mr turco, mrs schroedter and mr mastorakis, you have all stressed this point. i would point out that announce to you, actions in favour of equal opportunities and equality between women and men in the report for 1999. there has been a great deal of effort recently to improve the coherence of the structural funds with other community policies and, in particular, mrs flesch, with state aid. this is an area in which the commission adopted a communication in 1998 bringing the map of regional state aid closer to the maps of regions eligible for the structural funds, and i have had a very constructive and very regular dialogue with my colleague, mario monti, on this subject. the same is true for the environment, in the context of the new programmes 2000-2006. let us be clear here too: it is not a question of making the structural funds, ladies and gentlemen, the instruments of other policies. the structural funds are a policy of cohesion, of reducing disparities between regions and countries. the objective of the funds is to support the development of the weakest regions in order to strengthen economic and social cohesion in the union, and you stressed the insufficient progress in this area. the question is therefore not only to ensure - and this is not negligible - that structural assistance takes sufficient account of the community's sectoral policies, but also, in turn, to ensure that the union's other sectoral policies welcome or promote this dimension of cohesion. i am thinking in particular - to reply to mr sanchez garcía and mr theonas - of the outermost regions. you know, ladies and gentlemen, that i will continue to take personal care in the commission of the future and the development of the outermost regions. you have seen this when the commission's report on these regions was published: i have paid particular attention to them. i also say this in response to mrs sudre's comments on this subject. what i say about the outermost regions and the need for good cohesion and consistency between the various policies also applies to the most disadvantaged regions, whether they are urban areas, which are increasing in number, or whether they are island or maritime regions, to answer mr ripoll who asked me about this. in conclusion, i the commission is aware of the seriousness of the situation in latin america and the need to ensure that the community's policies are consistent with the principles of the united nations charter. overall, we have seen, in the last 15 to 20 years, an impressive process of democratization that has borne fruit in latin america. every time these advances are called into question, it is therefore necessary to say clearly: 'so far, but no further'. paraguay, which was one of the last latin american countries to undertake this democratization, is also the country that seems to be threatened. that is why we must show our solidarity with the democratic forces in this country, not just in words but in deeds. the european union has been active in paraguay for some years. our efforts to make a real difference are concentrated on two main areas. they are about developing and strengthening democratic institutions. i would like to send a very clear message to the paraguayan government that these efforts should not be seen as a task for europeans, americans or anyone else. we can help to develop these institutions, but only those who are in power in paraguay can show that they want them, that they want to fill them and that they want to use them. the programme to support the paraguayan parliament has already been carried out in three phases. there is a supplementary project entitled 'modernisation of institutions'. since we could be criticised for not using these means within the prescribed framework, i should like to make it clear that we have seen fit to put in place very strict control mechanisms for paraguay and other countries. the means made available therefore do not in any way pass through dubious channels - nor do they lead to them - because their supervision is ensured by an independent co-directorate under the direct control of the commission. the most important programme in terms of resources and perhaps also in terms of objectives to be achieved is a programme which deals with the social and regional causes of democratic instability in paraguay and thus with the living conditions of the population, especially in rural areas. a series of important programmes with considerable financial resources have been launched in this field. all of them aim to improve the daily lives of people living in rural areas - 46% of the population - and to integrate them more fully into the country's political and social structures. i would also like to point out that there is also a special programme to support the indigenous population of the chaco region. all things considered, the activities of the european union in paraguay are therefore of a scale that is uncommonly large for the size of the country. however, it must be acknowledged that there is no permanent union representation on the ground. i can inform you at this stage that the commission is currently considering a reorganization of its foreign representations, a new priority, and that this point is also being considered in the context of this reflection. however, no decision has yet been taken to change the situation in paraguay in this respect. let me conclude by saying that for us the defence of democracy and the rule of law throughout the world, and therefore also in latin america and paraguay, is the central objective of our international work. i hope that the debate on paraguay which is taking place today in the strasbourg parliament will not only be seen as a sign of european solidarity but also as a sign of european responsibility!

in writing. - (de) in 1993, the federal republic of germany abolished the right to political asylum guaranteed by the basic law. its borders have been closed to the immigration of asylum seekers. the federal republic of germany now grants asylum only on rare occasions. refugees are excluded socially and legally or forced into illegality. the schmitt report aims to extend this unworthy system to the whole of the european union. it is precisely this system that should be used to develop 'common standards for asylum procedures'. the problems of this asylum legislation are not, however, addressed in the schmitt report. there is not a word about the inhumane procedures of repressing. the social discrimination suffered by refugees - in germany, through the asylum seekers act - is also not highlighted. the report by mr schmitt ignores the fact that refugees are discriminated against in the labour market. in germany they are subject to a categorical ban on work. the rapporteur does not even mention the daily violations of the privacy of asylum seekers and data protection. eurodac and the schengen information system have made refugees the most well-recorded group of people. they're the first glass men. mr schmitt's report offers no outline solution to all these problems. the rapporteur regrets, instead, the so-called 'illegitimate use' of the right of asylum in europe. the amendment to the right of asylum means that some refugees are no longer legally entitled to apply for asylum - the desire to live in a place other than one's place of birth was, is and will remain the most legitimate. the most urgent task of this parliament is to develop such a policy and to create the conditions for its optimal implementation. instead, the report's comments contribute to the discrediting and criminalisation of asylum seekers. the schmitt report calls for 'burden sharing' within the union in the reception of asylum seekers. now the refugees are being insulted as a "burden". it is not on such an assumption that a humane asylum policy can be drawn up, one which takes account of the interests of refugees. the schmitt report also welcomes the 're-admission agreements'. these are the instruments of a policy of closure which has nothing to do with a policy of human asylum. readmission agreements have the effect that people seeking protection can be returned to their country of origin. they therefore facilitate the refusal of asylum by eu states. the report by mr schmitt also approves the regulations on 'third countries' and 'safe countries of origin'. it is because of these regulations that people prosecuted for political reasons cannot get asylum in germany - namely whenever they transit through a 'safe third country' or come from a so-called 'safe country of origin'. since these instruments prevent a fair and equitable asylum procedure, they should be rejected and abolished as soon as possible. the european parliament must make proposals on how the interests of refugees and asylum seekers can be taken into account within the union. we must insist that the policy of isolation, the dismantling of the right of asylum and the questioning of the geneva convention on the status of refugees be brought to an end. all people seeking asylum in the eu must have access to a fair and equitable admission procedure. mr schmitt's report unfortunately goes in the opposite direction. it is a question of the isolation of europe from the outside world and of further limiting the duration of protection for refugees and asylum seekers. i reject the construction of a fortress europe and therefore also the resolution on 'common standards for asylum procedures'.

the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think we have here a really excellent example of cooperation between the european commission and the european parliament. i should like to begin by giving a brief history of this proposal for a directive. there has been a proposal for a directive on combating money laundering since 1991 in europe. national legislation in this field is largely based on this directive. this must be relatively new information for many national citizens, because it is always assumed that this is legislation emanating from the national legislator. it has certainly contributed to this, but the origins of the fight against money laundering go back to this directive of 1991. following a series of reports, some of which were from the commission, the european parliament held a hearing on this subject in december 1995. the hearing revealed a clear lack of cooperation between the member states, which is explained by the existence of standards which differ widely from one country to another. some countries, such as the united kingdom and germany, have gone far beyond the requirements of the directive. others, such as luxembourg, have transposed the minimum. these differences caused big problems. at that time, the european parliament had already asked the commission to draw up a new proposal for a directive to replace the first one. we're there today. we thank the commission for this and i think this is a good example of how the commission can react and take over an initiative from the european parliament. on the other hand, i have to make some criticisms. i think the commission's proposal goes a little beyond its purpose. it has, in effect, transferred the rules applicable to banks and financial institutions to other professional sectors, which it incorporates into the second directive on money laundering, which are obliged to combat this scourge. but the rules applied to banking cannot be so easily applied to professions such as lawyers, tax advisers and accountants. lawyers, for example, are subject to professional secrecy and immunity from liaison with their clients. our problem was therefore to make the necessary changes at first reading. i think we've made it. we have been able to maintain the principles of the rule of law which preserve confidentiality when it comes to representing clients in court or in a legal case. only when lawyers are engaged in the same activities as banks, namely asset management and financial management, are they subject to the same rules as those applied to estate administrators. i see. and i think the amendments take that into account. i think we have put more emphasis on the practical application of the identification requirements laid down in the proposal for a directive. it makes no sense for a real estate agent to have a client's identity papers when he enters into a business relationship with him. that would make this kind of business impossible. the amendments tabled in this connection also have the merit of being more practical and closer to the citizen. we regret that the commission has not defined the concept of organised crime in the list of offences. our amendments fill this gap. as regards fraudulent operations which could harm the interests of the european union, we have strictly limited them to really serious offences and we have eliminated minor offences, contrary to what would have been the case with the commission's proposal. i would like to thank the finnish and portuguese presidencies from the bottom of my heart for the quality of their cooperation and i am sure that the forthcoming talks with the french presidency will be just as fruitful. with this directive we have tried for the first time to apply the new procedure laid down in the treaty of amsterdam, which makes it possible to apply codecision at first reading. unfortunately, this attempt failed, but not because of parliament. this failure was due to the fact that the various delegations to the council working party had no clear-cut mission. the council was therefore unable to present final texts suitable for negotiation. the commission has therefore decided to deliberate on the first reading before the summer, to follow the normal procedure for the first and second readings and then to await the council's common position. but this should not prevent us from continuing to cooperate with the council on this issue, because the tampere summit rightly placed the fight against money laundering among the top priorities. to this end, we must all strive to improve the fight against money laundering in europe as quickly as possible. i think our debate tonight is contributing to that. i think and hope that we will make rapid progress and that the european union will soon have a second directive on the fight against money laundering and that the member states will in turn speedily transpose it into their national legislation.
the commission has already submitted a proposal for a regulation to the council. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission is proposing a substantial amendment to the directive on the prevention of money laundering. since the directive was adopted in 1991, the situation has changed. firstly, we have gained some experience of the application of this directive, and secondly, we must take account of the amendments to the treaties. it is becoming increasingly clear that money is the main objective and driving force behind organised crime. it is therefore necessary to take measures to address its benefits. even the community's finances are falling victim to organized crime, as the commission's reports on the fight against fraud acknowledge. this is a burden on the budget of the european communities. the member states protect their finances by applying their national legislation, but the communities have no police or judicial bodies to take action against fraudsters, recover lost money and impose penalties. for this reason the community budget must be protected by directives, regulations and other measures. article 280 of the ec treaty clearly states that 'the community and the member states shall combat fraud and any other illegal activity affecting the financial interests of the community by measures taken in accordance with this article which are dissuasive and afford effective protection in the member states'. the commission proposal is closely linked to article 280 of the treaty. even the crime that harms the communities' finances is most often organized. the rapporteur is right on this point. but there are exceptions, and not all of them are international organized crime. on this point, the committee on budgetary control is rather on the side of the commission's proposal. but, aware of the difficulties of differentiation, our committee is prepared to follow the rapporteur and accept only a simple reference to article 280 of the treaty. the committee on budgetary control also believes that the primary objective of the directive on combating money laundering is prevention and deterrence, with the collection of evidence coming second. the conclusions of the european council of october 1999 recommend. i thank the rapporteur, mr lehne, for the spirit of cooperation in which we have been able to work.
- (de) mr president, public opinion often associates organized crime with spectacular murders, such as the murder of judge falcone, or with drug trafficking. actually, it's something else. organized crime is a set of recurrent, systematic offences that use professional structures. the systematic theft of cars, credit cards, and so forth are among them. this type of crime has two consequences: firstly, it causes considerable damage, because it is not limited to a single act, but accumulates a set of isolated crimes. second, the amount of money it produces is so great that an individual is unable to spend it discreetly. i always say in meetings that there is absolutely no way for organized crime to move these huge sums of money without being detected. that is why they try to disguise the money they have earned illegally as honest money. this is called money laundering. dirty money is turned into honest money. anyone who hinders or at least seriously complicates these activities is giving organized crime a boost, hindering its development and undermining its expansion. our colleague mr lehne pointed out that we have had a directive on this for a long time, which has made it possible to harmonize standards in the european union. however, this new proposal is essential because it allows the latest developments to be taken into account. we think it is a good thing that the scope of the directive is not only extended to banks, but also to other sectors or professions which can be used indirectly for money laundering, and that this is a satisfactory solution to the problems of the professions. we also find it positive that crime is not limited to drug trafficking but includes all forms of organised crime. we have attached particular importance to the inclusion fact that we can do that will lead the united states to rigorously enforce the system. paragraph 7 of the draft resolution states that a number of changes will have to be made before parliament can consider the safe harbour system to be adequate protection. apart from the question of whether parliament's present powers allow it to issue these conditions, i would first of all like to stress that none of these points are new to the commission. on the contrary, these are improvements which we have always advocated in our negotiations with the united states. but the government of this country logically refused them. this is not in itself a reason to abandon them. but the question is whether these changes are a prerequisite for the system to be considered appropriate. the commission, like all the member states, considers that none of these amendments, although all of them are desirable, are indispensable. and let me ask the members of this house to remember that the question here is whether the safety zone provides adequate protection and not whether it meets all the requirements of the directive. the first amendment that should be made is the recognition of the right of any individual to lodge a complaint with an independent public body in the event of a breach of the principles of the security sphere. this is also a point which mrs paciotti raised with some insistence. but the system of the security sphere already allows for independent settlements of conflicts, which are often the work of private conflict resolution bodies. we should, for a multitude of reasons, be in favour of, not against, this alternative dispute settlement, which is generally more "convivial" than judicial procedures. the security sphere also reserves a protective role for public bodies. it has not only a self-regulatory function but also a self-regulatory function supported by legislation. and the two protective authorities recognized in the decision are the federal trade commission and the u.s. department of transportation. of course, an individual in the united states may have his reasons for going to court. but alternative dispute resolution should not be an obstacle to bringing a case before a court. increasing the number of requirements would be dangerous, because we would then be moving towards a system equal to the directive, whereas we can only demand adequate protection. the officials responsible for data protection in the european union themselves have said in an opinion, which you quote in detail in your draft resolution, that the self-regulatory system in principle provides adequate protection. the second amendment aims to oblige the participating undertakings to make good any damage suffered by the persons concerned in the event of a breach of the principles. compensation will be required from participating companies in many cases, for example in the context of obligations under us law. the safety sphere does not offer as complete a guarantee as the directive, but again we are not entitled to demand the same requirements as those contained in the directive. and i don't think the difference is that big. we must not overstate this point. even in the european union, the number of cases resulting in compensation is low. the third amendment proposed by parliament is the right to have data obtained or processed unlawfully deleted. in the area of security, data erasure is a sanction that all dispute resolution authorities should be able to use, but it is for the latter to decide in what circumstances the sanction should be applied. the us argues that data deletion is not considered a requirement in the oecd guidelines. although the latter can be interpreted in several ways, the united states cannot be completely ignored. the data protection officials working party does not consider that data erasure is essential for adequate data protection. the commission therefore does not consider it necessary to implement these amendments in order to be able to qualify the level of protection of security spheres as adequate. to make these changes the conditions for the assessment of the safety sphere system's relevance would be to sign the death warrant for it and thus deprive ourselves of the improvements we want. i want to make this clear. the united states no longer wishes to discuss this matter, and the commission also considers that the debate on this subject is closed. the security sphere is necessary both for the persons concerned, who transfer the data, and for the economic actors. businesses on both sides of the atlantic have understood this. the safe area will simplify data transmissions and ensure greater legal certainty. but it will also offer much better protection to those concerned. as mrs palacio has just pointed out, most of the data currently sent to the united states is not protected in any way. the security sphere will not solve all the problems at once, but it will raise the level of security standards in the united states to a much greater extent than any other solution, and by simplifying the transmission of data, it will make fraud much less attractive. i would like to conclude by calling again on parliament to adopt a clear resolution which would put the security sphere system on track. parliament would thus be in good company. the working party of civil servants responsible for data processing issued an opinion on 16 may, which you have no doubt already seen. all these officials would have liked to see further improvements in the safety area system, but in the present context they did not reject the idea of a commission decision, as it would allow the system to be tested in practice. however, they stressed the need for monitoring and vigilance, which is essential if the decision is to be implemented. when asked for their views at the end of may, the member states, as noted earlier this evening, unanimously supported the draft decision. some of them expressed the same concerns as those expressed in the parliament's draft resolution tonight, but all agreed that it was time to give the system a chance. by supporting the commission's draft decision, parliament would not be isolated. by expressing its concern about this and urging the commission to be vigilant, parliament would be adding to the officials responsible for data protection, but by erecting obstacles it would not improve the security sphere: it would only prolong the current situation, which would harm the people concerned and the companies. the security sphere is not perfect, but the alternatives are not better. i'm going to stop here. if you will allow me, i would like to thank once again the rapporteur, mrs paciotti, the committees which have dealt with this matter most closely, and their chairmen, mrs palacio and mr watson. the work they have done has been constructive. i look forward to the vote in parliament.

- the next item is the report (a5-0179/00) by mr lehne, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a council regulation (ec) laying down the list of third countries whose nationals must be in possession of visas when crossing the external borders and the list of third countries whose nationals are exempt from that requirement (com (2000) 27 - c5-0166/2000 - 2000/0030 (cns)).
the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this regulation also has a history, a history which extends over the whole of the previous legislature. you will remember that after the entry into force of the maastricht treaty, the question of introducing a single european visa regime was raised for the first time. in other words, all eu member states were in principle required to apply the same visa requirements to third country nationals coming to the eu. at that time the commission had already put forward a very good proposal, which had also received the support of the european parliament. unfortunately, the council had fundamentally changed the very principles of this proposal and declared, so to speak, as almost indicative, everything concerning the list of third countries whose nationals are exempt from the visa requirement, saying that anyone could bypass it and impose this requirement on other states or exempt them from it by simple notification. at the time, the european parliament argued that it had not been properly heard and, moreover, that the result was contrary to the aim of the maastricht treaty. he had brought an action before the court of justice of the european communities. he won the case. the council regulation was declared null and void. the commission then presented a new version of the proposal to the european parliament which was very similar to the first. the king welcomed her. a further change was made to its legal basis - it was no longer maastricht but amsterdam - which was to lead to a new proposal. it is on this last proposal that we are debating today. the european parliament still maintains that the list referred to in this regulation must be definitive. this means that there can no longer be any exceptions, so no more black, green, blue, yellow, grey lists, but, please, one and only one list, binding, one point is all. this is a decisive element, because it will finally allow the european union to have a single visa regime. in addition, the commission has dealt with an important point which parliament had already considered as such at the time. this is the question of the visa requirement for the associated states which are currently well into the accession process, namely bulgaria and romania. parliament has always been of the opinion that these states should be exempted from the visa requirement. he came to this conclusion by noting the considerable progress these countries have made on internal security and other issues. the commission has now agreed to this opinion and is now proposing to add bulgaria and romania to the list of visa-exempt countries. we consider this to be progress. clearly, these countries have succeeded in convincing the commission. it is now hoped that, after listening to the european parliament, the council will show the same determination and that progress will be noticeable. i would ask the council to consider this directive as soon as possible. let me also thank the plenary assembly and, unusually, the conference of presidents, who have deviated from the original agenda by agreeing to add this item to it. the decision of the conference of presidents may make it possible to put an end to this directive quickly and to send a relevant signal. during the preparatory phase, the council has communicated to me a series of amendments which it would like to see adopted. for example, it proposes to introduce reciprocity. what's that? it is very simple: citizens of individual member states are partially subject to a visa requirement with certain third countries. therefore, the member states concerned should be able to require that the citizens of those third countries be subject to a visa requirement. i refused. not because i do not understand the demands of these member states, but because i believe that this is a further breach of principle and that we are thus again in conflict with the provisions of the treaty which provide for a single list of countries subject to the visa requirement and a single list of those exempt from it. that is why i do not think we can go down that road. europe has gone so far - i will cite the schengen acquis, the elimination of controls at a large number of frontiers as an example - that it is simply not possible to do otherwise. we need a single visa regulation and i think the commission has put forward a good proposal. parliament has deliberated in the same spirit, i hope. the council is now in the driver's seat. it must reach as constructive a result as possible as soon as the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, on 6 july we will be voting in plenary on the discharge to be given to the commission for the implementation of the auditors' report, such as, for example, the obligation to endeavour to obtain a positive declaration of assurance. in 1998, the court of auditors refused, for the fifth time in a row, to ensure that the commission had made a conscientious and careful management of financial resources. it also required that measures be taken to close and sanction the three major cases of fraud, namely fléchard, commission - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are debating today for the second time the discharge to be given to the committee for the 1998 financial year. on 13 april parliament decided by a majority to postpone the discharge and to request further reports and more detailed information from the commission. the commission has obviously responded to parliament's wishes and sent the following on 11 may: the report of the financial controller on the corrections made in the context of ex ante control, a report on the consequences of the inquiry committee on the customs system, a report and an overview of the contracts concluded with the scientific visitors, a report on the number and outcome of the disciplinary procedures relating to financial irregularities and implemented since 1998. the commission has indicated that it has taken specific measures, in particular with the assistance of olaf, and that it has drawn up specific binding action plans and implemented the first measures, as is also the case, for example, for the management of the european development fund. in fact, the court of auditors had granted the commission a statement of assurance - albeit limited - for the management. the committee on budgetary control and, in particular, its rapporteur, mrs rühle, were not satisfied with this and wanted and asked for additional measures to improve the result. i can say without any reservation that the action plan - which was not only drawn up at the invitation of parliament but also, really, in collaboration with parliament - is capable of increasing the transparency and effectiveness of external aid. i particularly welcome the cooperation of those who have just dealt with this subject and confirm that the commission will keep its promise and inform parliament every six months on the implementation of the action plan. in its report on the implementation of the 1998 budget, the court of auditors had given a statement of assurance to the commission on the revenue side of the budget and on commitment appropriations, but not on the management of payments made from the budget. the number of errors in the implementation of the budget is too high. the commission and i, as the commissioner responsible for the budget, fully share the position of the court of auditors and parliament. the commission has therefore already taken or decided on a number of measures to improve budget implementation and to reduce or avoid errors. this requires prevention first. such error prevention is the result of the measure - to give just one example - which aims to reduce the number of tendering and award procedures applicable to external aid - whether phare, meda or other programmes - from the existing 80 or so procedures to around 40. reducing errors also requires better control. this is the aim of much of the commission's administrative reform. in future, the various administrations which actually spend the money allocated to european policies will have more staff to monitor and will also be able to examine better the control systems in place in the member states. the reduction of errors also requires effective penalties, financial compensation and, where there is a deliberate breach of staff's status, appropriate disciplinary procedures. i would like to point out once again that my colleague mr kinnock will be submitting a draft reform of the disciplinary procedure before the summer break. this report criticises the current financial control as the ex ante control has not rejected any payment request. however, this is not an indicator of whether financial control is working or not. i would like to point out once again that the court of auditors has also stated that the errors it has found cannot be detected ex ante and the commission concludes that we must considerably strengthen the area of ex post control, also by setting up an independent and autonomous audit service. improving financial management, reducing errors, reducing delays, for example, and improving the efficiency of the use of reduced resources are not the only priorities of the commission; there is also the fight against fraud. it's about the future; it's also about the past. i repeat: the commission has nothing to hide and that is why i also address the questions that have been raised in the fléchard case. the decisions taken by the commission in 1994, that is six years ago, have been reviewed by the court of auditors. the commission has made sure that the report and the commission's reply, which also covers the chronology of events, do not remain secret, confidential, but are officially available, and that reply is also now available on the internet. in the debate between the court of auditors and the commission, however, there is a controversy as to whether the commission had the right, or even the duty, to apply the principle of proportionality when adopting financial penalties. the commission considers that it has that right. while the court of auditors maintains that only the courts can apply the principle of proportionality, we believe that it is a general administrative principle. this was also the view of the commission at the time and, as regards the fléchard case, i would like to echo the words of the commissioner responsible for budget and financial control, mr schmidhuber. he wrote that, in the opinion of the financial controller, this did not preclude the search for a negotiated solution, taking into account the principle of proportionality. the positions are therefore in agreement and, at the same time, the commission stated that, as far as it was concerned, it would have been desirable to examine more closely at the time why the exported butter had not reached its destination in russia but had been sold in poland. as regards the question of reimbursement, i would like to recall the following: this was dependent on proceedings before the irish high court, and a legal compromise was reached which has become a legal matter of fact, which is of course a measure which is also binding on the present commission. in the current fight against fraud and in the resolution of cases from previous years, the commission must safeguard the principles and rules of the rule of law. this also applies to information issues. where olaf is requested at a given moment in an investigation at national level to transmit information because of the secrecy of the investigation, this constitutes a binding legal basis for olaf. this applies to the director of olaf as well as to the commission. in this connection, i would point out that olaf is independent in the field of investigations and that this was emphasized by your assembly in the context of the development of the legal basis for this. this means that olaf is also independent in the reports it produces and that the question of whether olaf information can be published depends on the full responsibility of the director of olaf in this area. as regards the question of whether other contracts have been awarded to fléchard, i have informed the committee responsible that, as far as it is concerned, the commission can say that other contracts have been awarded through the tendering procedure. as to whether export contracts have been concluded or export activities have taken place at national level, i would point out that in the agricultural sector as a whole, payment to the various beneficiaries is made only at national level. this is because the paying agencies are responsible for the payments. the commission may then, in accordance with a regulation, request access to the data and investigate which payments have been made and who are the beneficiaries. i should point out, however, that regulation 2390/1999 provides that the commission guarantees the confidentiality and security of electronic data transmitted by the member states. if that is the decision of the committee responsible, the commission is quite prepared to ask the member states for an appropriate reply, to ask for permission to transmit the data. i would point out that these principles on the relaying of information are also contained in the agreement between parliament and the commission on the relaying of information. this agreement should provide a good basis for this important area of relations between parliament and the commission and, in so doing, provide a good basis for the discharge procedure. i would like to thank the members of the committee on budgetary control for their intensive cooperation not only on the report but also on the results, the evaluations, the comments and, above all, the many proposals for improvement. with the establishment of an independent audit service and the consistent implementation of the audit recommendation, the commission will implement the concrete measures of the action plan presented and the profound internal reform measures. it will consistently implement the reform of the disciplinary procedure, the personal and operational management of olaf, and the anti-fraud strategy by drawing up comprehensive legislation and in close and strengthened cooperation with the member states and other states concerned, with the avowed aim of restoring public confidence in the proper management of european funds, in collaboration with - above all - the european parliament and the other european institutions.

president described as a 'beautiful and necessary' project, and towards strengthening its institutions before enlargement. while welcoming the new presidency, i would like to comment on some of the points raised in your speech. first of all, i would like to express my unconditional support for the commitment to advance the european social agenda. in february, when i presented the commission's strategic objectives for the period 2000-05, i announced that one of the main objectives would be to redefine europe's economic and social priorities. less than five months later, i find the progress already made in implementing the economic aspects of this priority particularly encouraging. the social aspects of europe's development are the other side of the same coin; this is where we will be focusing our efforts in the next six months. in particular, the presidency will have to deal with a whole series of important issues on which the commission has already put forward its proposals. the commission has just adopted a social policy agenda, which sets out the issues to be dealt with over the next two or three years. this is so that the conclusions of the lisbon and feira european councils can be translated into concrete actions. in my view, this document strikes the right balance between the political guidelines defined in lisbon and feira on the one hand and the duties and powers conferred on us by the treaty on the other. it should therefore be able to bring together the consensus of all at the nice council. it is essential that the union does not create inequalities in our society, especially as economic conditions are favourable to reducing them. the commission therefore welcomes the emphasis the presidency is placing on these problems. the anti-racism directive was recently adopted in record time - just six months. for the time being, we expect the presidency to deal in the same way with the other aspects of this very important package of anti-discrimination measures. in fact, any programme to combat discrimination must first guarantee equal opportunities for men and women. we must also do everything we can to put an end to the abominable form of slavery which is the trafficking of women and children for sexual exploitation. one form of inequality still present in european society concerns access to education. an action plan was adopted in lisbon and is now being put into practice. for my part, i am convinced that the presidency will take strong action to ensure that all our young people acquire the skills needed to integrate into a knowledge-based economy. we also have a responsibility to advance knowledge by encouraging the mobility of students, teachers and researchers, both qualitatively and quantitatively, as was finally proposed at feira. i am glad that this topic has returned to the agenda, because it is a topic of fundamental importance, the ultimate consequences of which have not yet been sufficiently examined in depth. another source of inequality is the poverty trap that has trapped too many european citizens. in lisbon, the european council reaffirmed the commitment of the member states to work towards eradicating poverty. in addition, a high-level group on social protection is working with the commission on this ambitious strategy. it is truly scandalous that such situations of extreme poverty still exist in our societies. at the nice council we should reach a consensus on the attitude to be taken towards social exclusion, and in this respect the commission has already put forward proposals. the feira european council also strongly supported the commission's proposals on food safety. it also welcomed the commitment of the member states to move towards the establishment of an independent food safety authority as soon as the european parliament had delivered its opinion. i think that this opinion will be delivered at the latest during the first part-session in october. once our proposal is presented, i hope that the plans for the creation of this authority will go ahead under the french presidency. this is our specific commitment to the citizens, who are not prepared to tolerate any hesitation in the matter of food security. in this respect, we must also adopt a common approach in order to maintain our internal market. the problems we have recently faced have taught us a lesson and i think that each of us is now prepared to take on our responsibilities. european public opinion is extremely concerned about environmental problems. for my part, i stand with the french presidency and i support what has been said, namely that we should make the protection and improvement of the environment one of our main priorities. important decisions will have to be taken in this area at the sixth session of the united nations world conference on climate change in the hague in november. at this meeting - one of the most important after kyoto - the union must confirm its leadership role: we must uphold the commitments of kyoto and keep up the pressure on our partners to do the same. the impact of our transport and energy policies on the environment, and in particular on climate change, will be the main topic of two documents that the commission intends to present to the council and parliament next autumn. the first will be a green paper on the common transport policy and the second a strategy paper on the various sources of energy and on the security of energy supply. these are the concerns of european citizens, who expect us to intervene effectively, especially in the present situation. citizens are particularly concerned about the disasters caused by oil pollution on their coasts. as you said, mr president, if we are to prevent such disasters from happening again, the council and the european parliament must quickly adopt a set of measures on maritime safety, as we have already proposed. another major concern for citizens is the use of genetically modified organisms and biotechnologies. we must ensure adequate protection of human health and the environment and, at the same time, enable society to benefit from the advances of modern biotechnology. the new framework legislation on the deliberate release of genetically modified organisms should therefore be adopted as a matter of urgency. this set of provisions strengthens and improves the existing one, and a balanced response is essential to restore public and market confidence. so here's an ambitious agenda for the next semester. for my part, it seems to me that the various lines of action can all be summed up in a strong desire for a better quality of life. across europe, at all levels of society, citizens are demanding better social quality, better ethical quality and better environmental quality; and we need to listen to that request. that is why i would like to stress the need to establish constructive relations with our new neighbours. one of the main challenges facing the european union is the need to stabilise our continent and the promotion of stability in border regions must clearly be at the heart of this strategy. we therefore fully agree with the proposal to organise a political summit between the european union and the most democratically advanced balkan countries. the commission has already started laying the foundations for this summit on the balkans; we hope to work closely with the french presidency on more specific preparations. i recently had the opportunity to reflect on the increasingly important interaction between the european institutions. since the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, our legislative system has become more efficient under the new codecision procedure. this procedure applies to a wider range of legislative acts; however, the opportunities for recourse to conciliation have decreased. according to a recent survey, more than half of the legislative proposals tabled last year were adopted at second reading and in almost one fifth of the cases, only one reading was sufficient. this means that the legislative process is maturing and increasingly based on consensus. i think this is encouraging, especially since the commission has recommended to the intergovernmental conference an extension of the codecision procedure and qualified majority voting. in this way, the democratic legitimacy of the european legislative process will be strengthened, which is essential for the political health of the union. mr president, i welcome your commitment to the successful conclusion of the negotiations of the intergovernmental conference, namely the necessary reform of our institutions. this commitment sends a strong and positive signal to our partners in the negotiations with the candidate countries. in biarritz and nice, europe will need all your skills and a great sense of responsibility on the part of everyone. we all know that it is essential to strengthen our institutions and make them work more efficiently: this is a prerequisite for enlargement. we shall have occasion to discuss this matter in more detail again and again. today i would just like to stress an obvious point, which is the very purpose of nice and subsequent councils: a union of 27-28 or more states will need stronger institutions and not weaker ones; we need a stronger, not a weaker, democratic commitment, a stronger, not a more vague, legal system. in this respect, it would therefore be illusory to think of the "monne method" as a method of the past, which can be more effectively replaced by ad hoc solutions. the european parliament, the council, the commission and the court of justice are our institutions. they provide the safeguards, the system of checks and balances, without which nothing sustainable can be built. given their essential nature, we must work to improve them. this is the task we have all set ourselves for nice. in short, it is clear that the next six months will be a period of commitment. i am convinced that when france passes the torch to sweden, we will have made significant progress in building the europe our fellow citizens want and expect. counsel. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioners, ladies and gentlemen, first of all, i must apologize for my delay, which is not due to any food fantasy, but simply to the fact that the president of the republic, jacques chirac, was among us. mrs fontaine accompanied him home, which delayed the necessary trilogue we had with the president of the commission, mr prodi, by a few minutes. zimbabwe is going through a serious economic, social and political crisis. despite some human rights violations, which have been rightly denounced by the international community, it has remained essentially a state governed by the rule of law, thanks in particular to the dynamism of its civil society and the independence of its judiciary. over the past three years, a reversal of external conditions has weakened a structured but at the same time ageing economic fabric. authoritarian drift and lax economic management have subsequently tarnished the country's image, undermined the trust of the donor community and fuelled popular protest. this discontent was expressed in the february constitutional referendum, in which the presidential party suffered its first electoral defeat since independence in 1980. parliamentary elections were thus a major challenge for the government. to hinder the opposition's progress, the government risked stoking tensions through a tough election campaign, making the unequal distribution of agricultural land the mobilizing theme of the rural world and veterans of the liberation war. the head of state, in this context, has allowed a large movement of property occupation to develop and has established the legal framework for future expropriations. these diversions, which i have just mentioned, have led to the deaths of 33 people, aggravated the economic crisis and distorted the electoral competition, creating a real risk of instability in southern africa. the european union nevertheless considered it important that the elections should take place and that their results should be credible and acceptable. the commission has therefore sought the agreement of the zimbabwean authorities to send a mission of nearly 200 observers to the country as soon as possible before the elections, thus demonstrating its interest in the consolidation of democracy in that country. it is clear that this presence helped to calm tensions and to restore the climate as favourable as possible, in this delicate context, to the free expression of universal suffrage. i would like to pay tribute to mr pierre schori, who led this mission, and to the remarkable work done by his team. while our observers noted that the level of violence, irregularities and intimidation in the run-up to the elections did not make the terms of free and fair apply to the fifth parliamentary elections in zimbabwe's history, they also noted the good organization of the elections themselves, the high turnout - i believe it was the highest since independence - and the calm in which they were able to take place. the counting of the ballots has not been the subject of controversy. so let me, on behalf of the european union, congratulate the zimbabwean people, who, by participating in this consultation in large numbers, have shown their determination to take their destiny into their own hands in a peaceful and democratic way. i also note with great satisfaction the overall acceptance of the election results by all parties present. the entry of a significant opposition force into parliament - in fact, very close to the majority in the seats that were up for election - augurs constructive debate. there is no doubt that with these elections, zimbabwe is turning a page in its young history. there are, of course, the underlying problems, which remain unresolved. the union therefore calls on all political forces in zimbabwe to mobilise and engage in dialogue in order to put the country firmly on the road to recovery. it hopes that the new government, with the support of the new national representation, will take credible measures to restore order to the economy, which will restore the confidence of local operators and donors. for the past 20 years, the european union has been the leading development partner of zimbabwe, a friendly country and a partner in the lomé convention. it wishes to continue along this path, with reasserted respect for human rights, democratic principles and the rule of law. the commission is willing to continue to intervene in favour of the populations most affected by the crisis and is in particular prepared to resume its support for the necessary agrarian reform, provided that it is implemented in an orderly, transparent and rational manner, in the service of poverty reduction. the european union wants to believe in the future of a democratic and prosperous zimbabwe, a factor of stability and harmonious development in southern africa.
commission - mr president, let me say first of all that i would have been delighted, in this debate, to hand over the presidency to mr schori, who has undoubtedly done, as the presidency has said, a remarkable job in zimbabwe. i think that all of us who wish zimbabwe well would like to congratulate him, as would all the members of the eu observer delegation. they all did a wonderful job. they have done very well in achieving their objectives under very difficult conditions and have fulfilled their mandate with extreme efficiency. the deployment of a full and experienced team to the scene, less than four weeks after an informal decision by the eu foreign ministers, is a tribute to the enormous efforts of all those involved. the effectiveness and professionalism of the observer mission enabled its members to overcome many political obstacles. they have made this operation a reference for election observation missions in countries in crisis. it is a widely accepted fact that the eu mission has helped to reduce the violence. i think it can also be recognised that it helped build the confidence of civil society during the elections. i would stress once again that mr schori's reputation and the role he played were decisive in our assessment of the success of the mission. i think the mission was considered the most credible observation mission during this period of unrest in zimbabwe, as shown by the extensive coverage in the local and international press. moreover, the european union mission, by far the largest deployed in the country and operating throughout its territory, contributed to a significant extent to coordinating all the efforts to monitor the electoral process in zimbabwe. we have of course been able to see the main points in the report, although we are still waiting for the opportunity to study it in detail. i know that the first part follows on from the interim report drawn up by mr schori and that it lists the acts of violence and intimidation which unfortunately marred the beginning of the election campaign. we know from what he has told us that the report analyses the electoral process and the conduct of the vote and i think, without taking his words out of his mouth, that in general the conduct of the vote itself was quite satisfactory. finally and most importantly, the report highlights the implications for the future of zimbabwe and we look forward to hearing what mr schori has to say about this. the honourable members are right to recommend that in the weeks and months ahead the european union should be very closely following developments in zimbabwe and offering help and assistance wherever we need to do so. this is something we certainly want to support and you can be sure that my colleague, commissioner nielson, and i will be stepping up our efforts to strengthen communication, both formal and informal, with president mugabe and his government to facilitate the transition to a genuine pluralist democracy. mr schori said how important it was for the government to prosecute those who had committed political violence or other human rights violations; he also said how important it is that the courts decide any dispute over the election results and, most importantly, that the government abide by their decisions. these are two fundamental aspects which touch - need i say more? - at the heart of the credibility of the whole democratic process. it is clear that zimbabwe is at a crossroads. the outcome of the parliamentary elections could mark the beginning of a major shift in the country's political culture, the transition to a multi-party system in which parliament would replace the political bureau of the ruling party, zanu-pf, as the main political decision-making body. president mugabe's electoral strategy, focused on land reform and aid to war veterans, has left out the country's economic difficulties, a shortcoming that is clearly reflected in the votes his party has garnered. the new government of zimbabwe and all those who want to bring the country out of its current serious difficulties, whether it is the economic situation, land reform or the terrible ravages of the hiv virus, must now face all these challenges together, effectively and in a constructive spirit. our status as the main donor gives us considerable influence which we must use to encourage the government to take positive initiatives towards the restoration of the rule of law and good governance, as a first step towards a more general recovery. i know that this is something that my colleague, commissioner nielson, will want to develop in his speech following mine. that said, i would like to congratulate mr schori once again personally on his excellent performance in a very difficult task.

commission. - mr president, i would like to congratulate the members of the delegation of the union to observe the elections in zimbabwe. they have done a very good job in very difficult conditions. the outcome of these elections provides the eu with a further opportunity to review its cooperation with zimbabwe. according to the report of the mission's officials, there is potential for positive developments in zimbabwe in the political, economic and social fields. they believe that the eu should not dismiss any of the options available to it to contribute to this development. zanu-pf will have to devise new, more appropriate policies to try to convince the international community to financially support the stabilization of the economy and the revival of growth. however, the legitimacy of zanu-pf is in question, because of the many intimidations and other electoral irregularities that contributed to its victory and also because despite all this, the mdc won 58 seats, almost as many as zanu-pf with its 61+1 seats. the movement for democratic change will not share responsibility for the crisis the country is going through or the painful measures that will be needed for economic recovery. the national indicative programme for zimbabwe under the 8th edf, which has a budget of eur 110 million, is directly focused on poverty alleviation. its main areas of cooperation are agriculture, health and education. the commission's policy has been to maintain aid to preserve basic social services and strengthen civil society, even in times of crisis. a tranche of €19 million is about to be released for a programme of micro-projects which, in the interests of reconciliation policy, had been postponed after the elections. so now he can go back. the commission has continued its support for land reform through this programme of micro-projects which in reality provide aid to combat poverty through the legal acquisition of land under resettlement programmes. however, in april the commission froze the €2 million for technical and political assistance for land reform. it was of little use to continue a technical and rather theoretical discussion on the principles of land reform as long as the government did not specify its policy in this respect. i hope that changes. the commission and other donors are ready to support the process, provided it respects the legality and transparency and poverty reduction objectives, as agreed at the 1998 donor conference. the commission is busy developing a horizontal programme to combat the aids epidemic and the spread of hiv in zimbabwe, which in themselves constitute a development crisis and a major cause of poverty now and in the future. this programme is to be financed from the €33 million of the second tranche of the 8th edf. i will make a decision on this in the coming months, depending on the development of the situation in zimbabwe. in any case, the commission continues to support projects aimed at combating poverty. if the government can seize the opportunity offered by the last elections, the union could increase its assistance in the future. as the heads of mission in harare have pointed out, it is premature to draw conclusions about the elections and their consequences. i fully agree with the recognition that the future of eu-zimbabwe development cooperation will depend on real progress in the areas of democratisation, the rule of law, human rights and economic reform. in conclusion, i would stress that there is potential for more intensive cooperation with zimbabwe, but that this will clearly depend on how the situation develops in that country.
