- doc. a5-0180/00 by mr mombaur, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the second report from the commission to the council and the european parliament on the state of liberalisation of energy markets (com (99) 0198 - c0m (99) 0164 - c0m (99) 0612) - c0m (90) 297 - c5-0163/2000 - 2000/2097 (cos))
the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, the gas and electricity market is one of the essential foundations of europe's competitiveness and environmental protection. we have drawn up a report which echoes four commission documents and the main aim is to create a common market of 15 separate markets. as rapporteur for this committee, i would like to draw attention to a few points, but perhaps you will allow me, mr president, to interrupt for a few seconds as the vice-president is entering the chamber. i repeat: our report is essentially aimed at echoing four commission documents and establishing a common market for gas and electricity from 15 isolated markets. the commission is concerned about many things. i'll list them. firstly, the community's fundamental rights of freedom of establishment and freedom to provide services have so far been only partially enforced. we recommend that they be imposed swiftly. secondly, we welcome the emergence of new structures at the level of suppliers. however, we urge the commission, as the competition authority, to work closely with the national antitrust authorities to prevent the formation of new monopolies, to maintain free access to the network for new suppliers, to set up exchanges and to maintain the possibility of changing suppliers. thirdly, we are concerned about security of supply and we believe that it must be ensured that member states who wish to do so can impose obligations on all competitors in the general interest. the treaty contains relevant rules on transparency and clarity in this respect, but member states also have the possibility to do so if they so wish. we are committed to keeping it that way. fourth, the regulators. most member states have established regulators; no state has done that yet. we find that in the states with regulators, not only large consumers but also smes and small consumers benefit from better market participation and clearer conditions for the use of the network. perhaps the relevance of the negotiated network access model should be reconsidered as it makes life easier for large consumers, complicates life for smes and may also be a tool that hinders the whole market in europe. fifthly, for markets, networks are the crucial place. there must therefore be freedom of access, and that means that tariffs must be a sound signal of non-discriminatory access for all and establish acceptable prices at cross-border level - this is what the so-called florence process is about - which enable cross-border trade. a model is being developed whereby the costs of cross-border trade are paid into funds. these amounts are paid by the network managers and paid to those who implement the transit lines. commissioner, madam vice-president, i have two observations to make on this subject. first, the costs currently reported by the network operators seem to us to be fanciful and without any justification, as if they had fallen from the sky. we must examine very carefully whether these are not completely false figures. secondly, the costs reflected in the tariffs must in any case provide the appropriate market incentives and thus cover all losses and encourage investment. that's an important part of the process. sixthly, the crossborder lines do not yet have the necessary capacity. the aim is to look at this problem and, if necessary, to remedy it or to make an allocation in line with the market, perhaps by means of tenders. i would like to make two further points. we expect the commission to come and discuss with us in committee the attitude to be adopted towards imports of gas and electricity from the countries of central and eastern europe, because we do not want other safety standards or inappropriate competition instruments to damage the gas and electricity market in europe. finally, as regards electricity, the transmission system operators have formed an association with the help of which results have been achieved in florence. we ask the commission to instruct, as we are doing ourselves, the operators of gas transmission networks to set up a similar association so that successes similar to those achieved in florence can also be achieved in the parallel madrid process concerning the gas sector.

the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, madam vice-president, ladies and gentlemen, the committee on transport is proposing to the house that the rail transport market should finally be gradually opened up by 2010. only through such openness will we achieve our common objective of moving freight from road to rail and eventually achieving sustainable mobility in the european union. first of all, i should like to thank the vice-president, mrs palacio, and the finnish presidency of the council for the fact that the council was able to adopt common positions in december 1999. we are very grateful. however, in the co-decision procedure we will defend the view that these positions do not go far enough to secure the future of the railway. the council is only going to take small steps. we believe that, eight years after the completion of the internal market, it is time to at least set the milestones and regulate things definitively so that the liberalisation of the railway sector can be completed in 2010. this would be in line with the lisbon summit, where the heads of state and government insisted on advancing the liberalization of transport. that said, what are our essential amendments? firstly, we agree with the council that a specific transeuropean rail freight network should be opened up to the single transeuropean rail freight network in order to achieve efficient use of the rail networks. however, we believe that five years is enough to show the railway companies and their employees that they need not fear the opening up of the networks. we believe that railway access should be extended to the entire network of the 15 member states after five years for both international and domestic freight transport and that the same should be true for international and domestic passenger transport by 2010 at the latest. this gradual and cautious opening would finally lead to a genuine common network within the european union by 2010. in order to ensure that railway companies in all member states have effective access to the networks of other member states, it seems to me essential to implement a strictly mandatory separation of the management of railway infrastructure and the provision of transport services by the national railway company concerned. experience over the last 40 years shows that failure to separate the network and its operation systematically leads national railway companies to claim for themselves the best use of the infrastructure of their network and, in doing so, to deny other railway companies effective and railway companies. another element is the question of the remuneration of the railway workers. we believe that in the medium and long term this remuneration should be increased to cover the costs. the financing of these costs will only be possible if the users, i.e. the railway companies, actually bear the costs of operating and maintaining the network, in accordance with the principle that the president of the european central bank. - mr president, a year and a half has passed since the birth of the euro and the moment when the ecb was given the responsibility for managing monetary policy. during this period, the eurosystem, i.e. the 11 national central banks and the ecb, had to demonstrate its ability to implement the conceptual framework that had been carefully prepared in previous years. it also had to prove that it could achieve the objectives set by the treaty establishing the european community. in retrospect, these objectives were achieved both from the operational and from the monetary policy point of view. that is why i am very pleased to present to you today the second annual report of the ecb. it reports on the eurosystem's activities in 1999 and at the beginning of this year. today's presentation is, in my view, an important demonstration of the ecb's responsibility to the european parliament. it is in addition to the discussions which have taken place in your committee on economic and monetary affairs, in which i participate once every three months. in addition to this regular dialogue, the other members of the executive board of the ecb attended committee meetings on several occasions to present a report prepared under the responsibility of the ecb and to participate in the exchange of views on various issues. in view of the many subjects covered in the annual report, it will clearly be impossible to cover all of them at our meeting today. that is why i shall concentrate on some of the most relevant issues which have already been raised in the motion for a resolution by your committee on economic and monetary affairs. as regards the first year of the single currency, i will begin by saying that the first objective of the ecb, namely maintaining price stability, has been achieved. with consumer prices in the euro area rising by only 1.1% in 1999, inflation was at one of the lowest levels in the last 50 years. in line with its mandate, the ecb remains vigilant to threats to price stability, as demonstrated by monetary policy decisions taken to dampen inflationary pressures before they materialise, rather than reacting when price stability is already under threat. the eurosystem will continue to pursue this progressive strategy in order to maintain a stable price environment, which also helps to support economic growth and job creation in the euro area. i share the analysis in your motion for a resolution that governments should take advantage of the favourable economic environment to intensify efforts to consolidate budgets and reduce public debt and to go beyond the objectives set in the stability programmes. at the same time, vigorous structural reforms of the manufacturing and capital markets should be undertaken. the broad implementation of the policy timetable will help to contain inflationary pressures and thereby support the ecb in fulfilling its tasks. in your motion for a resolution you also briefly discuss the potential implications of a 'new economy'. i would therefore like to comment on the possible emergence of a new economy in the euro area. first of all, there are different definitions of the new economy. the most useful definition, in my view, is that which characterizes the new economy as a phenomenon which increases the rate of productivity growth over a long period. there is some evidence, though it may be controversial, that a new economy is emerging in the united states. however, it is still difficult to find clear evidence of the emergence of a new economy in the euro area. of course, it is necessary to continue to monitor developments in order to identify, as early as possible, new economic trends and potential structural breaks in traditional economic relations. it is important to stress that, for the euro area, the creation of more flexible markets is a prerequisite if the potential benefits of new technologies are to be realised in the form of a substantial increase in productivity growth. we recognise that the uncertainty factor is one of the essential characteristics of the potential emergence of a new economy, given, inter alia, the evolution of productive potential and the reliability of indicators derived from it, such as estimates of output gaps. in this context, the eurosystem's monetary policy framework is well-equipped to deal with such uncertainties. it provides the flexibility to cope with changes in the economic structure in order to maintain price stability over the medium term. the ecb's strategy is based on two pillars and explicitly recognises the uncertainty related to the structure of the economy and the transmission of monetary policy within the economy. in the context of this discussion, some observers urged the ecb to keep interest rates low in view of the new economy. in reply to this, i would like to stress the following point: the new economy is above all a question of supply. a too lax monetary policy would not improve the conditions for the emergence of a new economy. on the contrary, by threatening price stability, such a policy could seriously undermine the ecb's current means of action. this would undermine confidence, increase interest rate risk premia and undermine prospects for economic growth and job creation. for this reason, the ecb, in accordance with its mandate, will continue to preserve price stability in the euro area. it is the guarantee that monetary policy will contribute fully to overall economic well-being while providing an environment in which the new economy, should it emerge, can flourish. i would now like to turn to another point which has been frequently discussed in our regular dialogue, namely the question of transparency. i have already spoken about the regular dialogue between the european parliament and the ecb, the transcripts of which are published on the websites of our institutions. in addition, at the press conference held each month after the first meeting of the governing council, i present the ecb's assessment of the economic environment underpinning our monetary policy decisions. you are no doubt familiar with the wide variety of ecb publications, in particular our monthly newsletter, the many press articles and speeches by members of the executive board of the ecb. these are also available, as usual, via the ecb's website. these numerous communication tools, in which arguments for or against a particular decision are presented, are in substance similar to minutes. it should also be borne in mind that, thanks to the regular press conferences and the rapid publication of questions and answers on the ecb's website, detailed information on the governing council's deliberations is available very quickly. we therefore avoid the delays inherent in the publication of all forms of official minutes. we always make our decisions from the perspective of the euro area. this is fundamental to the conduct of a truly single monetary policy. the publication of the ecb reports on economic developments in each euro area member state, as indicated in your motion for a resolution, must be seen in this context. our intention is clearly not to alter the ecb's view of the euro area as a whole. the resolution also calls for the ecb to publish macroeconomic forecasts. i can assure you that the preparations for this publication are proceeding with great earnestness. i still intend to start publishing it towards the end of the year 2000, in line with the statement i made last september at the european parliament's plenary session on the ecb's previous annual report. i would like to make a warning, however. the forecasts are only a decision-making element for the governing council. the publication of the ecb's forecasts should not be seen as a panacea that will address all the communication challenges facing the ecb as a new institution in a new multilingual and multinational environment. the forecasts themselves have important shortcomings. they swim, for example, in the greatest uncertainty and can quickly become obsolete if the external environment changes. we are aware of these shortcomings. therefore, as is clear from the ecb's monetary policy strategy, monetary policy decisions cannot be taken on the basis of general inflation forecasts alone. the full analysis of the monetary and macroeconomic situation and of the economic disturbances affecting the euro area is the relevant element in policy decision-making. the ecb's approach to communication has always been one of honesty. to continue in this spirit, i think we need to publish forecasts in a way that accurately reflects their limited role in decision-making and the inherent uncertainties they contain. any other approach would not be transparent and would therefore be potentially misleading. i now turn to a related issue, namely the publication of the ecb's economic and econometric models. to be clear, the ecb does not consider only one econometric model but uses a wide range of models. the results obtained from these models are evaluated critically, with the help of experts. policy decisions are taken on the basis of analyses based on models developed by the ecb, in some cases with input from national central banks. these are only some of the elements used in policy evaluations and policy decisions. the ecb has established a series of working papers where technical economic research, produced under the responsibility of ecb staff, among others, can be reviewed and reassessed by national and external experts. the respective authors are responsible for the content of these documents. however, they do not necessarily reflect the views of the ecb or the eurosystem. through this and other channels, a dialogue and exchange of professional views is established between ecb staff and a wide range of external experts, to the mutual benefit of all. different econometric models have already been published in a series of ecb working papers. for example, an econometric study of m3 demand in the euro area, conducted by ecb staff, was published in september 1999. other models will be published shortly. a euro area-wide model used by the ecb, which studies the overall behaviour of the euro area economy, will be published in this series of working papers produced by ecb staff, probably at the end of this year or early next year. i would now like to talk about the contribution of the escb, the european system of central banks, to maintaining the stability of the system and to prudential supervision. in this connection, i would like to mention the banking supervision committee which supports cooperation between the ecb, the national central banks and the supervisory authorities of the 15 member states. the central activity of the banking supervision committee is the analysis of structural developments and the monitoring of potential weaknesses in the banking sector. the banking supervision committee also provides a forum for the exchange of relevant information between the eurosystem and the supervisory authorities. finally, the committee may also act as a forum for cooperation on controls outside the eurosystem's remit. the need for multilateral cooperation between banking supervisors has increased since the creation of economic and monetary union for two reasons. first, emu introduced an unprecedented geographical separation between the area of jurisdiction of monetary policy and that of prudential supervision. secondly, the introduction of the euro itself has fostered the future integration of the banking and financial sector. in this context, the banking supervision committee is, in my view, the main forum in which multilateral cooperation between banking supervisors must be strengthened. as regards the issue of crossborder retail payments, which has been raised on several occasions by the european parliament, it will be recalled that in september 1999 the ecb published a report entitled improving crossborder retail payment systems - the eurosystem's view. the report calls for the banking sector to provide significantly improved services by the year 2002. since the publication of this report, the banking sector has in principle subscribed to the objectives of the eurosystem. it has started to work closely with the eurosystem to identify and examine the practical obstacles to achieving these objectives and, where possible, to agree on effective solutions. i fully share the european parliament's concern about the little progress that consumers can see. however, there are important signs that banks are making considerable efforts to prepare the ground for more efficient management of crossborder credit transfers. in particular, there has been continuous progress in the standardization and simplification of balance of payments information requirements. the ecb will prepare an additional progress report by autumn, updating its estimates. the eurosystem would prefer to maintain its current position on cooperation but, if necessary, it will increase pressure on the banking sector. however, it would be unrealistic to expect that the level of service for crossborder payments will reach that of domestic payments in all respects by the year 2002. i would like to stress again that the introduction of the euro was indeed an important step in the ongoing process of european integration. the ecb, as the guardian of the single currency, will continue to pursue its monetary policy of stability in order to fulfil its mandate and deliver the results that european citizens rightly expect. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. if this proposal is accepted, there will be three types of patent. firstly, there will be national patents, which will be issued in the national language by the national patent office. this is the current procedure and it will remain so. then there are the european patents granted by the european patent office. the european patent should not be confused with the community patent. the first is a basket of national patents: an inventor, for example, files a patent application in the benelux, france and germany, in other words in 5 out of 15 member states. if his application is accepted, he gets a patent in these five countries, and the jurisdiction falls to the courts of these five countries. this possibility, which is the system currently in place, will continue to exist. the community patent, which we are now discussing, is the third possibility. it is a unitary patent, in other words it is granted and applies throughout the community. that is why it is called a community patent. let me stress that inventors have the choice of either applying for a european patent or a community patent. the commission has no intention of eliminating any of the possibilities currently available. i would like to answer mrs thors' question about decentralisation in this area. it can't go both ways. we can't have butter and butter money. a community patent issued centrally, say in munich, and valid throughout the community at once implies the existence of a centralised court which will adjudicate on the disputes in question. the commission has therefore proposed the creation of a tribunal for disputes concerning intellectual property rights. and it is in luxembourg that it should logically be. that's what i'd like to say to mr. maccormick. our concern is not geographical at all - commission - (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mrs garcía-orcoyen tormo, for her work on the commission's proposal on emas. before going into the details of the various amendments, i would like to address three fundamental issues, namely the notion of best available technology, the relationship between participation in emas and the obligation to meet environmental legislation criteria, and the frequency with which the environmental statement will have to be validated. the amendments proposed by the european parliament on the concept of best available technology would imply that all organisations participating in emas would be obliged to use the technology. the commission agrees with the principle that all emas organisations should strive to apply the best possible practice in their field of activity and to work with maximum efficiency, both in terms of the choice of techniques and materials and from an organisational point of view. however, the concept of best available technology, which is expressly defined in the directive on the harmonisation of preventive measures to limit pollution, applies only to industry. this is something which the european parliament has also noted in a number of its amendments. since emas is now open to all economic sectors, this obligation to use the best available technology would, in practice, mean that many sectors would be unable to participate in emas. the european parliament itself, for example, would be excluded, since the notion of best available technology cannot apply to public institutions. this obligation would also represent a major obstacle for small and medium-sized enterprises. they are not covered by the directive on the harmonization of pollution prevention and control measures. if this exception is circumvented by means of emas, which is a voluntary system, the result is likely to be a disincentive for smes to participate. as regards the amendments aimed at limiting the principle of best available technology to the scope of the directive on the harmonisation of pollution prevention and control measures, it should be stressed that emas is not responsible for playing the role of an alternative for monitoring the application of mandatory legislation. we all agree that it is important for organisations to comply with the environmental laws to which they are subject. it could be said that compliance with environmental legislation is a minimum requirement. the aim of emas is to help organisations do better by exceeding this minimum. however, the objective is not to provide the supervisory authorities with absolute proof that an emas registered organisation complies with the law in all circumstances. given the systematic structure of emas, it is clear that the organisations that will be part of it will be in a favourable position to apply the legislation. however, emas is a voluntary system. if the european parliament maintains its amendments to ensure compliance with environmental laws, the role of emas may change. it will then replace the checks carried out by the competent authorities in the member states. i am convinced that this is not the intention of the european parliament. how often should the environmental statement be validated? well, the environmental - the next item is the report (a5-0166/2000) by mrs breyer, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position of the council with a view to the adoption of a directive of the european parliament and of the council on limit values for benzene and carbon monoxide in ambient air.
the rapporteur. - (de) ladies and gentlemen, madam commissioner, i will try to be brief, because i do not think that this directive is controversial in parliament. this is the second directive in the line of the directive on the assessment and monitoring of ambient air quality, and the proposal is part of a package of measures on the fight against air pollution. the most important aspect of this second daughter directive is that it provides for the first time a limit value for benzene and carbon monoxide in the european union. it is a major step forward, i would even say a turning point in the legislation on ambient air quality, because for the first time a limit value is set for a carcinogenic substance, namely benzene, which can indeed cause leukaemia. we know that the sources of benzene are petrol and oil, and in the european union 80 to 85% of benzene is attributed to the combustion of benzene on the roads. until now, there was no threshold value for health damage and therefore no benzene was safe. the precautionary principle laid down in the ec treaty, however, imposes a limit value associated with an extremely low health risk. we therefore strongly support the proposal to set the limit value at 5 micrograms per cubic metre of air. the common position has clearly improved the commission's proposal. i am also pleased that it has been possible to take up many of parliament's amendments. one amendment in particular was essential to us. the commission proposal provided for derogations to be granted to member states almost as often as desired. it was almost a blank cheque that could have been renewed over and over again and by removing this derogation we have reached an acceptable compromise. in the context of the application of the directive, it is also important to take the problems of the southern countries into account and to find a compromise. the proposal also corresponds to what mrs schleicher suggested in the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy at first reading, namely that justified one-off derogations can be made, not only for countries but also for certain regions, certain territories and that the 10 micrograms cannot be exceeded. in the light of the enlargement to the east, it is also very important to show that our environmental policy is not a two-speed policy and that the member states to which the derogations apply must also prove that they are on track to meet the requirements themselves. the committee on the environment has also tabled a number of amendments which should not be controversial, because they relate mainly to the obligation to inform. in this respect, we have made it clear that the new internet tool should be used to improve information. we also clarified how information should be conveyed and highlighted a major problem, indoor pollution, which should be addressed in the european union's research programmes. indeed, when we talk about the outer atmosphere, it should be clear, in order to be credible, that we also want to make efforts at the level of the indoor atmosphere. we have also written that the member states should draw up better documentation. finally, it is very important in member states with a derogation that the public is also informed of this derogation and of the efforts being made to finally reach our target of 5 micrograms by the year 2010. i'll stay on that, so i don't exceed my allotted time. it is important that this directive be implemented quickly and i think that, given the effort we have made here, it should no longer be a problem.
- (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as mrs breyer has just pointed out, we are dealing today with the second specific directive which emerged from the framework directive - adopted in 1996 - on the assessment and monitoring of ambient air quality. the main objective is to set limit values for benzene and carbon monoxide concentrations, in order to improve ambient air and to prevent harmful substances from affecting human health and the environment. it is true that the main source of emissions of the two harmful substances, benzene and carbon monoxide, is road traffic. other important sources include fuel distribution, oil refineries and the chemical industry for benzene, or all combustion processes for carbon monoxide. this directive is a major step forward in the fight against the greenhouse effect and in the process of purifying ambient air. the european commission submitted the proposal in december 1998. the finnish presidency made a serious attempt to exploit the new legal possibilities of the amsterdam treaty and to bring the amended proposal of the european parliament into force immediately after the first reading in december 1999. our group would be very pleased. our group has of course supported the amendments which stress the danger to certain groups of the population and which consider the proposed environmental protection measures as minimum conditions which can be extended. in addition, at first reading we tabled the provisions for the one-off extension of the time limit and the maintenance of the limit value - which are necessary in the southern member states for climatic reasons - and for setting the limit value for the concentration of benzene at 10 micrograms per m3. mrs breyer has already indicated that the common position has evolved well since then. now it uses exactly the wording we want, and the other provisions of the common position are consistent and provide for feasible measures to improve ambient air quality in europe. our group approves this common position and can adopt it as it stands. the regulations guarantee a high level of health protection and are flexible enough to keep pace with technical progress. mrs breyer has worked very hard and has been able to impose many of parliament's demands during the negotiations. i must say, however, that we consider the amendments tabled again to be superfluous, that is to say, they are justified, but not worth delaying the adoption of this directive any further. we believe it is much more important - and you have also mentioned this, mrs breyer - that this regulation can finally come into force as soon as possible, after a delay of six months, in order to contribute to improving the air quality in europe. the commission has also proposed that the directive be amended to include a reference to the 'new' directive.
commission. - (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection for their excellent of unnecessarily delaying the adoption of this important directive, which for the first time sets limit values for the content of benzene and carbon monoxide in air. the commission cannot therefore accept amendment no 4. i would like to conclude by saying that this common position represents a valuable compromise, which i hope will be adopted by the whole of parliament without any major changes.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0164/2000) by mrs von jackson, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a recommendation of the european parliament and of the council laying down minimum criteria for environmental inspections in the member states.
commission - mr president, let me first of all thank the rapporteur, mrs jackson, and the committee on the environment for their work on this proposal on environmental inspections. i cannot resist the temptation to point out to mrs jackson that she reminds me of the promise i made to the committee not to constantly propose new directives but rather to concentrate on their implementation. the poor application of environmental rules has nothing to do with the absence of such rules and guidelines. we have a wide range of legislation and we really want to act. we want results. we have already tackled the main problem: recommendation or directive? you will not be surprised to learn that the commission cannot accept the transposition into a directive for the following reasons. the commission's 1996 communication on the implementation of community environmental legislation pointed to a disparity between the inspection systems of the various member states and recognised the need to ensure a minimum number of inspection missions. the idea of seeing officials in blue uniforms with gold stars performing these checks may not be so bad! it recommended the development of guidelines to be integrated into existing national systems, leaving the choice of structures and mechanisms to the member states. a recommendation may achieve results. some member states already have well-developed inspection services or agencies, and the guidelines will ensure that they operate in accordance with common standards without requiring them to make substantial changes to their systems. as a first step, the recommendation will enable other member states to develop their infrastructure and capacity, through community funding for eligible member states. some member states could face enormous difficulties if they had to comply with all the requirements of a directive. and the commission did not consider that psychologically or practically desirable. at the present stage of development of national inspection services, i am convinced that the carrot will be much more effective than the stick. some progress has already been made in this area through the impel programme, which allows for the exchange of inspectors and studies on inspections, their frequency, etc. this proposal should therefore be seen as the first stage of an ongoing programme and the experience gained in this operation will help us to determine, at later stages, how to extend the nature, scope and application of the minimum requirements. the proposal obliges the member states to report on the operation, and i will personally ensure that this is done. if it turns out that the member states are not applying these rules in practice, we will not hesitate to propose a directive. in the council, all member states, including those with developed inspection services, were in favour of non-binding legislation at this stage. let 's face it . if parliament persists in asking for a directive, we shall be left with no legislation. in this case, we would be neglecting the member states which are most in need of assistance and advice, which would not bring about any change in the status quo or any improvement in the enforcement of the legislation in those member states. for these reasons the commission cannot accept any of the amendments concerning the transformation of the proposal for a recommendation into a directive. the commission cannot accept the content of the following amendments: amendment no 5, which aims to help member states to distinguish between national legislation - for example, which does not originate in the eu - and community legislation; amendments nos 6 and 11, which aim to transform voluntary reporting and advice systems into mandatory the rapporteur. - (de) mr president, i should like to begin by thanking the commission, commissioner reding and my colleagues from all the committees concerned for their extraordinary cooperation, and the council, the portuguese presidency and now the french presidency for their cooperation so far. overall, the intervention in the media programme had two objectives: we all want to strengthen european cinema and we all want to guarantee future jobs in the audiovisual sector, which is a growth engine. consequently, it is important to note that the european audiovisual industry is still very insufficiently equipped for this development. the cross-border circulation of european works is still too low. in the cinema, the market share of american films is 80%, and that of european films outside their country of origin is 7%. in television, imported american fiction accounts for 74% of the total volume of imported programmes, compared with 14% for works originating in other european countries. in this context, building on the earlier media i and media ii programmes, the media programme focuses on this lack of circulation of european works and supports three sectors in particular: continuing training in the programmes with media training, development and distribution with the media plus programme. the new features are the general consideration of online systems and the introduction of pilot projects to use digital technology. on this point, madam commissioner, i can say on behalf of all the committees concerned and, i hope, on behalf of parliament, that we support your proposals and wish them every success. i would point out, however, that we tabled amendments which we consider very important on certain points. the budget is first and foremost a part of it, as is often the case. the commission proposes €400 million for a five-year programme in the audiovisual sector. this was already the commission's proposal in 1995, which was unfortunately rejected by the council at the time. if we want to seize the opportunities of the digital revolution, we must act now. that's why 400 million isn't enough! we are proposing a moderate increase: 550 million in all, 480 million for media plus and 70 million for media training. however, this increase alone will not have any lasting effect. we need two more instruments. on the one hand, we must link up with other eu programmes and on the other hand, we call on the council and the commission to allow risk capital to finally be placed on the european private market - as in the united states. the mobilisation of private capital is perhaps our main demand, with the pilot project on the european investment bank. i would also like to raise the question of the legal basis. we know that this is a serious problem for the commission, but we would like to see article 157 on industry, but also article 151 on culture, as the legal basis for the audiovisual programme. it is about culture and industry. this should be reflected in the programme and in the legal basis. finally, there are other important demands: the transparency and effectiveness of programmes must be encouraged, funds must be concentrated on smes, independent producers, member states with a low audiovisual production capacity and on linguistic areas of lesser importance. my final appeal to the council and the commission is that they should create a powerful lobby group for european cinema together with parliament. - (de) mr president, the committee on petitions is a rather special committee. as the two previous speakers have said, the commission receives complaints from european citizens who feel that their rights have been violated. as rapporteur for the opinion on the right of residence, i would like to make a few remarks on the specific problems in this area. the free movement of persons is one of the fundamental freedoms that has enabled us to achieve european integration. since the maastricht treaty, there has been a general right of residence subject to sufficient means of subsistence and cover for sickness risks. a restriction on freedom of movement and residence shall be permitted only for reasons of public policy, security and health. the experience of the committee on petitions shows that the right to free movement in practice faces many problems: (a) the hesitant application of community provisions by the member states; (b) specific occupational problems with regard to the recognition of diplomas and certificates of study; (c) the non-adaptation of social security provisions, for example with regard to the complexity of forms for reimbursement of medical expenses. an analysis of the 1996-1999 infringement procedure reveals in 97 cases a direct link between the petition and the infringement procedure before the court of justice of the european communities. it is regrettable that the council of ministers regularly ignores the reports of the committee on petitions on serious breaches of community law by the authorities of the member states. this is evidence of a negative attitude towards the right of petition of european citizens. in future, the council should pay due attention to the rights of the citizens of the union.
(de) mr president, the right to petition and to complain is not a recent invention. as early as 2,000 years ago, roman petitioners could express their concerns to the emperor. however, this right was constantly threatened, modified, limited or eliminated. the petitioners of the past have become the emancipated european citizens of today. no administration or institution is infallible. many petitions point to an imbalance between legislation and european integration. petitions are thus a barometer for assessing the relationship between citizens and the legislator. these petitions are numerous. a hamster population in an industrial area is as much a concern to us as a ban on silicone implants or the introduction of a tax on heavy goods vehicles. i now turn to the ombudsman. my group congratulates the ombudsman on the work he has done in 1999. mr söderman's main achievement has been and is to work for greater transparency and publicity within the european administration. since most of the complaints for which the ombudsman is responsible concern the european commission and are based on a lack of transparency, this task needs to be worked on. access to documents, not only for european citizens but also for the ombudsman, is one of them. even the introduction of new technologies in offices cannot be a reason for not being transparent. citizen-based responses build trust. the opposite behaviour leads to mistrust and an increase in the number of complaints that need to be dealt with, which generates new costs. the ombudsman's initiative to introduce a code of good administrative behaviour is therefore to be welcomed. citizens have a fundamental right to an open, service-oriented and accountable administration, which is funded entirely by their contributions. i believe that the independence of the european ombudsman, as an example for the introduction of national ombudsmen in the candidate countries and in my own land of thuringia, is of paramount importance.

the committee on budgetary control adopted an opinion on the proposal. mr president, the committee on budgetary control is unanimous in its support for the objectives of the ec investment partners programme. we are, however, critical of the way in which it is being implemented. first of all, the commission is currently operating in a free-trade area, since the proposal to continue the programme, which has already been extended twice, was not submitted until the end of january, i.e. one month after its expiry, and cannot be adopted before the end of the autumn. we support the legislative proposal as a bridging measure until the end of 2001, because we do not ignore the fact that, according to the figures communicated, 34 000 companies are involved as partners, creating over 1 300 joint ventures and 42 000 jobs. however, the deloitte & touche study reveals a number of serious shortcomings which need to be addressed. the commission has also been active in the development of the european union's financial instruments, including the european investment bank (eib) and the european investment fund (eif). management deficits and lack of coordination between the ecip unit and the scr also affected the commission's reputation, as did the unequal treatment of financial institutions. for example, the danish development bank holds 38% of the funds, while the spanish development bank only 23%. the commission has already taken a number of decisions on the basis of the commission's proposals, and i am sure that the commission will be able to take account of them in the future.
draft opinion of the consultative committee on foreign affairs. the commission is not the rapporteur, mr imbeni, has done an excellent job. there's no need to repeat anything. i would like to raise two questions and add to them. the first is of a very principled nature. humanitarian aid must be provided regardless of the causes of the disasters and other political objectives. the increasing politicization of the situation in recent years is unacceptable and ultimately inhuman. at the same time, however, it should be noted that the growing number of disasters is not simply a matter of natural events that cannot be controlled. the same cannot be said of wars in which humanitarian aid has to be provided by, for example, echo. the increase in natural disasters is clearly related to the fact that we are increasingly demanding the global ecological and biosphere. for example, the united nations intergovernmental panel on climate change (ipcc) has reported that man's influence on the global climate is already being felt. i am convinced that our approach to crisis management must therefore also have a socio-political dimension and be integrated into development policy and, for example, economic policy strategy. otherwise we will only be able to cure the consequences of our own policies, and the people of the countries of the south in particular will suffer from the disasters we have caused. the second problem is directly related and is of a very practical nature. i would appeal to the commission to link humanitarian aid more closely with development policy in terms of concepts, organization and operations, even if the problem of the scale just mentioned has not yet been solved. the commission already has approaches to this, but i think they need to be considerably strengthened and de-bureaucratized. i am convinced that the concept of development-oriented emergency aid, as the technical cooperation society is trying to practice it, is exemplary in this respect.

the council. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the european union, as our debate has just shown, is destined to be a full-fledged, influential and respected actor in international political life. our democratic values, our common desire to contribute to peace and security in the world, our history, guide us in this. the community's economic weight, its key role in development and its special links with a very large number of countries or groups of countries make this possible. finally, the instability of a rapidly changing world, right at the doorstep of the union, sometimes gives us a strong incentive to do so. the french presidency of the european council therefore intends to contribute, in continuity with the efforts made over the past few years, to promoting the union's presence in the world. i would like to briefly describe the four main objectives we have set ourselves. first, of course, to advance the process of enlargement of the union, the great task that awaits us in the coming years, and secondly, to promote the development of a european security and defence policy, which must help to make the union a major player in international life. we also want to encourage the development of strategic partnerships with our neighbours and with the major regional groups, which should enable the union to contribute to the emergence of a multipolar world, which is essential for the long-term stability of international relations. finally, the fourth objective is to improve the effectiveness of the european union's instruments, on the basis of a debate which the foreign ministers, on a proposal from the commission and in the presence of mr patten, have just had at the informal meeting held in evian on 2 and 3 september, that is to say on saturday and sunday. the first objective of the french presidency is to give a new impetus to the accession negotiations. the prospect of enlargement is indeed the essential question facing us europeans, the great challenge for the coming years. hence the insistence of the french presidency on the need to make the igc a success and to conclude a good treaty in nice, a nice treaty in nice, so as not to delay enlargement and to be able to welcome the first candidate countries into a union with more effective institutions. i would like to make a very brief comment here to express our somewhat worried attitude today and our feeling that it is time to move from a statement of somewhat static positions to genuine negotiation in order to reach compromises, otherwise the negotiations will have difficulty in forming and unforming themselves. i would like to return to the accession negotiations, to say that we will go as far as possible in their conduct, with the luxembourg six, of course, countries with which we intend to make progress in the negotiations on the most difficult chapters of the acquis. the six countries with which we are negotiating in helsinki also have to be included, and we intend to maintain the pace of the negotiations and, of course, taking into account the degree of preparation of each of them, to open a whole series of new chapters, 42 in all, ranging from 4 to 9 depending on the country. in general, our objective, in close consultation with the commission and commissioner verheugen, is to arrive at an overall view of the state of the negotiations in nice, in order to give effective guidance to the work of the next presidencies and to set the course for the conclusion of these negotiations. the various reports currently under consideration in our committees and the debate on enlargement scheduled for october will further feed our analysis. the main dates for our presidency will therefore be as follows: a ministerial negotiating session will take place with each of the 12 candidates, either on 21 november for some of them or on 5 december, preceded in the autumn by two meetings at ambassadorial level. as far as the fifteen are concerned, we will hold a policy debate at the general affairs council on 20 november on the basis of the overall report and the progress reports for each of the applicant countries, which the commission is to submit to the council at the beginning of november. it will be an opportunity to identify, with a view to the nice european council, the main difficulties to be solved, chapter by chapter, country by country, and to reflect on the continuation of the accession process on this basis. i would remind you that we will hold two european conferences, on 23 november in sochaux, at the level of the ministers for european affairs of the fifteen and the ministers of the candidate countries, and on 7 december in nice, at the level of the heads of state or government, at the opening of the biarritz summit. as you can see, we therefore want to give a strong impetus to the enlargement process. the union has indeed indicated in helsinki that it would be ready to welcome the first new members on 1 january 2003, once the ratification procedures for what we hope will be the future treaty of nice have been completed, but, as the heads of state and government stressed at the feira summit, the countries concerned must not only take up the acquis communautaire, but above all be able to implement and actually apply it. this is, of course, a very difficult task, and we know that it is difficult for the applicant countries, and the community is already playing its part in supporting the efforts of everyone. these efforts are essential if the enlargement process which has been launched is to be conducted in a serious and controlled manner and if the most advanced countries are to be able to join as quickly as possible. as far as turkey is concerned, and i should like to say a word about it, the recognition of its candidacy in helsinki was an important step, which my country, france, supported. the presidency will initiate work in the council with a view to adopting the accession partnership with the country and will continue the analytical examination of the acquis. it will also ensure that the union's financial assistance commitments are respected, with a view to establishing a single framework covering all the instruments of assistance to the country. it will in particular endeavour to enable the adoption of the regulation on the economic and social development of turkey. but it is clear that accession negotiations will not even be possible as long as turkey does not respect the copenhagen criteria, including the democratic criteria, whereas any progress in this direction will naturally favour the adoption of the measures i have just mentioned. we look forward to the adoption by your assembly of mr morillon's reports on these important matters. the second objective of the french presidency is to continue the development of the common european security and defence policy by implementing the decisions taken in helsinki and feira. the union now has the instruments it needs to conduct a common foreign policy. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the health of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one. our objective, as the crises in bosnia and, more recently, in kosovo have taught us, is to provide a comprehensive response to crises which today have many and extraordinarily complex dimensions, ethnic crises, of course, but also sociological, administrative, judicial, security and finally military crises. all these dimensions are present. this is the specific feature of the european response compared with other existing instruments, namely that it is capable of being global and of responding to all these dimensions. the french presidency is therefore taking part in an extremely ambitious project which will necessarily take several years. it intends to maintain the pace of work in order to enable the commitments made at feira to be kept at the nice european council, and the agenda is particularly busy. i repeat the three main themes: on capacity, the conference on engagement which we will be holding on 20 november will be an opportunity for the member states to specify their national contribution to the achievement of the overall objective defined in helsinki; the european union is not a military power, but a political one, and it is not a military power, but a political one. finally, we must implement the decisions taken at feira, with regard to relations with nato and with third countries for military crisis management and the continuation of the work begun on strengthening civilian instruments for crisis management. the third priority of the french presidency will be to develop the union's strategic partnerships with its neighbours and with the major regional groups. the priority within this priority is to strengthen relations with the union's neighbours, and particularly with the balkans, whose situation - as we know - remains a cause for concern. in order to show the importance which the union attaches to developing relations with a region of the balkans - which we wish to see peaceful and democratic - france has proposed to its partners that a summit be held in croatia on 24 november with the countries of the former yugoslavia which, at various stages, are the most advanced in their democratic development. it is a matter of accompanying the recent positive developments in several of these countries and of reminding the federal republic of yugoslavia that the door will also be open to it when it joins the movement and, to be more precise, when the conditions are met for it to join the movement. the development of the strategic partnership with russia and ukraine is another priority of the french presidency, which will host the eu-ukraine summit in paris in ten days' time and the eu-russia summit on 30 october. the framework for the french presidency's action vis-à-vis russia is set out in the conclusions adopted by the feira european council, which offered to support the efforts of president putin and the new russian government to modernise and reform their country. at the same time, the presidency will of course continue to give the greatest possible attention to the question of chechnya. the council also reiterated in july that only a political the meda programme at the ministerial meeting in marseille on 16 november and, if circumstances permit, at the summit which may then be held on 17 november, in order to define guidelines for giving a new impetus to euro-mediterranean cooperation. the presidency also intends to complete the work on the peace and stability charter. at this meeting, which is about the peace process, the union must play a major role in supporting the parties and the agreements they will conclude. the presidency is also working to implement the common mediterranean strategy adopted in feira and to secure the adoption of the new meda regulation. as regards the association agreements, it hopes - as i have said - to achieve the signing of the agreement with egypt and substantial progress in the negotiations presence of mr patten, once again set about thinking about improving the effectiveness of the union's instruments. the union - as i have said - has many instruments at its disposal to influence the development of international relations. the european union's diplomatic presence in the world, that of the fifteen, but also that of the commission, is unrivalled, both in terms of numbers and financial resources, are considerable. however, everyone knows the weaknesses of the union's external action: lack of visibility, sometimes insufficient coordination, a lack of flexibility, and too little influence in international institutions, particularly bretton woods. efforts have already been made to address these shortcomings, in particular by adopting the first common strategies. but the countries must be strengthened by a greater decentralisation in the management of community programmes and by better coordination of the community's action with that of its member states. at central externally and, to this end, that synthetic tools be available which integrate all the dimensions of external aid. it is also necessary to improve the management of community aid by improving the programming and implementation of community instruments, in view of the observation made by the commission and shared by the member states of the unacceptable gap between commitments and disbursements commission. – i very much welcome this opportunity to speak to the european parliament just a couple of days after the informal meeting of foreign ministers in evian, at which there was a serious discussion on the effectiveness and efficiency of the european union's external activities and the budgetary consequences, the first time to my knowledge that such a discussion has taken place. i want to congratulate the french presidency without reservation on the priority that they have given to this extremely important practical issue. i want to respond to the motion for a resolution, not least since i suspect that in it are the bones of the discussion that we will be having between the union's institutions on cfsp over the coming years. just before the summer break, as some members may have read in the newspapers, we discussed in the commission the demands, the constraints and priorities of the european union's external relations, our understanding of what should be the commission's external role and some of the problems we encounter in performing it. any such discussion should of course begin with the treaty. one of the five objectives of the european union, as set out in article 2 of the treaty, is that it should assert its identity on the international scene. that objective reflects a number of things. it reflects first of all the european union's political interests, including a growing role in the area of security, which the president-in-office referred to in his interesting remarks. it reflects our economic interests, trade and the external dimension of the single market, including our agricultural policy. the euro would also come under this heading. it reflects our responsibilities for external assistance which have grown exponentially in recent years. the european union and its member states now provide 55% of total international aid and two thirds of global non-refundable aid. it reflects our defensive external interests, issues such as drug trafficking, nuclear safety issues, environmental concerns and migration and last but not least relations with our near neighbours, including the whole process of enlargement, which in my view is the most important and challenging issue facing this generation of european politicians. it is worth remembering that less than 20 years ago relations with greece, spain and portugal were external affairs for the european community as it then was. our prime task in the european union's external relations is surely the projection of stability, both in our immediate neighbourhood and beyond. a more stable neighbourhood and a more stable world guarantee a more stable european union. the skills that the european union has brought to its own development are skills which offer an example and a model elsewhere in the world. we need to be more imaginative in drawing on our experience and using it beyond our shores. in discussing how the european commission can concentrate on this task, i want to be clear about the limits of our role. foreign policy is and will remain fundamentally a matter for national governments, in other words for member states. there are 15 foreign ministers in the european union today and there will be 15 for the foreseeable future. but it is equally important that the member states should acknowledge what you in european parliament and those working on the cfsp have long understood: that mere intergovernmentalism can be a recipe for weakness and mediocrity, for a european foreign policy of the lowest-common denominator. that is why the union chose to move on from political cooperation, why the treaty of amsterdam created the new high representative for cfsp and why there is an important role for the commission and for the european parliament in trying to make a common – i stress common not single – foreign and security policy more effective. the new structures, procedures and instruments of cfsp recognise the need to harness the strengths of the european community in the service of european foreign policy. it would be absurd to divorce european foreign policy from the institutions which have been given responsibility for most of the instruments for its accomplishment, for external trade, external assistance, many of the external aspects of justice and home affairs and so on. that is why the commission participates fully in the decision-making process in the council, that is why we have a shared right of initiative – not a sole but a shared right of initiative – in these issues. there needs to be a sensible and sensitive partnership in the external field between the institutions of the union, including the european parliament, and its member states. we should be engaged in a common effort to make sure that world's largest trading group also makes its presence felt politically. we have a real contribution to make and we must not be afraid to make it. another point i want to emphasise is that the commission is not seeking new powers or a new role, but we do want to be able to exercise the powers we already have under the treaty more effectively. i have every sympathy for european parliament's desire to do exactly the same. i am determined that the commission should make a coherent contribution to the external relations agenda. it is very easy in the external field, perhaps more than any other, to make grandiloquent statements about great issues such as peace in the middle east, a stable and productive relationship with russia, international development. but if these are to be transformed from aspiration into reality, we have to pull our collective european weight. what does that mean in practice for the commission? firstly it means better coordination between commissioners and directorates-general encouraging a habit of working together. i think we are starting to improve things. i chair the group of relex commissioners which meets regularly both formally and informally. we try to frame a single agenda to discuss the impact of what we are doing on other commissioners' areas of responsibility. i think it is fair to say that this has so far been successful and that we intend to continue in this spirit. we have managed to avoid the turf wars which i am told occasionally disfigured the harmony of previous commissions. secondly, we are feeling our way towards a new and more productive working relationship with the council and i hope with the european parliament. it was evident at evian with ministers this weekend. apart from the detailed foreign policy issues on our agenda like the situation in the middle east, we were looking at how we decide our overall annual priorities in external relations and how we apportion the budget. as i said before, when i made a presentation to the council on the budget and on our priorities in may it was the first time this had ever happened. earlier this year, as well as that presentation to foreign ministers, i hope that i gave the european parliament exactly the same candid presentation on our external relations budget. in the past commitments have simply built up from one budget exercise to the next, with almost no effort to pull things together into a coherent whole. we are now trying to create a more rational system in which we can all have a proper political discussion early in the process on what our priorities should actually be. that is important in the council and it is important in the parliament because you are the budgetary authority. we cannot spend more than you allow us to but in that case you should not ask us to do more than is possible and criticise us when we have to make judgments about priorities. however, i think we are in a much better position to make those judgments with political guidance from the council and parliament. thirdly, i am working with javier solana to create sensible structures and the right division of responsibilities between the commission and the high representative for the cfsp. the institutional relationship between the commission and the high representative is evolving, as is the precise role of the european parliament in the cfsp. but we have in this last year managed to develop a strong and sensible partnership and i think we can honestly claim that, whatever the difficulties, it is starting to make a difference, for instance, in the balkans where the challenge to the credibility of europe's foreign policy remains formidable. fourthly i am working to respond to new demands on the commission arising from the new security agenda. we have set up a new crisis management unit to help pull together the commission's contribution in that area, but i also want to adapt our structures so that we can have a greater input into aspects of external relations where traditional bilateral diplomacy has been less effective and where the commission has particular expertise which it should be able to deploy more effectively. one example is conflict prevention, which may involve issues that are not part of the normal diplomatic agenda. other examples are climate change, control of drug-trafficking, control of the other death industries, the creation of new civil structures including independent media and so on. these are the sort of issues on which i want to see the commission contributing its experience and resources. in the discussions we had in the g8 foreign ministers' meetings i was struck by the extent to which the foreign and security policy agenda is changing and bringing together disparate issues in which the community has almost unique competence, for example in the environmental field. we discussed yesterday mr galeote's excellent report on our external services and the importance of enhancing the effectiveness of what the european union does around the world. there was a lot of discussion about better coordination, better coordination between member states and all the institutions of the european union, which i know is a serious priority of the french presidency and one which i totally share. we have perhaps talked more openly about these issues in the last few months than ever before but now we have to put our rhetoric into practice and discharge our responsibilities.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. ladies and gentlemen, the european union faces many challenges, especially in the field of foreign and security policy. in recent years, considerable progress has been made, particularly with the cologne and helsinki decisions and the development of a european defence policy. we must see - and mr patten has expressed this - that we are carrying a large part of the world's foreign aid. but are we really well-positioned to meet these challenges? are the structures really appropriate? is it really that we are letting excellent people like patten and solana appear on the outside, or are we pushing them through increasingly false structures into an internal competition? it is true that the council wants to work as an executive in foreign, security and defence policy, but how can it do this with 27 foreign ministers at the same time if it sees itself as an executive de collectiv? all this leads to a situation which is ultimately intolerable! the european union has indeed largely communalised the instruments of foreign aid and trade policy, but unfortunately we do not have the chance to have this common policy promoted by the institution that is designed for this, because this leads to competitive situations with the foreign ministers who are not prepared to give up a bit of their powers de facto. the fact that you keep appointing new special representatives means that you are taking away the powers of the community institutions, the commission, without any real coordination. kosovo is an example of this: absolute chaos! we give most of the money, but nothing is really solved there, despite the best efforts of all involved, because the structures are not right. that's the problem with embarrassing ourselves. we should ensure - the agenda calls for the report (a5-0213/00) by mr bouwman, on behalf of the european parliament's delegation to the conciliation committee, on the joint text approved by the conciliation committee for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on port reception facilities for industrial waste and cargo residues (c5-0348/2000 - 1998/0249 (cod)).
- mr president, madam vice-president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. the epp group welcomes the outcome, with one reservation, because in the end the new directive is making progress on the protection of the seas and fair conditions in ports in the union. the importance of the directive lies first and foremost in the fact that it obliges all member states to ensure that port reception facilities are finally installed in all ports where they are needed within the next two years. furthermore, the masters shall be obliged to use these facilities. we hope that, by applying the principle of these two obligations, this will reduce the illegal dumping of marine litter into the sea, thus strengthening the protection of the marine environment and also improving the competitive situation between ports. i believe that the conciliation procedure was ultimately successful, because we were able to at least get the idea that ships must make a substantial contribution to the costs, regardless of the actual use of the facility. we would have preferred, as a parliament, to have got our demand for at least 90% to be 'essential' because that would have meant that parliament's demand had been met and there would have been no financial incentive to continue simply dumping marine litter into the sea. because you would have paid the cost anyway, so you could have used the facilities! but the council has not been able to get through to this system of no special fee. and we hope that the commission - if it is indeed the case that there is still dumping in the sea - will propose a change in the review in three years' time. but at any rate, madam vice-president, we are grateful to you for having set out in your statement - which is essential - at least a 30% threshold as the common opinion of the council and parliament, so to speak, and we are counting on the council to act on your statement. secondly, as my colleague has already said, we have achieved two further successes in the interests of the protection of the seas and the citizens of the european union. firstly, we have found that 25% of all merchant ships actually require inspection for proper disposal. marpol is nice, but not if it's just on the bookshelf! the only way to protect the sea is to actually check that the waste has been disposed of. secondly, we have also put pressure on the member states to fulfil their obligation to actually set up port reception facilities: we have insisted that member states have to introduce compensation schemes in the event that ships are unnecessarily stranded in ports simply because the disposal facilities are not available or are not sufficient. the ships must pay for this, but they are also protected. mr president, i would like to conclude by thanking the chairman of the committee, mr hatzidakis, and the rapporteur, mr bouwman, on behalf of the group of the european people's party, for the commitment and success of the negotiations.
thank you very much, mr. jarzembowski. i was surprised that mr piecyk did not wish to speak for three minutes.
- mr president, i would have been very surprised if you had not chaired this sitting again! it is a good day for the seas in europe and for you personally, mr president, because i know that you are an enthusiastic diver. if you can then dive in even cleaner waters in europe, we will all rejoice together. but the seas are the priority. i think we can congratulate each other today. we can congratulate the rapporteur, theo bouwman, and we can congratulate the delegation, because we have succeeded in improving a directive or a common position of the council in a number of important respects. it had been watered down, and i think that parliament has made clear rules - clear rules for everyone. firstly, it was said that all ports must have facilities for waste and cargo residues. that's a big step. secondly, all ships must pay, regardless of actual use. that is the very principle that is being reintroduced here. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. it's true that you can't be 100% satisfied with 30%. it's perfectly clear. nevertheless, the principle of a 'special fee-free system' with the 30% was introduced and fixed. of course it can be improved. but behind this principle, no one can be left behind. thirdly, everyone must inspect at least 25% of the vessels. i think we should also ask the member states to go beyond 25%. we should invite them to a competition to control more. we have often found that for ships in port -
