in writing. - (de) the partnership between the eu and the countries of the southern mediterranean has a number of positive elements. it should be pursued and even deepened. however, the report on the reform of the meda programme seems to me to be wrong in several respects. the european union is simply concluding free trade agreements with the southern mediterranean countries, which paradoxically lead to unilateral liberalization. the impact of such agreements is particularly negative for the most financially disadvantaged: existing free trade agreements have already demonstrated this. the report admits that this danger is real in the case of free trade agreements. otherwise, why describe and call for 'supportive measures' to mitigate the negative effects of free trade? if the dangers of the free trade strategy are acknowledged but the strategy is adhered to, the social, ecological and cultural components of the programme will never do more than repair and mitigate the damage - whereas they should be the guiding principle of such agreements. in addition, to be eligible for aid, meda countries must satisfy the bretton woods institutions (the imf, for example). even though the latter's programmes are known for their anti-social and purely liberalisation-oriented strategies. the aim of the euro-mediterranean partnership must be to address the imbalances between the regions north and south of the mediterranean, to improve the quality of life of individuals and to encourage convergence within the different regions. but if free trade is elevated to the status of a driving principle, the objectives are only facade and the winners are once again a small number of rich people. i also oppose the misuse of the euro-mediterranean partnership to prevent migration from these regions to the eu. for some time now, the european union has included the 'fight against illegal immigration' and the 'return' of 'illegal' refugees among the objectives not only of the conventions concluded with the mediterranean states but also of the agreements signed with one or more third countries. in this way, each agreement adds a new stone to the eu's fortress. this report is another example of the european policy of isolation towards migrants and refugees. the countries of the southern mediterranean are seen as the outposts of the fortress europe. they should ensure that 'unwanted' people do not end up in the eu. i wonder how europe intends to defend respect for human rights and individual freedom in the mediterranean partner countries if it does not even respect the rights of migrants, if it throws them into the illegal environment and if it wants to keep them away from europe at all costs, including murder. this report once again guarantees the free movement of goods, services and capital. once again, freedom and human rights are being trampled underfoot. that is why i voted against, despite some positive elements.

commission. – the european council of tampere of october 1999 called for the establishment of a european police college for the training of senior law enforcement officials which should start as a network of existing national training institutes. considerable progress has been achieved so far. the portuguese presidency submitted a draft council regulation at the end of june 2000. the french presidency aims at adding a council decision adopted by the end of this year. this would make it possible to meet the deadline of having the european police college in place by 2001, as mentioned in the commission's scoreboard on justice and home affairs. a number of member states are in favour of creating the european police college as a permanent network of national training institutes. other member states regard the current presidency proposal for a network as a temporary stage on the road to an institution at a fixed location. the commission has, from the beginning, insisted that the european police college will become a fixed institution after having functioned as a network for an initial period in line with the tampere conclusion. this has led to the draft regulation now containing the following approach. from january 2001 the european police college is set up as a network of national training institutes, a virtual academy. it will function in this form for three years. after that period a decision will be taken on the form in which to continue with the european police college. the commission continues to take the position, however, that the draft regulation should contain a clear obligation for the european police college to become a fixed institution after having functioned for a few years as a network.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i have to go. the report before us is parliament's opinion on a commission communication on the problem of undeclared work, which is also discussed under the term 'black labour'. the european level is dealing with this because this problem does not concern just one country, but all the member states. what's the point? the failure to declare employment causes considerable economic and social damage in the member states. health insurance, pension systems and the general public lose billions each year. the workers are not insured or protected in any way. the idea of a modern slave trade with fatal consequences for those involved is very clear. those who have a service provided to them by means of undeclared work have no guarantee or business rights. the people concerned believe that this is to their advantage, but it is to their own detriment and to that of the community. now, underground work is by its very nature and by its very definition difficult to record in all countries. long-term studies and estimates suggest that there are 28 million undocumented workers in total. the volume of undeclared work now represents 15% of the eu's gross national product. the sector as a whole is growing three times faster than the official economy. in this communication the commission is struggling to analyse and to take the necessary steps to curb undeclared work. parliament has worked long and hard on this problem and has identified a number of causes which have a multifaceted and reciprocal effect. in almost all the investigations, the reason given was that the tax and duty burden was too high. the committee lists other causes, however, such as poverty, dubious bidding, dumping prices linked to subcontractors, inflexible labour laws and poor administrative practices, as well as a marked decline in awareness of the illegality and illegality of undeclared work. however, the committee has taken different positions in drawing its conclusions, arising from a very different weighting of the causes. i still believe that the goal unites us, only the path separates us. the conclusions adopted by the committee at its last meeting call for an inventory, as accurate as possible, of the sectors and main groups of persons concerned, the involvement of the social partners in active measures to combat undeclared work, the inclusion of the issue in national employment programmes and the controls and sanctions for detecting undeclared work. the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has also adopted a been unsatisfactory, such as the posting of workers directive and the issue of professional domestic work, which is mainly carried out by women. i can only present a few important points in the report in writing. -the commission's communication entitled 'pricing as a policy instrument to promote the sustainable use of water resources' aims to achieve and harmonise the economic objectives set out in the water framework directive. the proposal to monitor compliance with the cost recovery principle through a price monitoring mechanism is aimed at eu countries where the water sector is still heavily subsidised by the state. in germany, the principle of cost recovery is already applied, and there is already control of abuse by the cartel office and administrative supervision. therefore, neither the water framework directive nor the commission's proposal on water pricing can be used to create additional control bodies in germany. similarly, the integration of environmental and resource costs into the price of water is aimed at those member states which are still overusing and polluting their water resources, which is not the case in germany where enormous efforts have already been made. the objectives set out in the framework directive in this respect cannot therefore be used to justify the introduction, for example in germany, of a national water or waste water tax. given the non-binding nature of the economic objectives of the water directive and the commission's communication, there is a concern that the countries actually targeted will at least slow down the implementation of these objectives. if the 'model pupil' germany takes particular paths, as is the case for the implementation of other directives, this would only further exacerbate the distortions of competition between national water management systems within the eu and would be in contradiction with the objective of the directive to create a single framework for the management of water resources in europe. germany must learn to implement the european objectives as the directive provides and not as the länder would like. once again, some member states will be left to implement the european water framework directive on their own.

the agenda calls for the report (a5-0225/00) by mr hernández mollar, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the portuguese republic's initiative for the adoption of a council decision establishing a secretariat for the joint data protection supervisory authorities established by the convention establishing a european police office (europol convention), the convention on the use of information technology in customs matters and the convention implementing the schengen agreement of 14 june 1995 on the gradual abolition of checks at common borders, signed by the governments of the benelux states, the federal republic of germany and the french republic (schengen convention) (7381/2000 - c5-0230/2000 - cns480).
the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i welcome any initiative that seeks to improve data protection for the citizens of the european union. the agreement on europol, schengen and customs cooperation, however, has serious problems. one of these is the lack of protection of data collected and processed in institutions. the fact that the proposed office must be independent of the institutions to be monitored, as the budget itself indicates, is self-evident to me. i cannot, however, agree with the report by mr hernández mollar. i wonder why the merger of the previous data protection officers into one office with a joint secretary-general should lead to better data protection, simply because there will certainly be savings in this area. the commission has also proposed that the data protection rules should be amended to take account of the new data protection rules. in the political field, i interpret the portuguese initiative and the report as another step towards better coordination between schengen and europol. the problems raised by the agreements mentioned go far beyond the lack of data protection. both europol and schengen are playing a major role in securing the fortress europe. fundamental human rights, such as the right to freedom of movement, the right to asylum or, in many cases, even the simple right to human dignity, are being violated, and this is supported and monitored by these institutions. i therefore cannot agree to any slight improvement which would in the end help to legitimize the institutions. i shall abstain, because i am critical of europol and schengen in general and because i believe that one secretary-general, rather than three, does not mean more data protection.

mr president, first of all i would like to thank mr skinner for his excellent report on this complex subject of safety and health at work, and also for his willingness to respond to important ideas put forward by the epp group. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he has not already said that. i don't like every point. the second reading requires some correction, but on the whole the epp group will accept it. in its present form it already takes account of the objections of small and mediumsized enterprises and requires expertise, of course only in the setting up of ladders and scaffolding as workplaces. as with all legislation, there are certainly national and regional phrases that can be laughed at, if the whole thing is even funny. i stopped laughing when i read the european statistics on accidents at work and i am still listening to them. i don't want to go into details. it's happened many times before. but i want to say something very basic. it's not just protective measures that cost money. the continuation of wage payments, sickness benefits, invalidity, widow's and orphan's pensions impose a high level of economic and social burden on the economy. the productivity of a moderate social policy is shown here. prevention is better, cheaper and more humane than social policy. don't wait until the child has fallen into the well to act, but prevent him from falling into the well! but subsidiarity, many say. this principle does not mean that europe must not act at all! i like the definition in quadragesimo anno best: subsidiarity in doubt, the preference for the smaller unit of life and for the social partnership solution over the state or i say this in addition also the eu system. but if the smaller unit cannot do its job in the interests of the greater good, the larger unit must step in. this is why european minimum standards were laid down in the eu treaties, especially in the 1980s, when europe was governed by christian democrats and conservatives; image of european development cooperation is out of proportion to the enormous contribution that the eu itself and its member states make to aid for the countries of the south. although the european union is by far the largest donor, its perception is unfairly far behind that of the major multilateral organizations such as the un and the world bank. some 60% of all aid comes from the european pot. complementarity, coherence and coordination are the infamous three cs around which the debate on european development cooperation therefore revolves. the european commission's cash crunch, which revealed a considerable amount of unspent funds, has reignited the reform debate. but theoretical treatises are not going to get us very far. nor should it be overlooked that there are achievements which should not be underestimated. the first thing to be changed is the practice, and this requires a certain amount of political will on the part of all concerned. let us take mozambique and the echo operation as an example. echo has already provided €750,000 for the most vulnerable people since the floods began in early february. since then, a further eur 9.65 million has been made available in emergency aid, and a further eur 21 million is to be used to finance the medium-term consequences. the member states also reacted quickly. the total aid from the european union and its member countries amounts to €85 million, while the un puts the global contribution at only €115 million, including european funds. what is missing are the three k's quoted above. coherence can only be achieved by aligning policies and measures. complementarity and coordination are important prerequisites for synergy effects. the parallelism of multilateral and bilateral development cooperation, services of the member states, which the council has to ensure. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the coordination of the activities of the european investment bank and the european contributors to development cooperation also have a right to be visibly reflected in operational practice and public perception. there are positive approaches to all this, but they must be developed the greatest obstacle to the satisfactory implementation of the three ks is the lack of political will on the part of the member states, which lack a genuine interest in effective, coordinated development cooperation, thus weakening the european image and preventing the optimisation of development policy opportunities, which is not least due to the member states themselves. the european capitals should learn that by strengthening the image of europe, they can also strengthen their own image.

process in asia and europe. the asem process is structured around three pillars: politics, economics and culture. the asem process has facilitated the asean+3 process, bringing north and south east asia even closer together. its structure of meetings between the ministers of finance, economy and foreign affairs, as well as summits, follow the asem model. in the union too we had and we have to learn how to manage effectively a process which aims to promote political dialogue in order to deepen the economic relationship between the two regions and to increase personal and cultural contacts. without an institutionalized secretariat, we have succeeded, despite some difficulties, in convincing our asian partners that we want to relate to them on equal terms, fleeing from a donor-beneficiary relationship and any postcolonial attitude. this approach is of particular importance in our efforts to consolidate, deepen and broaden the political dialogue. while our asian partners prefer to focus mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. the convention, with the applause of the courts of justice in luxembourg and strasbourg, has drawn up a draft charter of fundamental rights in a remarkably balanced way and has placed it in the hands of the council. what is the added value of this charter? first, it is the distillation of the basic stock of fundamental rights from more than 30 valid sources of law. secondly, transparency for citizens who now know their rights vis-à-vis those who apply and create european law, and transparency for those who do exactly that, create or apply european law. they too now have a clear view of the rights they must respect. thirdly, the convention has not stopped at the mere copying of old rights - this has even been acknowledged by the council of europe - but has taken up and formulated new threats to old rights: in crime, biotechnology, data protection and administration. the charter therefore guarantees greater protection than the european convention on human rights, and this must be said to all those who say the opposite here in the house, and it formulates political and social rights in a balanced way. it is the first declaration of human rights of the new millennium and the most modern charter of human rights available in the world. it makes people realise that the european union has always been a community of values. however, the eu has a lot to do to remain such. mr moscovici, i ask you, in all seriousness, to consider the following: if you want to go back to the cologne decision and think long and hard about whether this should be included in the treaties, what encouragement would those who disregard human rights get from our hesitation? it is true what mr barón crespo said: why waste time? the aim here is simply to make the law more visible.

in writing. - (de) the result of the vote in this house is that the objective of the directive, which was accepted and approved by all the speakers and the commission, has not been achieved. with the rejection of amendment no 3, the directive does regulate maximum values for length but does not harmonise maximum widths and heights for accessories such as ski boxes. however, it is even more decisive that the provisions on the testing of turning are not adapted to the current version - proven by practice since 1996 - of regulation no 36.03 of the economic commission for europe. rather, reference is made to directive 97/27/ec, which is based on an obsolete version of regulation 36.03 of the economic commission for europe and is currently being amended within the commission. this means that no adaptation to scientific and technical progress is necessary and that an old and impractical test method must be used. this will not allow rigid buses of 15 metres in length. in the hope that directive 96/53/ec will be adapted as quickly as possible to the amended directive 97/27/ec (if it is updated), i voted in favour of this report. i am astonished by the statement made by the commission representative after the debate that he would reject all the amendments with one exception. it shows that a debate is superfluous if the commission is not prepared or able to reconsider its position or to react to the arguments put forward.

in writing. - (de) the csu group in the european parliament welcomes the fact that this draft charter of fundamental rights brings together and makes visible the fundamental rights enjoyed by citizens vis-à-vis the eu bodies and institutions. however, the incorporation of this charter into union or european community law can only be approved if such incorporation is preceded by a clear description and delimitation of the eu's competences. the charter aims at comprehensive protection of fundamental rights and falls wholly or partly outside the eu's remit. we refuse to accept the fundamental rights enshrined in the charter without establishing the necessary powers and obligations of protection and action which fall to the eu. the csu group in the european parliament supports the horizontal provision which establishes that no new competence is created for the community and the union. other major shortcomings in certain areas of the charter, which should be addressed before the charter is proclaimed, are: · the charter should not be overburdened with detailed regulations and these should be left to secondary law. · there is no clear line in the field of social rights as regards rights of defence or rights of participation and protection. · the declaration on basic public services is the responsibility of the member states. · we are asking for the registration of a right of citizenship and protection against expulsion.

talking about substantial reforms and not just retouching one or another institution. however, we also know that in nice the maximum of what can be achieved will be less than the minimum of what is necessary. this means that we know that the reforms will and must continue after nice. but we do not want to see new, additional barriers to membership being erected in nice or afterwards. this means draft opinion of the consultative committee on agriculture and rural development. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. we know that the agricultural sector is one of the most difficult sectors to expand. but there is no need to worry; the committee on agriculture believes that if we use the pre-accession aid properly, we can do it. but there are a few things we need to be clear about: the structure of the applicant countries is so different, it cannot be more different. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. in the field of import-export, only hungary has a positive balance in agricultural trade with the eu-15. all the others import more agricultural products into their countries than they export to the union. this should give us cause for reflection, because many of our farmers are afraid that if unification comes, we will all go down because these are all well-established agricultural lands. it's not like that. the dangers are elsewhere. we in the committee on agriculture firmly believe that we are giving as much as possible to these countries and to the right places through the sapard funds in the pre-accession phase. we need reforestation in the positive sense of the structures, from slaughterhouses to dairies to processing. it is not reasonable for us to import the pig halves into the fifteen, to produce the added value here and then to send the finished products back to the shops in those countries. they're not gonna get up like that. everything we do now to start this process saves money later. it must also be clear - and this too should be discussed openly and honestly with the countries - that the common agricultural policy cannot be understood as meaning that it will be applied everywhere from the first day of membership without checking whether there are price losses in the individual product segments which must receive the same payments. this would be unfair to other structures in the union of fifteen. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. now, of course, we have the problem of transitional arrangements. in the veterinary and phytosanitary fields, these countries are asking for transitional periods of 10, 12, and sometimes 15 years. of course, that's not possible. and since that is not possible, it is important to do a lot now to make sure that wherever unavoidable transitional arrangements have to be created, they are as short as possible. it is better to take action now than to start a long debate five minutes before accession. all these purely agricultural matters should not blind us to the fact that in the agricultural sector in particular: if the institutional reforms are not properly regulated in our country before the first candidate countries join the eu, many things will not be regulated as we want them to be. it is not surprising, of course, that the committee on agriculture considers that the important sector of agriculture, which still needs almost half the budget - and will remain so for the most part - should be included in parliament's codecision. i say this with all the force of my committee to all the agricultural ministers of the member states, whatever their political views, because that is where the brakes are placed on those who do not want this. the future member states, our candidate countries, are entering a process of changing the eu's common agricultural policy. it would be a poor example of parliamentary democracy if they were to continue to be democratically excluded from the shaping of the future common agricultural policy in an area which is much more important to them than to most of our fifteen fellow countries. that is a very important point. i would add that at this stage of the intergovernmental conference it is necessary to say this clearly and distinctly to our member governments and above all to the ministers for agriculture. in some areas we will have conflict, we already have. it's about money. it is assumed that we did not want to give them the same blessings of the common agricultural policy in euros. that's not right. but justice does not mean that all things are done with the same yardstick. it means that everyone, depending on his situation in the candidate countries, will receive the same aid as those in the fifteen countries. and that does not mean that the same numerical sums have to be paid everywhere per hectare, per tonne and per head. that is not necessary, and we would actually be producing injustice. the bottom line is: do not panic, but the reforms must come to us, otherwise the integration of the agricultural sector will not work either.

i have to say that i am not in favour of this. - mr president, i have to go. article 13 of the amsterdam treaty is known as the sleeping giant. it is the basis for a europe-wide approach to anti-discrimination. my task was to deal with the employment and occupation framework directive, which will bring about major changes in business practice. the experience of the anti­discrimination act passed in the usa ten years ago gives a glimpse of what is to come for europe. it is therefore essential that the groups listed in article 13 are effectively protected against discrimination. at the same time, the legitimate interests of the workers must be taken into account. it is no wonder that the french presidency has made this issue one of its priorities. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a welcome one. all stakeholders must be involved. human resources can only be fully exploited when there is peace of mind. it is an economic and social gain. in companies, people are rejected for further training because they are too young or too old. older people are disadvantaged by being pushed out of the labour market or by having a higher age limit for recruitment. those who come from socially difficult families or neighbourhood structures or because they are disabled are often not accepted in job interviews. disabled people are rejected on the grounds that their sight is not suitable for customers or staff. the only intention behind this is to save costs on measures to accommodate the disabled. employers then claim that the employment of disabled people is what is known as unfair hardship. in the employment committee we have defined very precisely in article 2 (4) what are reasonable adjustments and also the circumstances in which companies cannot be charged costs, namely in the absence of size or turnover. i expressly share the wish of the disabled people's associations to create a separate directive. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the disabled are not excluded from the labour market. some important points in the regulation are: first, the burden of proof. article 9 of the draft directive provides that anyone who feels discriminated against, whether as a rejected applicant or as a dismissed person, may take legal action. he only has to go to a court or a competent authority to make it credible that there is discrimination. the defendant, on the other hand, must prove that he did not discriminate and must be able to document this. in order to avoid unreasonable logistical and financial burdens, especially for small and mediumsized enterprises, we advocate a limitation period of six to twelve months. secondly, the right to bring a class action. the commission's proposal that associations should only be able to take legal action if the parties concerned have agreed to it is to be welcomed. associations, organisations and legal persons with a right to bring actions should only be representatives of the interests of workers and of the groups protected by article 13. thirdly, the mediation body. in the event of disputes, independent mediation bodies shall be set up which shall take into account the interests of employers and employees alike. many problems can be solved internally before they become legal disputes. the majority of the employment committee wants these bodies to be set up in the eu member states and not as a central body at european level. fourthly, the involvement of the social partners. the social partners, as the main actors in the management of discrimination issues in the workplace, are best placed to develop practical solutions. and of course the ngos should be involved, but the autonomy of the social partners must never be in question. fifthly, religious communities, which is probably one of the most sensitive areas within our directive. question: can member states allow different treatment of religious and belief communities? i mean, yes! their indispensable contributions to society in social institutions such as kindergartens, hospitals, educational institutions are important. they see the danger of having to hire people who cannot identify with their values and beliefs. the employment committee agreed by a large majority to the compromise that different treatment does not constitute discrimination where religion and belief are essential requirements for the exercise of a profession. equal treatment and non-discrimination are fundamental principles of the eu. the vote tomorrow will show whether we can build bridges after the excellent cooperation of all the rapporteurs on the article - i can only name mrs swiebel as a deputy for all - and after the intensive discussions with the commission and the council presidency. the opportunity to persuade the commission and the council to adopt many of our recommendations is great.

the rapporteur. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i am grateful that we are still able to discuss today the proposal for a council directive amending directive 68/193/eec on the marketing of vegetative propagating material of vines, and i hope that tomorrow we will also be able to vote in favour of it. in terms of area, production and consumption, european viticulture is the world leader. in several member states, viticulture represents a particular and significant part of total agricultural production and in many regions this sector is the sole and decisive source of agricultural income. wine growing is often found in areas where other forms of agricultural activity would be difficult or impossible. the wine sector is a highly diverse sector with a long tradition and ancient cultures. the vineyard estate is the basis for optimal grape and wine production in terms of quality, quality and quantity, and it determines these factors for a period of 25-40 years. the vineyard is therefore of great importance and it is essential to guarantee optimum reliability in terms of quality and varietal purity. trade in and trade in vegetative propagating material of vines are so far regulated by directive 68/193/eec of 1968. the text of this directive contains various provisions which allow member states to derogate unilaterally from certain standards and the directive has been amended several times. i welcome the commission's draft amendment, which clearly summarises the necessary changes in a report, while also incorporating new changes resulting from new developments and findings. these include new types of propagating material from vines produced from green shoots or by in vitro propagation. the consolidation of the internal market which is now being sought is very welcome. it is urgently necessary to amend or repeal the old and obsolete provisions in order to remove existing or potential barriers to trade. i think that the french winegrower should be able to produce grapes for the german or italian market, and vice versa. the specific characteristics of wine production and its development, particularly in the technical and scientific fields, make it essential to lay down detailed technical rules. these will help to ensure the smooth functioning of the internal market and improve the marketing prospects, while protecting the legitimate interests of consumers and producers. the commission is to publish a community catalogue of varieties on the basis of the communications from the member states. this will bring greater security to european wine growers in trade. many amendments include a better definition of the term, such as the inclusion of the genotype. accompanying documents and controls are important and the commission must ensure that only one single document is required for each lot across europe. quality and healthy grapevine material is playing an increasingly important role. the report has been given a special edge in recent weeks. the commission proposes to create a legal basis which takes account of genetically modified varieties. the commission proposal refers to council directive 90/220 which is intended to regulate all genetically modified materials as a horizontal directive. we have created the same reference in the field of forestry and plantation. the fact that directive 90/220 is still under conciliation procedure should not prevent us from doing the same for vines as for forestry and planting material. all the amendments to directive 90/220 now being introduced in the conciliation procedure will later also affect vines. at present, no genetically modified grapevine material is on the market, but research is ongoing. whether the future will be favourable to the authorization of genetically modified vines or whether the wine producers and the wine industry will oppose it is not part of the directive today. i am sure that this will be discussed at length elsewhere. today's directive ensures that traditional grape varieties that have shaped the wine-growing regions are preserved and safeguarded. the traditional wine-growing sector is our strength in the european union and it is important to support it. i therefore ask that the report as it stands be approved by the house and that the european internal market can therefore also be used in the vineyard sector.

counsel. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to be back with you today to present to you - as the french presidency had promised on 3 october - the results of the informal european council in biarritz, to which you made, as always now, madam president, an appreciated contribution. as i said, the institutional reforms under discussion at the intergovernmental conference have taken up most of the time available, and i think that is a good thing, so i will start there. on the igc, work had progressed at ministerial level, before biarritz, as far as i think it was possible to do so, and this informal council has therefore arrived at the right time to confirm certain progress, to give guidelines for the final phase of work into which we have now entered. in biarritz we saw first of all, and i think this is fundamental, a general agreement on the need to reach an ambitious treaty in nice: this is what i have called the 'spirit of biarritz'; secondly, tangible progress on qualified majority voting and enhanced cooperation; finally, what i would call the opening of a substantive debate at the highest level on the two most delicate issues: the re-weighting of votes and the commission, which now allows us to really enter into negotiations on these two difficult points. i'll be more specific about qualified majority. there was a fairly broad agreement on more than half the items under discussion and, on the sensitive points, the way to possible solutions was outlined. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we have noted, and this is not insignificant, that there is a clear openness on cooperation in the fight against tax evasion. in the social field, i believe we should also be able to make progress, provided, however, that we do not touch on the principles underlying the various national social security systems, which leaves a certain margin of manoeuvre. in the field of external trade policy, progress will also be possible, but only if we find ways of giving special attention to the most sensitive issues and, moreover, prevent a misguided extension of community powers. in the area of justice and home affairs, i am optimistic about a solution for civil judicial cooperation. however, the issues of asylum, visas and immigration remain more delicate. finally, some difficulties remain, notably on non-discrimination and the environment. substantial progress has therefore been made, although some progress is to be welcomed. all the member states now agree on the usefulness of enhanced cooperation and the need to make the procedures for initiating it more flexible. they also agree that they must remain open, that there is no need to move towards a two-speed europe, that the institutional framework of the union must be respected and thus, in particular, the role of the commission and that of the european parliament; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. finally, in the field of foreign, security and defence policy, i believe that appropriate provisions will have to be sought to take account of the specificities of these issues. on the commission and the re-weighting of votes, two closely related political issues, the discussions showed agreement on the need to make the commission stronger and more efficient, but having said that, i admit that not much was said, because there is still a very clear division on the modalities. some advocate a definitive cap on the number of commissioners, with equal rotation between member states, others defend the one-state/one-commissioner formula, without always ruling out a profound reorganisation of the college. both approaches therefore remain on the table and will have to be assessed in terms of their ability to ensure that the general interest of the community is respected. the two well-known options for the weighting of votes also remain on the table: simple weighting, where a slight, very slight majority is confirmed, or double majority, but with different formulae, double simple or re-weighted majority or a form of "demographic fillet". it is clear that we will only be able to decide on these questions at the end of the negotiations; the commission will continue to work on the basis of proposals in order to prepare the final decision in nice. the work will now continue to nice, in a very intensive way, on the basis of the informal guidelines adopted by this european council. so we have a little less than 50 days left. in the meantime, the preparatory group met yesterday to work on qualified majority voting and enhanced cooperation on a very concrete basis. it also pursued its work on the amendment of article 7 of the treaty in accordance with the positive guidelines issued at biarritz. the preparatory group will play its full role until 19 november, the date of the next ministerial meeting. we will therefore have a total of six working sessions at ministerial level by nice, four of them in a restricted format, two in the form of a conclave, and we intend to take advantage of all these opportunities to keep the spirit of biarritz alive. finally, a word on a related but fundamental subject for the european parliament: the charter of fundamental rights, to tell you that the european council unanimously welcomed the quality of this text which could therefore be solemnly proclaimed in nice in the form in which it was transmitted to it by the convention. the question of its incorporation into the treaties was not dealt with at biarritz. it is clear, however, that the majority of states are not ready for it at the moment and i am convinced - this is not a wish, it is an impression - that it will probably only be formally put forward afterwards. i now turn to the international issues which were also very much present in biarritz. you all know the context in which this summit took place, with the situation in the middle east on the one hand and the change of regime in serbia on the other, which resulted in the arrival in biarritz of the new serbian president, mr kostunica. i'll be brief on the middle east. i would simply remind you that from the very beginning the european union called on the parties to do everything possible to put an end to the violence, to resume dialogue and to preserve the achievements of camp david, and the european council in biarritz called on both parties to hold a summit meeting. the union continued to make its voice heard, the voice of reason and appeasement, in sharm el-sheikh, where it was represented for the first time, i stress this, because i am not one of those who think that europe is weakening in the middle east, although it is gradually returning to it, through the voice of mr solana, high representative for the cfsp. unfortunately, we have since seen that the agreement reached in sharm el-sheikh has not been implemented and that tensions remain, to say the least, extremely high on both sides. the european union is therefore naturally following the situation with the greatest vigilance. we must recapture the spirit that presided over the oslo accords. this is the ambition of the presidency, of all the member states, of the high representative, of the commission and, finally, of your parliament. the second important event that marked biarritz, in a happier way, was the return of democracy to serbia and, even more so, the consequences of the created a radically new situation in the federal republic of yugoslavia, paving the way for the democratization of the country and, hopefully, for a wider reconciliation in that region of the balkans. the european union, true to its commitments, has been drawing the consequences of this political upheaval since the general affairs council of 9 october last, when it decided to lift the sanctions, including the oil embargo and the air embargo, which had been imposed on the federal republic of yugoslavia since 1998, with the exception of the sanctions against mr milosevic himself and his entourage. president kostuniça therefore accepted the invitation of the presidency to go to biarritz for a lunch with the heads of state and government. at the joint press conference with the french general affairs council also confirmed the union's willingness to contribute to the restoration of navigation on the danube and to participate actively in the modernization of the infrastructure of the federal republic of yugoslavia from a regional perspective. the european council in biarritz also decided to grant the federal republic of yugoslavia an initial emergency humanitarian aid of eur 200 million, without prejudice to an assessment of needs and the coordination of economic and financial assistance to the federal republic of yugoslavia, which will be entrusted jointly to the political perspective by proposing to conclude a stabilisation and association agreement along the lines of those currently being negotiated with the other countries in the region. it is precisely in conditions. in a few minutes, here are the main results of the european council in biarritz, which was, i say this with all sincerity, because i am convinced of it, very productive and therefore very useful for the union's progress, which we have of course yet to conclude.

and he himself has said this - largely agree with the concerns expressed by the member states in biarritz. first of all, mr president, i note your agreement with the reasons for relaxing this mechanism so that it can be really implemented in enlarged europe. i note your concern for respect for the institutional framework of the union and the need to devise an open system, as well as your wish to see the veto in the council abolished, all principles which were widely agreed upon in biarritz. i also understand your wish that what you call the 'institutional unity' of parliament or the commission should not be affected. we are all in agreement once again that the institutional framework of the union must be respected. it is not a question of withdrawing from the treaty or of questioning what exists. the fact remains that we are dealing with a special provision of an exceptional nature and necessarily somewhat specific in relation to ordinary law. i would like to stress that there is no question of using this mechanism to compensate for the fact that qualified majority voting has not been introduced in certain areas. the first objective of the intergovernmental conference is the qualified majority vote. nor is it a question of creating a europe to the letter. however, despite the clear guarantees that must surround enhanced cooperation, it is an exceptional type of cooperation. they will reflect the fact that at one point we were unable to agree on a further deepening of cooperation in a specific sector. it is therefore difficult to say that everything is happening exactly as if we were fifteen, forgive me for insisting on such an obviousness. so, while respecting the existing constitutional framework, it seems to me difficult - perhaps even two thirds - of the member states are not involved in such enhanced cooperation? what legitimacy would the vote of a majority of members of parliament from states not concerned by such enhanced cooperation have under these conditions? would that not be to reinstate, by a roundabout way, the veto which you yourselves wish to override? there is a real question of principle here, which is why we cannot - in my view - apply exactly the same rules as in the union in every case of enhanced cooperation, and all the more so in the very specific and delicate field of foreign, security and defence policy. i think we must bear in mind the particular situations to which this system must respond. it must not become the norm and it must be given real flexibility, while respecting certain principles. i now turn to the constitutionalization of the treaties. i could simply thank olivier and simply point out that there is a very low-level attack on president prodi in his text - he is speaking with humour, of course - or else i could point out that he did not quite say how he wanted the constitution to be achieved. fortunately, his report is here and the term constitution covers several requirements. first, the need to simplify and clarify the treaties. secondly, the need to establish a genuine reference text which clearly defines the union's values, principles and objectives and, finally, the need to allocate powers between the various decision-making levels within the union. this is a question which your assembly - and we must give it credit for that - asked very early on, when it was set up, in fact, in july 1999. it is a response to real needs, the ones i have just mentioned. but it is also true that we as the presidency must take account of the fact that the member states have indicated up to now that they are not yet ready to talk about the constitution, even though a distinguished list of political representatives have raised this issue. in fact, it is easy to see why the member states are not yet there. if a constitution can provide at least a partial answer to the questions i have raised, it is a project that goes much further. a constitution, by definition, is a fundamental act of immense political significance, in the best sense of the term. it cannot be seen as an exercise in editorial clarification or even in the allocation of responsibilities. it seems to me that a constitution goes far beyond that. it is precisely this future stage, the exact outlines of this european future, that we are not yet clear about. i believe that we will only be able to talk about the constitution and the way in which it is to be drafted when we know what we want to put in it. as you know, this requires us to make certain political choices, which go far beyond the three requirements set out above. i have noticed that, for example, the heads of state or government who have spoken on this term do not all have exactly the same meaning. i would like to return to the three questions i raised. first, the simplification of the treaties. yes, it is a laudable goal, and brilliant jurists have tried to do it. the european institute in florence in particular, at the commission's request - and i imagine michel barnier will speak about it - has done so with a result which i would call very honourable, despite the particularly arid nature of the exercise, but i do not feel that the authors of the report - to whom olivier duhamel refers - have been able to escape a form of contradiction between the objective of clarity and the objective of legal certainty. the treaty is not rewritten in a constant manner. that's understandable, you know. it is extremely difficult to rewrite treaties that have been negotiated, sometimes with a comma missing, as the next point in our discussion provides a striking example. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i am thinking, for example, of the equal presentation of the common policies adopted by the authors of the report, even though their respective weight is obviously very different and this translates into provisions of a very different nature. i shall not go any further, because we are not here - at any rate i am not here - to discuss the report of the florence institute. i also noted that your rapporteur proposed another formula which, if i understand correctly, would distinguish between provisions which would be part of a framework treaty and other provisions, in particular common policies, which would be part of an annexed protocol. what i want to suggest, whatever option is chosen, while being personally not only open to, but supportive of the idea of a constitution, is that this approach raises substantive questions. it is not a technical or trivial exercise and we must ask the fundamental questions first. secondly, the distribution of powers. a well-known and less often debated question. so far no conclusive results have been obtained, but this should not discourage us from resuming the work. the exercise is complex. we must be careful not to destroy what has been the community's identity from the beginning. this mixture, which varies from sector to sector but is always very subtle, of shared competence. an exercise must not lead to a change in the balance or to a retrogression in the name of the principle of subsidiarity, as some seem to wish. that is what i wanted to say at this point. i cannot go any further as the representative of the presidency-in-office, because, as you know, we have chosen to concentrate until december on the four main items on the agenda. we are aware that the other questions are still being asked. some members raised them. the commission and parliament are also concerned. they will probably be discussed very soon, at least for some of them. there will be nice, there will also be the conclusions of nice and therefore an after nice. it will not necessarily be in the form that your rapporteur would like, because - cooperation and mr duhamel's report both live up to the reputation of the committee on constitutional affairs. i would like to pay tribute to its members and to its president, mr napolitano. as regards the second report, mr duhamel, we welcome your report very much. it seems to us to provide an excellent starting point for the discussion on the constitutional work we will have to undertake immediately after nice. this reflection does not prevent me from saying at the outset that our duty here and now, for the success of the intergovernmental conference, is to concentrate all our energy and all our efforts, and we need to do so because we are far from the point, on the igc agenda as it stands, particularly as it is extended to enhanced cooperation. mr duhamel, you will probably agree in nice, open the door to enlargement, open the door to new and future reforms, but first open that door and that is the aim of this negotiation. but inevitably certain questions are being asked now, as you are doing with great force, and they must be asked in nice, even if they are not the subject of the discussions of the intergovernmental conference. i think that nice could announce the next steps in thinking about several themes which are linked. first, the reorganization of the treaties. i thank you for your positive reference to the work of the florence institute which we had commissioned, as i have noted mr moscovici's constructive approach to it. i would like to remind you, however, that we had asked for a report to be drafted as a single document, and that is what we were given to do, but naturally, once we have brought together in 93 articles what is currently scattered among several hundred articles and several treaties, we can work as a single document - as i believe the florence institute has done - but the legal interpretation of this new text is necessarily different. it is a good piece of work which forms a basis for the future exercise of reorganizing the treaties. that's the first point. secondly, the legal nature of the charter of fundamental rights, a question which, as the presidency has said, is unlikely to be resolved in nice. but we think, as many of you do, that this work cannot stop here and that perhaps article 6 will have to give legal force to this charter, and i will fight for that. thirdly, and finally, the possible clarification of the delimitation of competences within the union. i know that the report by olivier duhamel is essentially based on a broader perspective: that of constitutionalisation which would go far beyond the current institutional framework and whose outcome would be more long-term. but it seems to me, mr president, that it is necessary first of all to clarify the current legal and institutional situation, as your report also proposes as a first step: 'a reorganized treaty', as you say in paragraph 9 of your resolution. like you, mr duhamel, i believe that the european union must be given a clearer and simpler basic text. it is a necessary and possible task. it is not a question of changing the institutional framework established by the treaties, and it is certainly not a question of increasing the union's powers, but of making the construction of europe more readable. it is indeed essential for european democracy, the first reason for our being together, as you have said, that citizens should have access to a constitutional treaty, a text which, as vaclav havel hoped, all the children of europe could learn in school without much difficulty. the important work carried out by the european institute in florence at our request, to which i have referred, shows that it is legally possible to bring together all these essential elements in a single text comprising a small number of articles. the preparation of this basic text will provide an opportunity to answer other constitutional questions which will be raised in nice and which i have just mentioned: the legal nature of the charter and the clarification of powers. a reorganized treaty enriched with other constitutional elements, is it already a constitution, or should this expression be reserved, as you yourself recommend, mr duhamel, for a new fundamental text drawn up according to new methods? i am not afraid of the word 'constitution' and i think i used it before you, ladies and gentlemen, at the very beginning, when i was not yet officially a member of the european commission. i mentioned this work on the constitutionalisation of the treaties during my hearing before the european parliament, the hearing before the commission was inaugurated. i want to assure you of my personal availability, and even my passion, mr duhamel, which will be at least equal to yours to participate in this work. i also agree that in our work on this subject we should move as far as possible away from the references you yourself have rejected: those on the left are those of karl marx and those on the right, you said, those of joseph de maistre, although i would like to point out, in the case of the latter, that he had the quality of being a savant, even though i disagree with many of his writings. i would therefore like to express my readiness and that of the commission to work in the direction you wish, respecting the stages of this constitutionalisation work. in any case, ladies and gentlemen, one thing is clear and must remain clear: none of the issues we are discussing can be a prerequisite for the enlargement of the european union to the countries of central, eastern, baltic and mediterranean europe which are currently candidates. the commission does not encourage the convening of another intergovernmental conference before the first enlargement. the institutional reform necessary to enable this enlargement must be done now and there must be no leftovers from nice, certainly not from amsterdam. after that, there will be no more pre-conditions on our part. the conclusions of the nice european council could announce, in the sense you recommend, a mandate and a timetable for work on constitutional matters. i think again that any discussion after nice will have to be open to all, to the member states and to the candidate countries, in an appropriate form which we will have to define. finally, i believe that the commission, which has actively participated in the work on the charter and, as is its role, in the work on the institutional negotiations, will also have to contribute to the collective reflection after nice, which is clearly linked to another exercise we have undertaken on governance. i hope, ladies and gentlemen, that the commission, in liaison with the other institutions, will set the stage. it is prepared to do so by means of a report drawn up following nice on these questions of clarification of competences and simplification of the treaties, which could be available before the end of the period of ratification of the treaty of nice. as for the rest of the work, i should also like to say that the report you have presented, mr duhamel, contains many very interesting ideas. like you, the commission has been impressed by the quality and form of the work of the convention which drew up the charter of fundamental rights and i think that this method must not be left unchecked and that lessons must be learned from it.

the rapporteur. mr president, mr president-in-office, i should also like to welcome our commissioner, ladies and gentlemen. budget advice is almost always given under the heading 'money is not the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. the ecsc treaty expires in june 2002. that means that 2001 will be the last full annual budget, strongly support this proposal. however, the distribution of resources is not optimal in our eyes. we see that there is still room for change and we ask the commission to examine this. the main issue is the ratio of administrative expenditure. we are proposing a reduction in adjustment aid, research aid and social measures, which i shall go into in more detail. that is to say, we do not support the cuts in research. on the contrary, we believe that the research sector should be strengthened, particularly with regard to the applicant countries. the accession countries will double coal production, steel production will be increased considerably and we believe that we therefore urgently need a process of modernisation and restructuring. we must push it, we need research into environmentally friendly technologies. we propose that, once the ecsc treaty has expired and the funds have been transferred to the eu budget, the applicant countries should be allowed to participate in coal and steel research financed by the community, following the example of the socrates and leonardo programmes. we believe that this is an important proposal for the environmentally friendly modernisation of steel and coal production in europe, and also for the financing of these sectors and the conversion measures. the second point is to examine the relationship between social measures and adjustment aid. the council's proposal reduces social measures from eur 31 million to eur 29 million. we cannot understand that. we believe that structural adjustment aid is needed in this area. the employment rate has fallen from 15% to 5% since 1999, and we must respond to this. we are, however, of the opinion that the adjustment aid can be reduced. the adjustment aid has not been used up in recent years. in 1999, for example, only half of the appropriations allocated were actually used. the commission, on the other hand, intends to increase the ceiling for the whole period up to june 2002. we think this is absurd, since there will still be an operational budget in the second half of 2002, and we therefore want to review the relationship between adjustment aid and social aid. we also want an audit of administrative expenditure. parliament has been proposing cuts for a long time. in view of the reduction in ecsc activities, in view of the changeover, it is questionable whether the administrative budget at this level is really justified. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission is also proposing this, and we support it subsequently. each separate structure creates additional costs without added value, and we should rather form a specialist subcommittee within these bodies. we also propose that parliament should continue to be kept regularly informed. in a statement to parliament in 1973, the commission undertook to accept the binding nature of parliament's opinions on the ecsc. we expect that this commitment will be extended to the new structures.

draft opinion of the consultative committee on legal affairs and internal market. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us in the past. the european union is a community of law because european law is respected and enforced. the european court of justice is responsible for this. it has thus made a significant contribution to the success of the whole integration project over the last forty years. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption by the end of the year. we have 1 600 pending cases before the european court of justice, 120 000 pages of translations are still to be translated. the european court of justice has thus become a needle-punch for european legal certainty. the committee on legal affairs and the internal market has already been working on this issue at first reading, to help citizens to get back to their european rights and to ensure that the eu as a community of law is not discredited by delay. i am very grateful to the committee on budgets and the rapporteur for having agreed to this line of argument and for having supported our proposals. we are proposing again, in particular at the second reading, that 60 new posts be created at the european court of justice and that not only the posts be created but that the corresponding budgetary resources be made available. we also propose to use 3 million euro as an immediate measure to employ freelance translators. these measures are intended to restore full functioning to judicial control, to restore confidence in the eu's legal certainty and to consolidate the european union as a community of law.

commission. – as one or two honourable members may know, i had been due to attend, alongside javier solana and bodo hombach of the stability pact, the special summit of south-east european leaders in skopje today, which has been organised by president trajkovski to welcome yugoslavia back into the family of south-east european nations. but i told president trajkovski that much as i would have liked to have attended, i needed to be here in this parliament today, demonstrating democratic accountability in action. i have had several debates and it has been a pleasure to take part in them. but i am pleased to be able to report back to the house on my visit to yugoslavia yesterday and on monday. like many honourable members, i had long hoped for the chance to report on such a visit and on our efforts to build ties with a democratic belgrade. many of us have been surprised and inspired by the triumphant return of democracy to serbia in recent weeks. i guess we should not have been surprised that democracy always wins in the end. the european union made abundantly clear before the elections which took place just a month ago today that democratic change in yugoslavia would mean a radical shift in the european union's policy towards that country. what a difference a month can make. in the summer i reported to this house about a serbia that was an outcast among european nations, about the repression of the brave, independent media, about our support for the opposition. today, although it is early days, the opposition are in government and the independent media suddenly find that they are no longer embattled and alone but in the vanguard of a new effort to create a truly open and pluralistic media for the whole country. from the moment the people of serbia made their democratic will clear and from the moment they insisted it should be respected, the european union has been as good as its word. barely four days after the democratic transition on 5 october, european union foreign ministers announced the lifting of sanctions and the immediate repeal of the oil embargo and the flight ban. they announced the extension of the european reconstruction agency to serbia and montenegro. they underlined our willingness to press ahead with clearing the danube and to provide the resources to do so. they asked the commission to draw up proposals to extend our recently announced trade preferences for the balkans to the whole of yugoslavia. they expressed a wish for member states to re-establish or normalise diplomatic relations with yugoslavia at the earliest opportunity. they underlined the willingness of the european union to contribute to the institutional and economic rebuilding of the fry and they extended an invitation to president kostunica to attend the informal european council in biarritz and to participate in the regional summit that the presidency is organising and which is to be hosted by the croatian government in zagreb on 24 november. the day after the foreign ministers' meeting, foreign minister védrine representing the presidency, flew to belgrade to inform president kostunica in person of the measures decided by the european union to honour the promises it had made to the people of serbia during the election campaign. the same day, just five days after 5 october, a team of commission officials arrived in belgrade to discuss with president kostunica's advisers an urgent, short-term assistance package. later that week, the european commission proposed to the european council at biarritz that the budgetary authority, including this parliament, should approve an emergency package of assistance to serbia worth eur 200 million, 180 million of it mobilised from the emergency reserve. in the last few days, a team from our reconstruction agency has been in belgrade, working out in close partnership with president kostunica's team, and in particular with professor labus and the g17 group of economists, as well as with other donors, precisely what assistance we can deliver and how we can ensure it arrives on the ground in serbia as rapidly as possible in the next few weeks, given the onset of winter and given the upcoming serbian republic elections on 23 december. following these initial missions i went myself to belgrade on monday and yesterday afternoon i visited podgorica. in belgrade i met president kostunica and held a separate meeting with him and some 80 mayors from democratic municipalities. i visited the headquarters of the students' resistance movement, and met the brave independent journalist, marislav filipovic, jailed by milosevic for telling the truth and recently freed under president kostunica. i met with professor labus and his colleagues of the g17 group of economists and with colleagues from the world bank to discuss both short-term help and the longer but vital task of long-term reconstruction, especially institution building and building the rule of law. i met the mayor of belgrade and visited with him a belgrade school being renovated under the european commission's schools for democracy programme. i visited the independent media centre, a kind of haven for independent journalists which the european commission has helped to support; and gave an interview. i also visited the studio of the independent television and radio station, b92, which was harassed by milosevic and supported amongst others by the european commission and whose journalists, like other independent journalists, will deserve prominent and flattering mention when the history of the last few weeks in serbia comes to be written. they were infinitely braver than i have ever had to be. i also had important meetings with representatives of the democratic opposition of serbia and with ngos and representatives of civil society, including the impressive head of the civic democratic alliance, goran svilanovic. i briefed european union heads of mission before my departure to montenegro where i had meetings yesterday evening with president djukanovic and prime minister vujanovic. let me just say a word about my meeting with president kostunica and the emergency assistance package that we are finalising for serbia. i set out for president kostunica our determination to provide assistance to serbia as rapidly as possible. i was impressed by his commitment to democracy and made very much aware of the huge challenge he faces in consolidating democracy in serbia, especially in the run-up to the serbian elections. i made clear to him our willingness to be as helpful as possible. i applauded the approach he had taken at biarritz and during his recent visit to sarajevo, in particular his willingness to establish diplomatic relations with bosnia and herzegovina without delay. others will have seen the comments he made during a recent cbs interview. it seems to me that president kostunica has made an impressive start in formidably difficult circumstances that few of us predicted a few months ago. he deserves a certain amount of political elbow-room, as he tackles those problems and consolidates his position, and all the practical support we can muster. that is why we have moved fast to put together a large-scale emergency assistance programme for serbia. our priorities which have been drawn up, following close consultation with democratic leaders in belgrade, are to provide help, above all, with energy supplies as well as with medicines and possibly with food. as part of the same package we will extend country-wide our highly successful schools for democracy programme which for some months now has been providing basic improvements to schools in municipalities which were run by the opposition. now we will do that serbia-wide. we are going to launch a new programme called towns for democracy to provide basic municipal improvements and services and we are going to reinforce our support for the media and civil society in this critical phase. it is clear that serbia faces a formidably difficult winter, especially on the energy front. we are going to do everything we can to alleviate the problems but it will still be tough because milosevic has left serbia's new leaders with a spectacular shambles. on energy we are looking urgently to extend our energy for democracy programme across serbia. in particular we are envisaging shipping in diesel and heating fuel, both to keep the power plants running and to fuel district heating plants. we will operate mainly through the municipalities, as we did last year under our pioneering energy for democracy initiative. i had an extremely useful meeting with president kostunica and many of the mayors to discuss priorities. i hope i have made it clear what a formidable task we face. we will have to work with others and, despite our efforts, serbia faces a difficult period. but we are working flat out to get our help on the ground as rapidly as possible, which means from the second half of november. the people of serbia know that, from now on, they do not have to face the future alone but with the staunch support of the european union and the entire family of european democracies at their side. it was clear from my meetings with the mayors and others that expectations of the european union are very high. we must not disappoint them. i hope there will be rapid agreement in the commission and in the management committee on the programmes we have in mind so that deliveries can indeed start in the second half of november. the people of serbia will not understand if bureaucracy stands in their way and nor will i. we simply must get moving very fast indeed. let me make a further very important point: none of the assistance that i have described is at the expense of our efforts elsewhere in the region. i and, i believe, ministers in the general affairs council are acutely aware of the european union's obligations to croatia, to bosnia-herzegovina, to albania, to fyrom and to the people of kosovo and to montenegro. we are not going to relax our efforts elsewhere in the region. if anything, we are going to redouble them. that was one reason why i visited podgorica yesterday, my third visit since march and the first time i was able to fly in with a visa from belgrade. i discussed our considerable assistance programme with president djukanovic. we have given eur 55 million to montenegro this year in recognition of the pressure that montenegro was under from the milosevic regime and the brave democratic path that it has taken in the last three years. i informed the president and prime minister of our plans to extend the activities of the european reconstruction agency to montenegro and i informed them, in the light of the welcome democratic change in belgrade about our proposals to extend the full benefits of our recently implemented asymmetric trade measures for the region to montenegro as well as to serbia. this will be a big boost to montenegro's economy. i listened to the views of the prime minister and the president on recent developments and on relations between montenegro and serbia. i made clear to them and to the press that i had been impressed by president kostunica's commitment to democracy and the formidable challenge he faced in consolidating it. the european union was determined to do all it could to help, which was why we were putting together a substantial emergency package for this winter. speaking as a friend of montenegro, i said that when elected democratic leaders held out the hand of friendship it was very important to grasp it. i underlined my view that with milosevic gone, remaining problems should be resolved through a process of rational and calm dialogue displaying understanding of others' points of view, a certain generosity of spirit and a degree of patience. (these are attributes that have not always been widely available in the region in the last decade – i understate the point.) now a new generation of leaders was in power who want to do things differently, i concluded. let me just finish today by saying that this year began with democratic change in zagreb and this autumn we have seen much hoped-for democratic change take root in belgrade. there is still much to do. democracy, although i believe it to be irreversible, is still young and fragile in serbia. what we have now before us is the best prospect for a generation of building lasting peace and prosperity across the whole of south-east europe – the chance truly to draw a line under the traumas of the recent past and to look to the future, a future in europe. the european union is ready for that task and stands ready to do all in its power to deliver on the hopes of so many whose lives have been blighted by the horrors the milosevic regime inflicted inside and outside the borders of serbia. it is an enormous challenge, but this is the challenge for which all of us have been working for so long. now we have a duty to rise to it.
