commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has maintained a consistent position throughout its contacts with morocco, a position which reflects the mandate approved by the council in october 1999. it is now time to open a new phase in our relations with morocco, in a spirit which is best exemplified by our concrete proposals for the support that can be given to the growth and development of the moroccan fishing sector, in accordance with the priorities set by the moroccan government in its five-year plan. all the efforts we have made in recent months, whenever the parties concerned have held meetings at technical or political level, have essentially been concerned with the outlines of a new partnership in the fisheries sector, a partnership which must be mutually beneficial and well balanced. after mr fischler's last visit to morocco on 16 october, when he was received by his majesty king mohamed vi and had the opportunity to speak with the moroccan prime minister, mr youssoufi, and the minister for fisheries, substantial progress seems within our reach. the talks referred to above can be considered to have led to the effective launch of negotiations on the content of a new partnership in the fisheries sector. we agreed that the new form of cooperation thus established must take account of the interests of both parties and we noted that morocco considered the potential employment benefits of a new partnership to be an important element of our cooperation. the commission reiterated, on behalf of the community, its readiness to assist morocco in the development of the fisheries sector, but that the achievement of this objective should not lose sight of the european interests linked to the possibility of fishing in moroccan waters in a sustainable manner. we believe it is of the utmost importance that community fishermen resume their activities at a level compatible with the obligation to ensure sustainable resources. we have therefore reached a consensus to work towards a responsible partnership, after which morocco will present its views at a meeting which will take place, as you have pointed out, in brussels on 30 october, that is to say on monday. finally, i would like to stress that if the european union and morocco wish to cooperate in the future, flexibility is needed on both sides, because maximalist demands will not get us anywhere. it is clear that all our efforts are now focused on finding a fair agreement with morocco, but the commission, in consultation with the member states primarily concerned, is also considering what measures could be taken to help the sector in question in the event that there is no consensus on a new partnership. the commission is hopeful that a balanced partnership can be established with morocco. it stated that it was too early to foresee the exact nature of the measures that would be taken if the moroccan side adopted a negative attitude.

first brought before the court of justice in 1989. a history of almost 12 years of office reluctance, holding tactics, hopes, even personal distress, to placebos for those affected, to the tenacious defense of old rights against citizens who sought nothing but their good right. the case is that of the union citizen allué and coonan against the university of venice, the case of the union citizen allué also against the university of venice and the case of the union citizen david petri against the university of verona. the european court of justice has made its position clear. in three judgments the european court of justice has given legal aid to these citizens who, before the first of these judgments, were employed as lecturers in italian universities. the tenor of these judgments is clear: the rights of the persons concerned to freedom of movement for workers within the union and to freedom from discrimination on grounds of nationality were infringed by italy's failure to offer the lecturers the same conditions of employment and job security as italian nationals with corresponding teaching posts in universities. i'm afraid nothing has changed since the first verdict. the amendments to the law which followed in 1995 are still not able to guarantee full protection of the rights of teachers with teaching assignments. in the end, even the ombudsman came out in support of these citizens. but i don't know if this wordplay is accepted in all languages, in german you say "it makes a difference whether you are right or whether you get right". the legal affairs committee has taken a clear position on this matter, taking the side of citizens of the union whose rights are being restricted. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would like to mention only two examples of attempts at the last minute to improve parliament's position or even to reverse it in individual cases: the original recital h proposed by the legal affairs committee reads: whereas, during this long period, the union citizens concerned have suffered setbacks, stress and uncertainty after being involved in hundreds of court cases over 12 years in protracted and recurring disputes, and whereas the legitimate expectations that they will be able to pursue their profession with adequate career prospects have been disappointed. the commission has already made a number of proposals, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. the text would then read: whereas the persons concerned, who are citizens of the union, have been involved in lengthy and recurring disputes in hundreds of court proceedings over a period of 12 years and whereas their legitimate expectations have been disappointed. this is not only a marked difference in the german language. but i come to the more serious matter. amendment no 9 now proposes: 'whereas the italian government considers that it has fully complied with its obligations towards the lettori under law 236/95, which is in accordance with the principles of the treaty.' apart from the fact that this was not discussed in the legal affairs committee, we would argue here that the legal basis in italian law corresponds to the bases of the treaty, and the court of justice has said exactly the opposite! i think this is a very dangerous approach. if you think that these practices are legally correct and politically desirable, then you should act as a legislator and change the foundations, but if you want to use parliament counsel. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would first of all like to express the presidency's condolences to the european parliament on the disaster that occurred near salzburg, austria, and to say that we share the pain of the families of the victims in this very serious accident. i am particularly pleased to be here today to debate in depth this fine draft of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union before you adopt the final position of your assembly on this text. we have certainly already had two exchanges on this subject, the first on 3 october last, in the context of an oral question by the chairman of your constitutional committee, giorgio napolitano, and the second on 24 october, when i came to present the results of the informal european council of 13 and 14 october in biarritz, where the charter was precisely one of the main items on the agenda. but i do not think that the debate today is a repetition of what has been said. on the contrary, it is particularly important, since it is today that your assembly is going to decide whether, as the conclusions of the cologne council call for, it will proclaim this text, together with the council and the commission, at the european council in nice, which will be held in less than a month from now. this is clearly a major political decision and a new opportunity to show the european citizens the full extent of this initiative. as regards the position advocated by your constitutional committee, for which i would like to congratulate the rapporteurs mr duff and mr voggenhuber, i understand that they are calling on you to adopt the text of the charter as it stands and, therefore, to give your president a mandate to proclaim the charter in your name in nice, together with the presidents of the council and the commission. this position, as you know, is in line with that taken by the heads of state or government at the european council in biarritz, who themselves unanimously and unreservedly approved the charter, and i can therefore only invite you, on behalf of the council, to follow this position, perhaps giving you some reasons. the council presidency regards this charter as a double success. firstly, the method chosen was successful: the one-tiered convention, composed of members of the european parliament, the national parliaments, the european commission - and i take this opportunity to welcome the presence of mr vitorino, who brought all his expertise - and personal representatives of the heads of state and government, all under the enlightened presidency of mr roman herzog, former president of both the court of karlsruhe and the federal republic of germany. the diversity and quality of the members appointed has, i believe, been an undeniable factor of wealth. i also find the twofold concern of the convention to work in full transparency and in full interaction with citizens, particularly through the internet, equally remarkable. in the course of its work, it has thus, in a spirit of openness which has paid off, consulted the major european non-governmental organisations, the social partners of our continent and, which is also important for the future, the candidate countries. this transparency and openness has actively contributed to the progressive improvement of the various versions of the draft charter and has made it possible for the last one to be the right one. i know that the experience of the convention is already clearly emerging as one of the ways - i do not say the way, but one of the ways - that europe could now follow in order to be more transparent and more attentive to its citizens. members of your assembly, particularly in our previous debate, have already expressed the wish that we should be able to repeat this experience. i have no doubt that this opportunity will present itself. the second and main success is the result achieved by the convention. the charter is first of all - and this is rare enough to be emphasized, as i see particularly in the preparation of the igc - a clear and well-ordered document. by bringing together some fifty articles, making it a short text divided into six chapters, whose titles sound just right, perhaps a new motto for europe: dignity, freedom, equality, solidarity, citizenship, justice, it undeniably responds to the concerns of conciseness and clarity and therefore also to the concerns and expectations of our fellow citizens. the charter is then a very coherent text. its drafters were able to meet a double requirement which was not easy to satisfy: on the one hand, not to create a right ex nihilo and, on the other hand, to give an accurate, but evolving, dynamic picture of the extent of fundamental rights in force in the union. but i am convinced that the charter will be a success mainly because of the strength of its content. first of all, it clearly reaffirms the fundamental rights as they are essentially derived from the european convention on human rights. as such, the drafters of the charter were constantly concerned to avoid - as was also stated in the specifications - any risk of divergence of case law between the european court of human rights, responsible for compliance with the convention, and the court of justice of the european communities, in particular by adopting the wording of the council of europe convention when it appeared to be sufficiently complete. similarly, under the general provisions, article 52 (3) states that where the charter contains rights corresponding to rights guaranteed by the convention, 'their meaning and scope shall be the same as those conferred on them by the convention'. i sincerely believe that in this way the drafters have precisely limited as far as possible the risk of divergent case law between the luxembourg and strasbourg courts. moreover, as we have just celebrated the 50th anniversary of the european convention for the protection of human rights, i believe that we can trust the judges of the two courts to nourish and extend the dialogue they are already having, which is undoubtedly an insurance against any risk of a two-speed europe of human rights that some have mentioned. of course, the charter, which would otherwise have been a bit disappointing, does not simply reaffirm, or even update, pre-existing rights. it enshrines many new rights not contained in the convention, which correspond to the changes in our societies, whether it be the development of technologies, the emergence of new dependencies or the increasing complexity of our administrative and public systems. it is particularly important for citizens to know, for example, that the union prohibits all human cloning for reproductive purposes, or that it guarantees its citizens protection of personal data. finally, i am of course pleased that this text attaches importance to economic and social rights. france has made a strong plea for this aspect to be substantial, but this was also the wish of many other member states, the wish of the european parliament, the wish of many national parliamentarians, and the presidency of the council can only be pleased about this. it was a question of the innovative power and the driving force of the charter and of the consolidation of the european social model, to which we are so deeply attached. first of all, it is important to stress the importance of the inclusion of a chapter entitled 'solidarity'. i would therefore like to pay tribute again to the person behind this, i believe, president herzog. this value of solidarity is indeed the one that best sums up the european social model, which is the very essence of community construction. and it is this solidarity that the charter guarantees, through the right to free education, through the right of workers to be informed and consulted, through the right to negotiate and to take collective action, including strike action, even if it was not easy to put this into the text, but also through the right to protection against unjustified dismissal, the right to social protection and the prohibition of child labour. i would also stress article 23, which is particularly clear on equality between men and women, stating that equality must exist in all areas and that this principle does not preclude the use of arrangements providing for specific advantages for the underrepresented sex. in sum, i would say that this text is undeniably the greatest collective advance in the affirmation of social rights, both because of the importance of the rights enshrined in it and also because these rights are for the first time included in the same text as civil and political rights, which solemnly marks the indivisibility of the set of fundamental rights. it is true, however, that some criticism has been levelled at the content of the charter. some criticise the text as reflecting "the political choices of the promoters of a liberal europe". they criticise the 'obligation of consensus' as a way of adopting the charter within the convention. i quote the words of a recent appeal by some members of parliament, particularly from the european parliament, calling for a revision of the charter. on the method, i would like to point out that the convention itself has determined its rules of procedure, without anyone from outside forcing it to do so, and that the rule of consensus appears to be a particularly constructive way in a context as diverse as the convention was. i am sure that the members of the convention who will be speaking here will be able to confirm this. i think that this has certainly helped to produce a text which i believe is balanced and ambitious. the european trade union confederation, for its part, was able to complain about what it considered to be shortcomings, such as the absence of reference to the right to a minimum income, for example. i would therefore like to clarify certain points. the charter was intended, regrettably, and perhaps later, to bring together fundamental rights and not to constitute, at this stage, a social treaty, and the mandate of the convention, specified in the initial specifications, did not allow it to create entirely new social rights from scratch. i am sure there will be further steps along the way. the charter is not the only initiative of the french presidency of the union in the social field, quite the contrary. the presidency has placed the promotion of a more united europe at the heart of its priorities. as you know, the presidency, building on the conclusions of the lisbon council, has launched the initiative of a social agenda, which should make it possible to determine the actions that the european union will undertake in the coming years to take account of existing needs, in particular by ensuring a quantitative and qualitative improvement in employment, as well as greater social cohesion. these approaches - the charter on the one hand and the social agenda on the other - are complementary to me and reflect the desire to put the social dimension at the heart of our european construction. i would also like to point out that the presidency, and i believe the other institutions, have reasons for satisfaction with the overall position of the european trade union confederation, which stresses the link between the charter and the social agenda and which concludes by stating that the proposal for the convention, adopted by the heads of state and government, is an important step on the road to a social and citizens' europe. i think that is an important position and i welcome it. it is with this in mind that the heads of state and government have, for their part, if not adopted - this will be done in nice - at least approved the text of the charter. the balance struck by the drafters was welcomed by all and the presidency does not want to reopen the discussions, nor, i believe, do your rapporteurs. i now come to a question which we have already discussed, namely the legal value of the charter. i have heard your rapporteurs once again express the wish that the charter should be the preamble to a constitutional treaty, and i am known to be in favour of this. but i would remind you, because we have to be very precise in view of what is happening today, that the european council in biarritz could only note that a majority of the member states were not ready to discuss, at least for the time being, the incorporation of this charter into the treaties. i can therefore assure you that, since this question will not be formally put until after nice, the french presidency intends to ensure that this perspective is included in the conclusions of the nice european council. however, several prominent figures, including members of the european parliament, have proposed that an explicit reference to the charter of fundamental rights be inserted in article 6 of the treaty on european union, which already refers to the european convention on human rights. they have thus underlined what is in fact a paradox, namely a situation where the treaty does not mention a new text specific to the european union, whereas it already mentions an existing text which belongs to the council of europe. you know that i have personally expressed my openness and even my support for this proposal, and i repeat it here. but the presidency, again on the basis of its bilateral contacts, can only say that several member states do not want this. and i would also like to inform the european parliament that yesterday, at the initiative of the presidency, there was a discussion in the preparatory group on this matter, which informs me that the discussion was not completely conclusive, which means that perhaps some of the governments could take inspiration from a clear position taken by the european parliament as a whole. i am convinced that this text, by its clarity, its coherence and its content, will become the reference text that the union so badly needed. and so, on behalf of the presidency of the council, i can only encourage you once again to adopt the charter of fundamental rights with a view to its joint and solemn proclamation in nice. i am convinced that this will be one of the important moments of this european council concluding the french presidency. (applause) i would like to thank
the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. one of the main tasks of the directly elected members of the european parliament, who represent the 370 million citizens of the european union, is to bring europe, the work of european unification, closer to the people. it was therefore right and important that the european parliament attached great importance to the drafting of a charter of fundamental rights of the european union and that it cooperated intensively and constructively in its creation. it was a great success for us as a parliament - and here the political groups came together, that is a positive result - that we succeeded in having the european parliament represented by 16 members in this convention on fundamental rights. the result now before us also charter of fundamental rights. the charter of fundamental rights has emerged from a variety of european and national sources of law. it is committed to the spiritual, religious and moral heritage of our continent and to the indivisible and universal values of human dignity, freedom, equality and solidarity. the charter presented is based on the principles of democracy and the rule of law. by putting the person, the human person, at the centre of the charter, by establishing citizenship of the union and an area of freedom, security and justice, it creates full transparency. citizens are clearly informed of their fundamental rights. the institutions, bodies and agencies of the european union are made aware of the legal positions they must take into account and respect when acting on behalf of the people of europe. the present charter is, in my view, a great achievement and, as a major european newspaper headlined it on 26 september 2000, it can become the calling card for europe. i have already pointed out in the plenary debate on the eu summit in biarritz on 3 october this year, and in connection with the discussion on the further treatment of the charter, that the future of the european union is now at stake. we are pleased to entrust you, madam president, with the task of proclaiming the charter together with the president of the european council and the president of the european commission at the eu summit in nice in a few weeks' time. but this solemn act in nice can only be an intermediate step in our view. the european union is now much more than an economic community. if we, as the representatives and guardians of the citizens of the european union and of europe as a whole, wish to pursue the unification of our continent with greater ambition and commitment, then the solemn proclamation can only be a first step. we, the european people's party, are united and unanimous in our support for the charter of fundamental rights to be incorporated into the treaties as soon as possible, so that it can also become directly binding on the people of the european union. i have to say, madam president, the charter of fundamental rights is a very important political project for the future of european integration, and i support it. why would you do that? firstly, it guarantees the rights of citizens vis-à-vis the institutions and bodies of the european union. secondly, it fills a gap in the protection of fundamental rights for people living in the union. thirdly, the charter also ensures the existing level of protection of the european convention on human rights in the union, and in some cases even goes beyond the european convention on human rights. fourthly, the charter - and this is particularly important to me - is based on the indivisibility of civil and political human rights and fundamental social rights. as a member of the convention i have been committed to even more extensive social rights, in particular the right to work and to a living wage, which should have been included in the existing social charter. however, i share the overall view of the european trade union confederation that, despite the narrow interpretation of social rights, the charter of fundamental rights is an important step towards promoting a social europe and a europe of citizens, and represents an added value compared to the current situation. madam president, i think what we need now, particularly with a view to nice, is a broad public debate with the citizens on the text of the charter, and we must also think about giving them the opportunity to vote in favour of this charter. i therefore personally support a europe-wide referendum on the charter, so that we can finally have democratic legitimacy for european construction by the citizens themselves.

marseille conference should reduce its ambitions. i am not saying, of course, that the current context will have no impact on this meeting. i am thinking in particular of the charter for peace and stability, which has been the subject of very thorough discussion among the 27 partners, but whose adoption is likely to call for a calmed regional environment. mr brok, who joined us, was asking view of the political context in the middle east. the main thing, i think, is that we continue the work and that this project is not abandoned. in this respect, i believe that the 27 partners are determined to adopt this text as soon as circumstances permit. let us not forget that the barcelona process is a recent one, only five years old. and when we started the partnership in 1995, we knew that we were embarking on a long-term project. it was not easy to bring together 27 partners from such different backgrounds overnight in a context of political tension, sometimes even more so, and in an original setting such as that of barcelona. we have also managed to maintain dialogue on sometimes sensitive subjects such as stability, terrorism, immigration and human rights. we intend to continue in this direction. this cooperation in political and security matters, the so-called 'first strand' of barcelona, is essential, even though we know that it is the most delicate and the longest to implement. but there are also other "wings" of barcelona, the economic and financial wing on the one hand, the social, cultural and human wing on the other. and this leads me to emphasize a fundamental principle of the union's mediterranean policy, and i will thus answer mr brok's question directly. i am talking about the overall process of parallel and balanced development of these three areas, which is the basis of the spirit and originality of barcelona and which we must preserve. and while it is true that the economic part of barcelona is the one which, despite its slowness, is performing best, the main thing is not to lose sight of this global aspect, without which the process would be condemned to being just one free trade area among others, without a political vision, without a human long-term vision, and that would be regrettable. our mediterranean partners are our immediate neighbours. we have much in common with them, a heritage, a history, a culture, exchanges, shared interests. finally, as mr brok has stressed, we have challenges to face together against racism, intolerance and xenophobia. there is also a great deal of scope for cooperation in the fight against trafficking in all its forms, migration and the strengthening of the rule of law. we europeans have experience to draw on. it is also in our interest to support our partners in their process of structural reforms, upgrading and opening up their economies to competition. the new impetus we want to give to the process in marseille will therefore have to be based on all its political and economic components, which are, as i have said, complementary and inextricably linked. it is true that barcelona is an ambitious partnership which requires means adapted to the objectives assigned to it. mr brok is talking about financial resources. of course, they will never be enough. the challenges are such, the needs of the countries of the south are so great that the union's resources will always seem insufficient, especially as the union's external commitments have increased extraordinarily in recent years. this is a debate which we have had on several occasions in the council, as you know, and which is at the heart of the reform initiated by commissioner patten. the council has, however, endeavoured, particularly since 1995, to provide the mediterranean with greater resources, in line with the challenges of the partnership. the french presidency had already been working on this since 1995, particularly at the european council in cannes, where we had succeeded in rebalancing the resources of mediterranean policy with those devoted to the countries of central and eastern europe. it is in this spirit that the meda i programme was launched with eur 3.4 billion committed between 1995 and 1999. the multiannual amount must now be fixed for 2000-06, and i can only hope - i cannot give a figure at this stage - that it will be commensurate with the union's mediterranean ambitions. you know that we are trying at this very moment to secure an agreement at the fifteen, if necessary by holding an extraordinary council meeting tomorrow in marseille. we have already reached agreement on the terms of the meda ii financial regulation. i believe that in the future we will have a more efficient, faster, more visible and therefore more credible instrument. the management of the programme will be simplified and the pace of repayments and disbursements will be accelerated. and then there are the eib loans which are essential for the development of the partner countries, particularly through its major infrastructure projects. i believe that with a multi-billion euro mandate for the mediterranean over the period 2000-07, we will be able to meet the expectations of our southern partners in the coming years, and this is essential. today, on the eve of marseille, the french presidency naturally wants to see this mediterranean priority of the union confirmed, including in financial terms. in reality, it is no longer just a question, as in 1995, of restoring a balance with eastern europe, but also of preparing for the future enlargement of the union. let us not forget that barcelona, like all the union's external relations, is an integral part of the community acquis and that the applicant countries should prepare themselves to see the mediterranean countries as privileged partners, because they are the privileged partners of our europe. this is a major challenge for the future of europe, whose centre of gravity will, it is true, shift to the east of the continent, but without contradiction with the south. this is all the more reason, in our view, for affirming the mediterranean dimension of the union, which wants to be a global player in the world and for which the mediterranean must remain, and will remain, a 'uniting sea', in latin a 'mare nostrum'.

commission. – mr president, let me engage in a bit of continent hopping. before reporting on the third asem summit and evaluating its results, let me briefly say a word about the asem process. the first summit in 1996 was at a time of huge optimism about asia when people were talking about the asian economic miracle. the second summit, in 1998, came at a time of economic crisis when many people were saying that asia had had it and all had been much exaggerated. we saw some reality at the third summit. there was not an asian economic miracle but a great deal that is very exciting has happened in asia and it has recovered very rapidly in most parts from the crisis of 1997/98. where it has done so most successfully, it has managed it by combining economic and political reform. that has been the background to these summits. the challenge for the third summit in seoul was to deepen the asem process both for governmental participants and for the broader public. it had to demonstrate that there need not be dramatic events occurring to justify meetings of european and asian heads of state or government. we outlined our goals for asem iii in our working party, we discussed it with the european parliament before the summit on two occasions in the asean working party and in the plenary which resulted, i believe, in your resolution of 5 october, the aims of which we not only took into account, but also managed to achieve in most cases. in addition to adopting three important documents, the leaders of the summit actively engaged in discussion of sensitive issues like human rights, the south china sea, east timor and burma. they pledged to promote and protect fundamental human rights and uphold respect for democracy, the rule of law, equality, justice and concern for the environment. it was agreed to intensify asem's high level political dialogue by drawing strength from the diversity of members while not excluding any issue. leaders agreed to an expanded and updated asia-europe cooperation framework 2000 which forms the work programme for the coming decade. the need for common efforts to implement the kyoto protocol was confirmed, a consumer-producer dialogue to stabilise world prices for oil was advocated as well as closer cooperation to develop energy saving technologies. trans-national crime was discussed, the exploitation of migrants, people trafficking, the fight against illegal drugs, all those issues which, alas, form the darkest side of globalisation. the summit adopted the separate seoul declaration for peace on the korean peninsula, welcoming the inter-korean summit in june, urging both sides to continue building on its success and underlining the importance of engaging the democratic people's republic of korea in multilateral dialogue. on enlargement, the two-key approach was adopted whereby a candidate country first needs the support of its regional partners before seeking endorsement from the other region. the final decision is made by consensus, by heads of state or government. no specific candidates were discussed at asem iii. in the field of economic and financial cooperation, leaders agreed to work together to address the challenges posed by globalisation, information technology, e-commerce and the digital divide by expanding research and information networks between the two regions. leaders also confirmed the preparation of voluntary annual reports on the status of efforts to overcome barriers to trade as identified under the trade facilitation action plan. there was an acceptance by all asem partners to work towards a new comprehensive wto round as soon as possible, taking into account the special needs of developing countries. in the social and cultural field, leaders recognised the vital importance of better educational links with specific initiatives for promoting mutual awareness, including an enhancement of inter-university cooperation and electronic networking between schools. in the related people-to-people field, the principle of opening the asem process to a larger segment of civil society was maintained, although the ngo initiative to establish a social forum could not be realised because of the resistance of certain asian partners. i am sure parliament can see these results are in line with the resolution of 5 october which i mentioned earlier. human rights and the rule of law are embedded in the process; there was a clear understanding of the need for the early start of a broad-based wto round but i am not sure that has been entirely reflected so far at the discussions at the apec meetings in brunei. while the proposal to establish a social forum was not accepted, we actively engaged with civil society and the ngos and i very much hope that this area will see further progress in the run-up to asem iv in copenhagen. finally, leaders agreed to encourage an intensification of contacts among parliamentarians as set out in the cooperation framework. inevitably, asem iii was dominated by the momentous developments on the korean peninsula which have resulted in the very worthy nomination for the nobel peace prize of the president of south korea, a man whose career has been distinguished, both by his commitment to democracy and human rights and the rule of law and, most recently, to his commitment to reconciliation between the south and north of the peninsula. i think that reminded us in europe of the important role that we have in asia, not just in economic and trade terms, though it has to be said that one of the reasons for asia's recovery has been that we have kept our word to keep our markets open to asian exports over the last two years. this year it seems very likely that china will have a surplus of eur 40 billion with the european union. we have kept our word in economic and commercial matters which, among other things, encourages asia to take us rather more seriously. it is important to remember that we also have a political role in asia, not just in our advocacy of democracy and good governance, but also in the contribution we can make in the korean peninsula and elsewhere to stability and security for the future. the asem process is an important one. this was a very valuable meeting. the process is developing and strengthening with time and i look forward to the next asem meeting in denmark in a couple of years' time when i am sure we will be able to build on the progress already achieved.

be able to accept them. the court reiterated that over 80% of the european budget is managed by the member states. the commission's proposal is not to hide behind the member states when it comes to political responsibility, but to give the european commission political responsibility for the implementation of the budget in accordance with the european treaty. but if the member states, for their part, are using this provision of the treaty as a shield to hide behind it and not take the necessary measures, then that is not acceptable either. i do not want to make a blanket argument. the financial protocols for the structural funds and the procedures for financial corrections in agricultural expenditure, for example, are common steps to improve controls. but i am really surprised that in the field of customs, for example, member states refuse to accept financial responsibility when their administrations make mistakes and thereby fail to collect customs duties, and then they do not take on this revenue loss, but all member states have to be jointly responsible for the revenue loss. the european parliament has been a very active participant in the debate on the future of the european union. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the court also makes clear in its report that errors found by the court do not constitute fraud and do not constitute budgetary damage. i do not mean to say that i am relieved of the burden, but i do so to clarify matters. the emphasis is naturally on the fact that the european commission's task is to avoid both formal errors and to combat fraud, especially since the question of how to define what is what and when is what is what is always raised. the european commission is therefore doing its utmost to tighten up the controls to protect the european taxpayer, to protect the european budget. the recent annual report on the protection of the community's financial interests and the annual report on the fight against fraud show this. olaf was established in 1999. new measures have been introduced to prevent fraud in the contracting sector, a very important area. now legislation has been introduced to combat money laundering, to combat the counterfeiting of the euro. cooperation agreements with third countries, and not least with the applicant countries, have been tightened up to ensure that fraud prevention does not stop at the eu's borders. last but not least, the commission's action in the us courts against tobacco companies for suspected involvement in cigarette smuggling has made it clear that the commission is not afraid of the big boys when it comes to fighting fraud. i would also like to mention in this context, and on the occasion of the date, that we have put forward a proposal for the intergovernmental conference in nice to amend the european treaty to include the establishment of a european public prosecutor's office to prosecute fraud against the community's financial interests. i very much hope that this proposal will not simply be put aside or swept under the carpet at the intergovernmental conference in nice, but that it will be seriously considered. but under the slogan 'we want our money back' we are also, of course, here and now, making financial corrections and recoveries. mr president of the court of auditors, you have announced that you will be making a special report, a special audit, on this, which i can only welcome. in the agricultural sector, some eur 600 million of financial corrections are made annually and, for example, some 2% of eligible areas are not paid as a penalty for often incorrect area figures, a problem area that the court of auditors has very clearly identified in its 1999 report. the court of auditors has increasingly started to draw up special reports. i would like to welcome this on behalf of the commission, because these special reports are very timely and can therefore be valuable for current decisions. i'm saying i can be. the commission is often not satisfied with simply listening to what the court of auditors says, but the council and parliament must also do so. i am referring specifically to the special report which has just been published on the sugar market regulation. the commission has proposed to extend the current market organization for two years only, with a view to a thorough revision. but unfortunately the council is saying that it is too early, that it must be extended for a longer period. i think that this shows that the observations made by the court of auditors in its examination of the past and the valuable information it provides for shaping the future must of course also be discussed together with the council. of course, timely audit reports should also be used to draw timely conclusions. this was the case, for example, with food aid to russia, which the court had examined in a report. at the end of last year, when it became clear that the humanitarian aid objectives could not be achieved with adequate control and monitoring measures, the commission decided to suspend the operation, although funds were still available. i would also like to mention briefly in this context that the improvement of external aid as a whole is an area of focus for the commission's work, both in terms of the institutional restructuring of this whole area and in terms of the need to increase and reduce the high legacy burdens in this area more rapidly than in the past. the commission has submitted a paper to the committee on budgets on this subject. the commission is on the right track with the reform. but we have not only chosen the right direction, we have also covered a significant part of the way. the 2001 budget, for example, was a milestone, the first time the commission had presented it in the form of an activity-based budgeting. the commission has re-arranged its priorities and the allocation of staff accordingly in the so-called peer group. the commission has strengthened the inspection capacities in the various directorates-general. it has set up an internal audit service to monitor the control systems in each department and a central financial service to assist all directorates-general, for example in drawing up contracts or in helping to implement the rules of the financial regulation. but we are now facing a difficult road, one in which we need the support of the european parliament, the council and also the court of auditors. this applies, for example, to the amendment of the disciplinary procedure, but it also applies, in particular, to the recasting of the financial regulation. mr president, you said that a lot of things are still on paper. the commission has already made a number of proposals. the court of auditors, for example, has undertaken to deliver its opinion on the proposal for the revision of the financial regulation very quickly, for which i am very grateful. i hope that parliament and the council will be inspired by the court's ambitious approach, so that this milestone in the reform will soon be no longer just a proposal but a legal instrument for improving budget implementation. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. a directive on general product safety has existed since 1992. the present debate should serve to revise the existing directive, to incorporate the experience we have gained and to eliminate any shortcomings. i doubt whether we have succeeded sufficiently. sure, there are some difficult legal issues. the scope of the directive must be defined in relation to the numerous national and community product regulations. the same safety aspects are also regulated there. it was necessary to ensure that we could ensure that consumer protection was fully guaranteed without, however, having to regulate things in a number of ways, or perhaps in a way that was contradictory. the possibility of having the conformity of a product certified by an external attestation would certainly be very helpful in this respect and would provide greater clarity and overview. it would have been better, however, to have introduced a general european regulation by means of a regulation and to have eliminated the overlap between european national provisions. in the food sector, for example, there are also many regulations which are currently being revised and reviewed by means of proposals for regulations, and i believe that this will enable us to achieve a high standard of safety. in other areas, this directive has been extended to cover other areas of application. the inclusion of service-related products will lead to an increase in the burden on trade and craft industries of obligations which are the responsibility of the manufacturer. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the rules are applied in a uniform manner. the export questions are two sentences. we are demanding very different safety standards and, like mr blokland, we are demanding that regional and national requirements be respected, and then we are exporting national provisions to other countries. i think there is a fundamental contradiction in the approach of the directive, which we cannot accept to the extent that it is proposed here.
commission. – first of all i wish to thank the rapporteur, mrs gonzález álvarez, the draftsmen, mr rübig and mr lehne, and the respective committees for their very comprehensive report on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on general product safety. the current commission proposal is in response to the numerous problems related to the health and safety of consumers which have occurred recently. although the review and revision of the directive are formally required by the directive itself, this coincides with the reinforced commitment by the commission to safeguard the health and safety of consumers. the revised directive will be of relevance for food safety for only a limited period of time but it will, in the long term, improve the possibilities for dealing with non-food product safety problems. i would only say a few words to present the main aspects of this proposal. the idea behind the directive is simple: that only safe products are placed on the market. this means european products as well as imported products. the two key objectives of the general products safety directive are: ensuring a high and consistent level of protection for consumer health and safety throughout europe and ensuring the proper functioning of the internal market. we had extensive consultations with stakeholders – as the rapporteur has acknowledged – on implementation of the present directive, which brought to light certain weaknesses which we are now trying to correct. we first clarify the scope of the directive. this directive is meant to provide good and consistent assurances of the safety of products for consumers. it is also meant to fill possible gaps in sectoral legislation, for instance, market surveillance or emergency procedures that are rarely provided for in specific legislation. however, it does not apply when specific sectoral legislation covering the same aspect applies. this also means that when new sectoral legislation is devised it supersedes the corresponding provisions of this directive. for example, in the foodstuffs area – as you well know – when we have a food authority, the authority itself should provide a notification system which will take over from the general product safety provisions. we wanted to make sure that the directive gave the best coverage possible to products used by consumers. this also means products which have migrated from the professional field to personal use: for instance, laser pointers; and, secondly, products which are used to provide a service. we wanted to have a more efficient system. this implies additional obligations for producers and distributors to provide information. the present situation is less than ideal. it is incredible, for example, that authorities in our member states are sometimes informed by the us authorities that a certain european product is dangerous. the notification is compulsory in the united states but not, so far, in the european union. as you know, law is no good if it is not applied properly. member states will now be required to strengthen the tasks of competent surveillance authorities. they will be required to establish sanctions. they will have to develop links with other member states as well; in particular, through a network of enforcement authorities of member states. this is also extremely important from an industry point of view in order to make sure that a level playing field is maintained between competitors and especially with imported products. improvement of rapex (the rapid alert system operated by the commission) is also necessary. the scope of rapex is extended to include voluntary measures taken by industry to withdraw a product. the practical operation of the system will be improved. we now also provide for the possibility of opening the system to third countries, in particular to the candidate countries: simplification of procedures for emergency measures at community level so that we can take rapid action following the advice of a regulatory committee. we have now introduced an export ban for products withdrawn at community level. another point to which i wish to draw your attention is the question of improved transparency. consumers often lack confidence because they do not know what is happening. nothing undermines consumer confidence more than a belief that something is going on that they do not know about. we believe that, in line with the general policy of the commission, citizens have the right to know which real dangers they are exposed to and the measures taken to prevent that. the limitation to this is professional secrecy as defined in article 287 of the treaty, except when there are overriding public health reasons. i expect that exception will be drawn and interpreted narrowly. i am very pleased that the report of mrs gonzález álvarez endorses the main principles of the commission proposal. many of the proposed amendments of the report are an improvement on the text and can therefore be accepted by the commission. allow me to address first the amendments with which the commission cannot agree. firstly, amendments nos 1, 8 and 18 propose to exempt second-hand goods sold by charity shops and non-profit organisations, private persons, flea markets and car boot sales, as mr whitehead has said, from the obligation to provide information and documentation on product risk and product origin. the obligations of distributors, which have been a part of the directive since 1992, are formulated in a very generic and flexible way. the only new requirement is that distributors, within the limits of their respective activities, are to safeguard and provide to the authorities on request the available documentation necessary for tracing the origin of products. this does not imply that distributors should actively inquire about the origin of a product, but just that they should not destroy identification of the product and/or manufacturer and keep trace of any useful information available on the product origin. this new requirement does not imply any substantial additional responsibility in the case of these kinds of shops. charity shops normally receive, as a gift, single used products which they in turn sell to consumers. the nature of their trade is such that they could not be required to play a proactive part in product tracing. in addition, the interest in terms of market surveillance of tracing the origin of single second-hand defective products is simply non-existent. in conclusion, there is already a lot of flexibility in the requirements of the directive on distributors. these requirements can be applied to these kinds of shops in a way compatible with the nature of their activities. however, to meet the concerns raised and in order to further clarify the situation we could consider including in the recital dealing with this article a statement that it may prove impossible to provide the competent authorities with information and documentation on the possible risks and origin of the product in the case of isolated used objects donated by private individuals. secondly, amendment no 3 proposes a deletion of part of the motivation for having clear conditions in the annex of the directive for the duty of business to inform the authorities about dangers. this motivation is needed in order to prevent excessive bureaucracy. thirdly, amendment no 4 proposes adding, in a preamble, a requirement that member states draw up factual reports with the cooperation of competent and independent public or private institutions. to require member states to engage external institutions for this runs counter to subsidiarity.amendments nos 6 and 29 require the commission to consider approaches or submit a proposal relating to the safety of services in amendment no 29 before a specified date. the commission is in fact already analysing and considering this issue, but it would go too far against the commission's right of initiative to introduce this in the directive in such a prescriptive way. amendment no 7 proposes certain changes in the references to paragraphs. the first part is acceptable to the commission, but it is not common practice in community legal texts to explain the content of articles referred to, as proposed. to replace the word "producer" with "supplier", as proposed in amendment no 11, would create more confusion than clarity, as there is no definition of supplier in the directive. the definition of producer already covers suppliers whose activities may affect the safety properties of the product. amendment no 13 proposes adding a reference to the precautionary principle in the general obligation for producers to place only safe products on the market. the precautionary principle is a general principle of risk management by the competent authorities and cannot be enforced as such as a direct obligation on producers. the commission does, however, share the view that the principle is important as a background for the revision of the directive, and a reference to this principle could therefore be made in the first recital of the directive. although the idea of publishing a full text of the european standards in the official journal, as proposed in amendments nos 14 and 16, is understandable, it would require fundamental changes in the relationship between the community and the european standardisation organisations, probably implying higher levels of subsidies from the community budget. the reason for this is that the standardisation organisations own the standards and that most of them finance part of their activities through the sale of the standards. this issue, with implications for most product-related community legislation, cannot, therefore, be dealt with in the context of the current revision of this directive. amendment no 19 proposes harmonisation of member states' monitoring approaches on the basis of guidelines prepared by the commission and the consultative committee. although the commission is in favour of cooperation and common principles, the proposed wording runs counter to subsidiarity. to require member states to take measures also in cases when business has already taken satisfactory measures to prevent a risk, which would be the consequence of the second part of amendment no 21, is not acceptable. this would also run counter to the objective of encouraging business to take proactive measures on its own initiative. amendment no 23 proposes the introduction in the directive of provisions on compensation in respect of damage. these are civil law aspects, regulated by the directive on product liability, and should not, therefore, be dealt with here. a requirement that the product safety network should be established within a specified time-frame is proposed in amendment no 24. although the commission is in favour of quickly establishing a network, this has to be agreed between the member states. it is therefore not realistic to set a time-frame. the first part of amendment no 27 proposes that only information related to the risks that have been established should be made available to the public. this is not acceptable, as consumers should also have a right to obtain information on on-going investigations – provided that this information is not covered by professional secrecy in the manner that i described earlier and drawn narrowly. finally, amendment no 28 proposes that the commission should submit a report on the implementation of the directive every second year instead of every three years. although the commission has sympathy for this idea, this cannot be done within the current limitations of the resources of the commission. the commission cannot agree with most of the additional amendments proposed for the plenary session. allow me to explain first the commission's position on the amendments to which we cannot agree. amendments nos 30, 32, 42 and the main part of amendment no 33 propose rewordings of the existing text of the directive which is not subject to revision. no problems have been reported to the commission with the existing wordings and the changes would weaken the provisions. amendment no 36 proposes that services directly associated with the product should be excluded except when provided by the original producer. the discussions in council go in the direction of dealing with the services within the definition of product which is, in fact, acceptable to us. amendment no 43 would totally exclude the application of this directive to products regulated by specific legislation. this is not acceptable, as these directives often lack provisions on market surveillance, notification systems and so on. a possibility of proving that a product conforms to the requirements through external certification is proposed in amendment no 37. such certification can always be used for providing evidence but cannot, in itself, be regarded as foolproof. amendment no 38 proposes limiting the time period for emergency decisions to six months which is, in most cases, not sufficient for adopting permanent measures. it also proposes an exemption from the export ban when the producer can show that the safety requirements of the receiving state are complied with. this is not acceptable as products judged at community level as posing serious risks and requiring rapid intervention should not be exported. the amendment also proposes that the possibilities for parties to submit their views on a community measure taken should be without prejudice to domestic remedies. as this is not any type of appeal procedure, this seems unnecessary. in addition, amendment no 41 proposes that the export ban should not apply when a product has been banned while carrying out further checks. this is a period during which there are real dangers of exports taking place. if the checks confirm that the product is safe, the ban will automatically be lifted. amendments nos 39 and 44 propose that information on dangerous products should only be available to the public once a banning or withdrawal decision has been issued and that exchange of information protected by professional secrecy should not be possible between market surveillance authorities. as the consumer should also have the right to information about risks not yet firmly established, including in cases when the measure taken is not a ban or withdrawal, this is not acceptable either. in addition, effective market surveillance cannot be carried out under the proposed limitations regarding confidential information. amendment no 40 proposes a deletion of the duty for business to notify the authorities about dangerous products they place on the market. that is not acceptable as this is a key improvement in comparison to the existing directive. still on the notification obligation, we believe that to use the term "ascertain" instead of "conclude" for triggering the moment when information is to be notified, as proposed in the first part of amendment no 34, will create more uncertainty than clarity. having extensively explained why the commission cannot accept amendments nos 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11, 13, 14, 16, 18, 19, 23, 24, 28 to 30, 32, 33, 36 to 43 and, in part, amendment no 7, the second part of amendment no 21 and the first part of amendments nos 27 and 34, i can inform you that the commission can accept amendments nos 2, 9, 10, 12, 15, 20, 22, 25, 26, 31 and 35 and, in part, amendment no 7, the first part of amendment no 21 and the second part of amendments nos 27 and 34, as these amendments constitute an improvement and clarification of the commission's proposal. in the case of some of these amendments, however, in particular amendments nos 2, 15, 22, 25, 31 and the second part of amendment no 27, further editorial changes might improve the text. to conclude, i wish to thank again mrs gonzález álvarez for the excellent report which can be supported by the commission to a large extent.

commission. - mr president, the commission has today adopted three recommendations for two council opinions on the updated stability programmes in germany, the netherlands and finland; they are the first to be presented updated from the 2000-20001 round. as you will recall, the stability and growth pact provides for increased and continuous monitoring of the budgetary position of the member states during the third stage of economic and monetary union. the central element of this monitoring process is the stability programmes, which euro area member states have to submit each year. the non-euro area countries present their convergence programmes, which are largely similar to stability programmes, although the objectives they seek to achieve are different. the medium-term strategies for public finances are included in the stability programmes. how can we achieve a budgetary position in the medium term close to balance with a surplus? the aim of this initiative, as you will recall, is to try to create the margin necessary to ensure that, in the event of a crisis, the government deficit does not exceed the budget deficit of the 3% of gdp reference value, which could of course be reached in a crisis phase. this means that we must take advantage of the upward phases of the cycle to bring the situation back into balance or surplus. in updating the programmes each year, member states include an additional year in the programme, analyse the budgetary policy implemented during the previous year, explain and describe the budgetary policy measures they have adopted and also revise their budgetary forecasts and objectives. this is the second time we have updated these programmes; we did so in 1999 and we are doing so again in 2000, including one more year. on the basis of the document submitted by the member states, the commission makes the appropriate assessment and, on the basis of this assessment, the council may adopt the recommendation submitted by the commission. it is true that in carrying out this process, the economic and financial committee pays special attention to the analysis of the commission's recommendation and the programmes themselves. within this framework, and in order to keep parliament informed, the commission considers it essential to also inform it of the state of play of the process. the commission also has the possibility, in the context of the regular annual budgetary evaluation procedure, of making recommendations - of a different nature - which may, where appropriate, highlight the non-compliance of some member states with the deficit situation. the use of this instrument for the coordination of economic policies has not been necessary so far; so far, budgetary compliance is functioning in accordance with the provisions of the stability and growth pact. more and more member states are reaching balanced or even clearly positive budgetary positions. this has led us to reflect on a different matter and to ask whether the stability and growth pact has been exhausted by the achievement of the quantitative target of a certain final figure, or whether other aspects relating to the quality of public finances should be introduced in the next programmes. the commission has opted for the latter option, and so let us now also assess in our annual assessment other aspects which we did not consider in the past: firstly, the budgetary policy orientation of each member state in relation to the cyclical situation in which it finds itself, that is to say, whether this type of budgetary measures are pro-cyclical or counter-cyclical and to what extent they help the market situation or create tension within it. secondly, we are also trying to assess the extent to which budget cuts, tax cuts are consistent, in accordance with a number of principles which can enable us to adopt a common position on this point. thirdly, we assess - and this is a very important question - to what extent there is a restructuring of public spending which is favourable to growth and production and which therefore avoids inflationary tensions in the future. finally, we assess the extent to which the national budgets presented each year are compatible with more ambitious medium-term strategies for public finances. in this respect, for example, problems such as the ageing of the population are becoming increasingly important. i would simply remind you that the last ecofin council asked the commission to include this long-term aspect of public finances, which relates to the ageing of the population, in the evaluation of the stability programmes from next year onwards. in the three programmes i shall now discuss, one of them, the one in the netherlands, already includes in an annex a specific analysis of this particular problem. i shall now turn very quickly to the three recently updated programmes. firstly, the three member states whose stability programmes the commission has examined today have made very significant progress towards the establishment of sound public finances since 1997, when they took their decisions to enter the single currency; in fact, finland already went into a budget surplus in 1998 and the netherlands did so in 1999. in its new programmes, which run until 2004, finland aims to maintain a budget surplus of more than 4% of gdp; the netherlands will achieve small surpluses, which could be higher depending on the growth path of its economy and some economic policy decisions still to be taken; germany is different: it will gradually move closer to overall balance. but in all three cases there is enough room to absorb the effect of fluctuations in the business cycle; in other words, in all three cases a crisis situation, if it should occur, could be dealt with within the 3% ceiling for budgetary imbalances. the three countries are proposing to introduce major tax cuts in 2001 and in subsequent years, tax cuts which will reduce the tax burden on labour and encourage employment and investment, so they are positive and necessary as long as the stability of public finances is maintained. in germany and the netherlands, the budgetary situation is expected to deteriorate next year as a result of these tax cuts. this is particularly important in the german case, as it represents a break in the path of gradual reduction of the public deficit. it is clear that one of our concerns with regard to the german programme is to insist that this change in trend is only a matter of one year, as a result of the reduction in these taxes, and has no future effects. in the case of the netherlands, the commission is concerned about other issues, such as the adequacy of the policy mix, and the risks associated with the fiscal stimulus effects of tax cuts in a context of strong economic growth, which could create a situation of overheating in the netherlands. our basic message is therefore that the margin for tax cuts must be complemented by strict control of public spending. germany and the netherlands have obtained substantial revenues from the sale of third generation mobile telephony licences this year. in the case of germany, for example, it represents 2.5% of gdp and in the case of the netherlands, 0.7% of gdp. both countries have very consistently made good use of these revenues by using them to reduce public debt. this, and in particular improved budget balances and stronger economic growth, will lead to a clear downward trend in government debt ratios over the coming years. this year, for example, germany is expected to fall to the 60% of gdp reference level and the netherlands to fall below that level in the same year. in the case of finland, the public debt situation is already well below this target and is also continuing to decline steadily. this debt trend leads to lower interest payments, which in turn will help to provide the necessary framework for tax cuts and, in some cases, specific increases in public expenditure. one of the positive features of the dutch programme is that it pays special attention - as i said earlier - to the impact of population ageing on public finances over the coming years. this is a problem which will also be raised to a greater or lesser extent in other member states, as was highlighted at the recent meetings of the eurogroup and the ecofin council. given that costs will increase in the future, some decisions will have to be taken shortly in order to contain them and ensure their long-term management. the dutch government will have to take important decisions on the use of its budgetary margins on the basis of its own programme and it would be appropriate for it to use these resources to accelerate the reduction of the public debt, which would allow it greater scope to deal with these problems in the future. the ambitious budget surplus targets of the finnish government are already motivated in large part by this ageing factor to which i have referred earlier. we also hope that the next update of germany's stability programme will pay more attention to this aspect, taking into account the impact of the pension reform being carried out. the commission welcomes the rapid submission of updated programmes by germany, the netherlands and finland. in the last two countries the programmes were adopted at the same time as the budget proposals for the next year, which in the commission's view is a more appropriate practice than the previous ones, when we knew about these updates after the presentation of the budgets of each country. this ensures that annual budgetary decisions are taken within a multiannual strategic framework and provides the community institutions with an up-to-date, global view, based on the latest data, of the economic situation in each country. the commission therefore recommends that the other member states which are still drawing up their updates follow this example, not this year, which unfortunately will not be possible, but in the years to come. these are the fundamental remarks i wanted to make on the three programmes we have presented today. i am at your disposal for any further comments, to hear your views and to answer, if necessary, your questions.
the commission has already done so. we are grateful to you, commissioner, for this report you have given us on the development of net new debt in the european union. i think that, on the whole, a positive conclusion can be drawn. when the maastricht treaty was created, it was assumed that the maximum new debt should be 3%. today, if you take the average of the eurozone, it has been reduced to a value of around 1%, and we are moving towards balanced budgets, which means that we are moving in the right direction. mr commissioner, are you not concerned that the situation in the federal republic of germany is such that this net new debt will rise by another half a percentage point next year instead of being reduced, and this despite the fact that the umts licences have brought a kind of warm rain to the federal republic's finances this year? we see this happening in the largest country in the eurozone, while in the netherlands and finland we have already achieved what we are asking for, namely surpluses to pay off the excessive debt. again, my question is, are you not concerned about this? i would like to stress once again that we in the european people's party consider the consistent application of the stability and growth factor, alongside the independence of the european central bank, to be one of the essential foundations of price stability in europe.
