commission. – madam president, i am glad of the opportunity to update you on the latest developments in the on-going crisis in relation to bse. i had already anticipated addressing you on the phillips report released earlier this month by the uk government. however, events in france over the past week clearly call for an earlier discussion of these events. only the dangerously complacent or naïve could assume that we have safely put the bse crisis behind us. once more we are reminded that bse is not an historic event, but a real and present danger. there has been a worrying increase in the number of cases of bse detected in france over the past year, in part due to the introduction of targeted testing. moreover, the marketing of beef from a herd found to be harbouring a clinical case of bse ignited public fears over the adequacy of controls to protect public health. clearly, we need to look at these developments and draw the appropriate lessons. that process must begin with a look at the facts. the current incidence in france is of the order of 7 cases per million cattle aged over two years. this falls far short of the international criterion of 100 cases per million used to define high incident countries. however, this relatively low incidence is no reason for complacency. the fact is that the incidence is rising in several member states. in the absence of clear and transparent evidence that the incidence of bse is falling in all member states, we must remain extremely vigilant. more importantly, we must learn from this latest experience. let me briefly outline my main observations in this respect. first, the increased incidence of bse in france is, in large part, due to the introduction of random testing by the french authorities. this follows from a commission decision requiring all member states to introduce such testing by 1 january 2001. all member states should follow the french example. second, the absolute necessity for the implementation of rigid controls on bse cannot be over-emphasised. the fact is that there is a battery of controls provided by legislation. if these controls are respected and implemented, the risk to the public is reduced to a minimum. i will return to this point later. third, we must have total transparency in our approach towards bse. the consumer reaction to bse has been variously described as a psychosis, irrational or driven by panic. a lack of clarity and transparency in addressing the issue has contributed hugely to this unfortunate situation. finally, we must not overlook the huge progress in recent years, in the past year in particular, in putting in place a framework to tackle bse. in the process, we have also begun the task of ensuring that eu systems are in place to avoid similar tragedies in the future. i was, frankly, disappointed that there was no acknowledgement in prime minister jospin's statement yesterday of the hugely positive role played by the community in recent years. inspired by this parliament, the commission has been the driving force in pressing for the adoption of measures to eradicate bse. and this was done notwithstanding the frequent lack of support in member states. this work is not complete. important proposals, for example, on animal waste and on transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, are currently before the council and parliament. the proposal adopted by the commission last week on the establishment of a european food authority is an even more significant initiative. we must not allow recent events to undermine this progress. i expect a strong endorsement of the commission's proposals on the food authority from the european council in nice – and i note what you, madam president, said on that issue only very recently. parliament can equally signal its commitment to the proposal by giving it the highest priority with a view to its adoption in the shortest possible time. returning to the issue in hand, the events of the past few weeks already call for a response. the commission view that targeted testing is essential in establishing a true picture of the real incidence of bse in the community has been fully vindicated by the test results in france. however, it is necessary to put in place such tests on a much larger scale. the public needs reassurance that the controls already in place are effective. extensive testing now appears to be the most effective means of providing such reassurance. the commission intends to put proposals to the agriculture council on monday next, which will fully answer public demands in this respect. the european parliament has been a consistent and strong supporter of such testing and i count on your support for the commission's approach. the implications of recent events for the community measures on meat-and-bone meal are also at issue. clearly, explanations are necessary for the increased incidence of bse, not only in france but also in other member states. time and again the finger of blame points in the direction of contaminated meat-and-bone meal. france decided, yesterday, to ban meat-and-bone meal on a provisional basis. i look forward to the forthcoming opinion of afssa, the french food safety agency, which will help inform the decision of the french authorities on whether this provisional measure needs to be continued. the evidence still strongly suggests that the increased incidence in some member states has its origin in the period before the introduction of reinforced controls in 1996 and subsequently. and it is certainly the case that the current controls are very strict. for instance: there is a ban on the feeding of mammalian meat-and-bone meal to ruminants, notably cattle. meat-and-bone meal must be processed, that is, pressure cooked, to very high standards. specified risk materials must be removed and destroyed. active surveillance measures, including random testing, are in progress to prevent cases of bse from entering the food and feed chains. however, these controls can only be effective if properly implemented. many inspections by the commission's food and veterinary office point to weaknesses in the implementation of these controls. in some cases, the follow-up to these reports in member states is not taken with the seriousness which it deserves. this, frankly, is unacceptable. it is unacceptable on public health grounds. it is also foolhardy, as the alternative to these controls leads towards an outright ban on meat-and-bone meal with the attendant huge financial and environmental consequences. public health and financial considerations, therefore, both argue for strict implementation. the commission, for its part, will continue to impress on member states the importance of this issue. the commission's food and veterinary office already affords top priority to member states' controls in relation to protective measures against bse. i am asking the food and veterinary office to carry out once more a fundamental and thorough inspection in the member states in this respect. for example, the requirement to remove and destroy srms only entered into force from 1 october 2000 and i want urgent on-the-ground confirmation that this requirement is being enforced. parliament's assistance in this respect would also be most welcome in alerting the public in the member states to the importance of these controls. moreover, there is currently a major proposal before parliament and the council for a regulation on animal waste. this proposal provides the opportunity for putting in place a comprehensive framework to ensure that all the relevant issues relating to animal waste are addressed. again, i hope to work with parliament in putting this proposal on the statute book as a matter of urgency. a number of speakers have raised the issue of a total ban on meat-and-bone meal. let me add a few comments on what i said earlier in this respect. in the situation confronting us it is always tempting to look to a magic solution, a solution which can, in one step, both eliminate risk and restore confidence. i have gone on record in stating that i will be fully transparent with consumers. this includes in my view the responsibility not to mislead them into believing that there are magic solutions to a very difficult problem. a total ban on meat-and-bone meal is an example of this. my only concern in relation to the use of meat-and-bone meal is whether it is safe or not to use in animal feed. i leave it to others to make the economic and environmental case for its continued use. in relation to its safety, let me repeat that there is an extensive range of controls already in place to ensure that mbm does not pose a threat of transmission of bse. it may be that mbm cannot be fed to ruminants and i have said this already. the scientific advice is that mbm produced under these conditions is not a danger. this parliament also accepts that there is a place for meat-and-bone meal produced under safe conditions. parliament acknowledged that in its report on bse in 1997 and i quote: "the recycling of carcasses and slaughter waste by the production of meat-and-bone meal for animal feed offers the best alternative on economic, environmental and health policy grounds". as i stated earlier, however, the safe use of meat-and-bone meal is conditional on the required controls being respected and implemented in full. if there is a weakness in the controls, clearly there is a problem. i am insisting, once more, that all member states accept their responsibilities in this respect. the commission's food and veterinary office will redouble its efforts to ensure that member states respect their obligations. i would add that if the french decision to ban meat-and-bone meal is motivated by fears over the adequacy of their controls it is a decision i fully endorse. i welcome in this respect that prime minister jospin yesterday also announced a substantial strengthening of controls on the food chain including a big increase in staff. i will be asking member states on monday if there are concerns that weaknesses in the implementation of controls over the past several years, in contravention of the community legislation in the matter, are a factor in the current increased incidence of bse. finally, madam president, i would add that the commission has recently presented a proposal to parliament under codecision for a regulation on animal waste. this proposal aims at putting in place a community framework which will address all relevant issues governing the treatment of animal waste, especially its use in animal feed. it is notable that in the discussions that have taken place already on this proposal with the member states, a ban on the feeding of meat-and-bone meal to animals has not been suggested as a necessary measure. by that i mean a total ban. instead, the consensus view is that the community must ensure that only material from animals fit for human consumption should be used in the production of meat-and-bone meal. it remains to be seen if this changes in the light of current events. let me recall, madam president, in this respect that i succeeded only five months ago in securing the council's agreement to a ban on the use of specified risk materials in the food and feed chains. yes, difficult as it may be to believe, it took four years to agree a measure which i consider to be fundamental to public health protection. the obstacles in securing support for a ban on meat-and-bone meal should be viewed in this light. let me assure you, however, that if and when i consider that a ban on the feeding of meat-and-bone meal to all animals is a necessary measure to protect public health, i will present such a proposal irrespective of the obstacles. parliament itself now has its opportunity to shape decisively the future direction of policy towards waste at community level. all options are open in this proposal on animal waste including a total ban, if thought necessary. i await your report and suggested amendments and assure you of my full cooperation for suggested improvements. the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the report under discussion today is, as i have just said, about the promotion of electricity from renewable sources in the internal electricity market. we are therefore in the first legislative procedure in the field of renewable energy. commissioner de palacio, i would like to thank you and the commission staff for bringing this legislative proposal to the table. the proposal for a directive is a logical consequence of the european union's strategy to double the share of renewable energy sources in energy consumption by 2010. the committee's report shows that we agree with the strategy set out in the draft, namely not to proceed with european harmonization of support systems but to leave it to the member states to orient the support system to national objectives. but, agreeing to the strategy does not necessarily mean agreeing to the detail. the committee's report proposes, in my view, important and necessary changes to the draft directive. first, however, a few preliminary remarks. it is about promoting renewable energy. this is a matter of the european parliament's own responsibility. in reality, the only reason why subsidy schemes are necessary for the production of electricity from, for example, solar, wind and biomass is that we are still directly or indirectly subsidizing other forms of energy. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. the promotion of renewable energy is therefore a compensation for the external costs of other sources of energy, a consideration of the positive environmental effects of this form of energy production and a compensation for existing distortions of competition. as long as the internalization of the external costs of fossil and nuclear energy is not carried out, as long as there is a subsidization of other energy sources, compensation schemes for renewable energy are necessary. the commission proposes that the member states should set indicative targets for the implementation of the directive. only when interim reports show that the targets are not being met in line with the overall strategy of the european union are binding targets set for the member states. we don't have that kind of time! we need to have binding targets now. the european union and all member states have made commitments in kyoto because of the dramatic nature of climate change. the european parliament has been a very active participant in the negotiations on the gatt agreement. renewable energy can undoubtedly make a significant contribution to achieving the binding greenhouse gas reduction targets set in kyoto. if the commitments made were serious, why not commit the instruments which will help to fulfil them, especially since i have, as the committee has confirmed, built a bridge to the council and the member states? the drafting of these binding national targets is to take place within one year, with the involvement of experts from the member states. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the second important change is that the commission is proposing a series of objectives for five years. if we define a clear, binding framework for the member states, the different systems which must meet these requirements should have a longer probationary period. after ten years, we can then very well judge which system is the most successful and the most efficient. we want to convince people in europe to switch to energy that nature provides every day, that does not cause environmental and climate damage, that makes a positive contribution to reducing co2. so there should be no controversy about what we mean by renewable energy sources. so, we don't want to have to seriously tell people in our regions that we are looking at household waste, which is a large proportion of plastic waste today, as a renewable energy source. should we not also ask them to produce more and more of this waste so that we can be sure of reaching our goals? i need not say that we would be discrediting ourselves and eu policy. i'm not against the incineration of waste. i would even call for a separate proposal for a directive in this respect in the report. no, i am opposed - as is the committee - to the use of fraudulent labelling in a law. you see, the draft report includes separate organic waste because it is part of it. you see, untreated wood and cork waste is considered a renewable energy source. even if hydropower is to be included in the support schemes only up to 10 megawatts, any hydropower is of course a renewable energy source and is taken into account in achieving the target. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the waste incineration system is not used for the production of waste. the committee also agreed that the problem of grid connection and access to renewable energy sources was another important point. the commission proposal to give priority to renewable energy access to the grid is not up for debate. i think there is a consensus here. the commission's general text on the question of cost sharing has, however, been clearly specified in the report. this is necessary because only clarification will create legal certainty and avoid disputes. these are the main points on which i wanted to comment today. i hope that tomorrow the house will take a step forward with this bill, with our opinion, and that you can tell us on behalf of the commission that you can accept our amendments and then the council can be the first to live up to its responsibilities! the commission is aware of the fact that the council has not yet adopted the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. this stable framework within which electricity generated from renewable energy sources can be developed significantly within the european union in the medium term, green electricity, and facilitate its mr president, one might ask why the european parliament is so concerned about vietnam. some might say that vietnam is very far from the european union. but i can tell you that in germany and bavaria, for example, vietnam is very close. if you drive across the border from bavaria to the neighbouring czech republic, you see vietnamese markets, you meet many vietnamese who are particularly active in the border region. if you go to the east of the reunified germany, you will find vietnamese who have found a home there within the framework of the communist bloc, and in the west there are vietnamese who have fled from that very communism and have come to germany as asylum seekers and refugees. this shows how closely we have long been a community of destiny in this eurasia. this is very clear when one considers the parallels in the history of europe and germany and also vietnam. germany and europe were divided. they were reunited ten years ago, under the banner of freedom. vietnam had suffered terrible wars, torn apart by the interests of the great powers. this vietnam was also reunited one day, but not peacefully, but by force of arms, and it was reunited under the sign of a communist system, under the sign of a dictatorship. now we have a situation in vietnam where economic reforms are being carried out. many people thought that this would automatically lead to political reforms. but we see in many countries in asia, including the last one discussed, burma - this is a parallel case - quite clearly that economic reform, trade and cooperation, as much as we welcome them, do not automatically lead to more freedom and more rule of law. in asia in particular, there is a danger that economic reforms will be disconnected from political reforms, that economic progress and economic liberalisation can take place without political liberalisation and without strengthening the rule of law, although i believe that without a functioning rule of law, trade, subsidies and investment are lost in the long run. that is why the economy also needs a rule of law framework. that is why it is so important that we clearly stand up for the rule of law, for the dismantling of the so-called re-education camps and, above all, for religious freedom. in vietnam this year a catholic monastery was confiscated, protestant minorities were persecuted, missions were closed and missionaries imprisoned, and the traditional buddhist church of vietnam was also brutally persecuted, although it was the one that had a great part to play in the national rebirth of vietnam. it is therefore our duty to speak for these political prisoners and to make clear our demands for democracy and the rule of law in all legitimate economic interests, and not to be blind to human rights, but to say that we, as the world's largest economic power, want to cooperate with vietnam and will do so, but only on the condition that democracy and the rule of law are increasingly respected there and that the overdue political reform process is finally put into motion. freedom of religion, freedom of conscience and freedom of the media are the crucial criteria we use to judge this.

disastrous human rights record is the best way to revive the relationship between the union and asean. given the importance which both they and we attach to this relationship, we hope that they will continue to convey our concerns - which, in our opinion, are shared by most of them - about the military regime. i believe that the eu-asean ministerial meeting should be used as another opportunity like to make the following point: it should be remembered that viet nam is a country in transition, that its government has initiated a process which led to the adoption in 1986 of a reform programme covering external relations and changes in economic and political matters. vietnam has since pursued an open-door foreign policy, which has given the country its rightful place in the sphere of our international relations. the process also led to the signing of the cooperation agreement between the commission and viet nam in 1995. during this period, viet nam has made progress towards a market economy, which has led in particular to its application for membership of the world trade organisation. in addition, and i think it is worth pointing out today, under the new constitution adopted in 1992, viet nam has an elected national parliament, which is responsible for enacting legislation and to which the government is accountable for its policies. according to our information, parliamentarians rigorously perform their role of examining legislative proposals and monitoring government policies and initiatives. i think it is important to recognize these advances and the context in which viet nam is still advancing; it is obvious, therefore, that things have been done but it is also, as you have pointed out, that much more remains to be done. i fully share the concern about the problems raised by some members: while it is true that almost 23 000 people have already been released under general amnesties, we must remain concerned about those who continue to be detained for their political or religious views. it is satisfactory that there is no official censorship in the vietnamese press, but it is also absolutely clear that there is occasional censorship in the foreign press. there are also clear pressures from the vietnamese authorities to have their own press self-censorship regime. moreover, although the recent reduction in the number of crimes punishable by the death penalty is a positive development, it is clear that, from our point of view, the death penalty must be abolished completely. the circumstances surrounding the execution earlier this year of a vietnamese canadian citizen certainly support our convictions in this regard. the commission is involved, with the member states, in all the initiatives taken by the union to the government of viet nam with regard to human rights and i can assure you that in this process we will continue to raise concrete problems and specific cases and encourage the continuous improvement of the human rights situation in viet nam.

the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the effects of climate change, and that the commission has already taken action to combat the effects of the floods. on the first point, i would like to point out that we attach great importance, as does parliament, to the problem of climate change and to the conference currently taking place in the hague. we have taken an active part in its preparation and have stressed that the union must take a strong lead in it. we agree with some of the statements made above that in this way we will contribute to the protection of environmental integrity and the credibility of the environmental protocols, with a view to their ratification in 2002. we are aware that the global destabilisation of the climate caused by the accumulation of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere will be the most important challenge in the energy sector in europe. the energy and transport sectors produce 85% of total greenhouse gas emissions in the union. therefore, it is these industries that must make the greatest effort to reduce emissions. the transport sector, with its projected continued growth of over 38% over the next decade, will be the one most in need of action. on this basis, the commission will shortly propose two strategic documents: a set of policies and measures to respond to the kyoto commitments and to the transport and energy objectives. the first will deal with the security of energy supply and the second with a revised common transport policy. but apart from the environmental problems, i would also like to comment on what we can do at this time. as you know, we have a fundamental difficulty: the legal basis for action. historically, as you know, there has been a budget line for emergency aid to populations in exceptional situations. this line was removed from the budget some time ago on the grounds that these were subsidiarity issues, which should not be dealt with at community level but at national level. the commission's room for manoeuvre is therefore very limited. the commission has taken two initiatives in this respect. a very clear one, relating to civil protection: on 27 september 2000 we presented a proposal for a council decision to strengthen the community instruments for coordinating the various civil protection systems at european level. this is going to be efficient in helping to solve problems, but it's not going to solve problems like the ones we're raising now. from there, what we are left with are the funding instruments that already exist. mrs ghilardotti raised the possibility of seeking funds. it's not so easy to get funding. the funds, as you know better than anyone, are well measured and there is no general surplus of funds, although there may be no budget execution in some specific cases. the fact is that if there is no legal basis for the use of these funds, it is very difficult to dispose of them. that is why the commission's proposal, which commissioner wallström has set out in detail in this parliament, is to use the existing eaggf funds, the structural funds of the interreg funds. the commission's proposals are not, however, to be regarded as a comprehensive programme, but as a model which can be changed completely, or else as a response to the requests of the member states, with programmes or specific actions depending on the use of the funds. we are absolutely open to these specific projects, we said so at the time and i want to stress this point today, but it is absolutely essential to have these proposals in order to be able to act. finally, as regards the possibility of using article 87 (2) of the treaty as a basis for community aid, i think there is an exorbitant interpretation of this article. all this without counting the budgetary problems it would raise. the article does not concern community aid but the compatibility of national aid with community law. what this article says is that in the event of natural disasters national aid may be compatible. whenever the commission has raised the question of the compatibility of these national aids as a result of natural events, there has always been compatibility. we are therefore fully prepared to act at this stage within the legal and budgetary margins available to us.

president of the commission. - madam president, mr minister, ladies and gentlemen, next week the european council will meet in nice. this summit will provide the heads of state or government with a historic opportunity which they must not miss. it will be an opportunity to address a whole range of issues: the european union is committed to the lisbon process and a social agenda, to the solemn adoption of the charter of fundamental rights. these are all important issues, but today, as you have suggested, i want to concentrate on the important decisions that will have to be taken in nice. the debate is on various issues, and i shall briefly touch on three aspects: firstly, the need to conclude the intergovernmental conference by adopting a treaty which provides real added value. secondly, the aspect of our security policy relating to crisis management; finally, the need to plan the way forward after nice. first, therefore, a new treaty. the fundamental purpose of a new treaty is to enable the union to continue to function after enlargement. in fact, our institutions, originally designed for six member states, will soon have to manage almost five times as many. we must prepare for this unprecedented enlargement. any unresolved problems in nice would end up blocking our way and so, just as we ask the candidate countries to meet all the criteria before accession, we too must be true to our commitments. this means ensuring that the union can take effective and democratic decisions that meet the expectations of european citizens. throughout the past winter, the commission has spent a lot of energy explaining why and with regard to which specific issues the initial agenda of the intergovernmental conference should be extended; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i am pleased to see that the negotiators are now close to agreement on those provisions which relate, for example, to enhanced cooperation, the court of justice, the democratic values referred to in article 7, and i note a greater involvement of european political parties in the democratic life of our member states and our institutions. i also have the impression that we are getting closer to a reasonable compromise on the composition of the commission and the weighting of votes in the council. as long as a number of fundamental principles are respected, i believe that the conference can proceed and reach an understanding in this respect, an understanding which meets the expectations and needs of countries large and small. whatever the number of commissioners, it is important to give the president of the commission all the powers necessary to manage the college effectively. similarly, whatever change is introduced in the weighting of votes in the council, it must be ensured that decisions cannot be taken contrary to the will of the majority of member states. the best way of doing this, and the simplest, is through the system of the double majority, although we are aware of the great difficulties it faces. (applause) i would like to thank so, little by little, we are moving in the right direction. however, there is one issue on which i find the lack of progress very worrying and which, in the view of both our institutions, is the most important issue we will have to solve in preparing for enlargement: the question of qualified majority voting. for the union to be effective, the conference must make significant progress in this respect, and this also means extending the codecision procedure. (applause) i would like to thank it is obvious that member states find it politically difficult to give up their right of veto in sensitive areas such as social policy, asylum and immigration, the common commercial policy, cohesion and taxation, even when it is only about the technical changes needed to make the single market work. if everyone stays on their side, however, i think it's worse for everyone; the fact is that the mathematics and even 50 years of experience show beyond any doubt that a modest enlargement is enough to make unanimous agreement much more difficult. in a union of 27 or more member states, the unanimity requirement will simply end up preventing any progress in any area where it is maintained. pay close attention to what i say: if the member states' right of veto in the area of justice and home affairs is retained, the implementation of the programme agreed with tampere will be seriously delayed or even impossible. and i will tell the heads of state and government in nice, without any further ado, that they should have no illusions about this. the particularly sensitive areas i have mentioned also include trade policy. i should like to dwell on this for a moment, since the house has insisted that it be given special prominence on today's agenda. as you know, modern economic activity is essentially based on services. under the current rules, some aspects of the negotiations on services are subject to the requirement of unanimity, precisely because our treaties were established as trade treaties on goods and not on services. the problem that is currently plaguing our trade policy is that, as the negotiations cover a wide range of sectors, including services, unanimous votes almost inevitably end up holding back any progress, not only in services but also in material goods. our trading partners, or let us call them our rivals in some cases, are enthusiastic about this because they can count on 15 veto possibilities and soon, thanks to enlargement, there will be many more. the situation is even worse when one of the member states imposes conditions, sometimes financial, in order to give its consent. the simple and natural solution - and this is the majority view during the conference - would be to change the current rules so that qualified majority voting applies to all aspects of these negotiations, including services. unfortunately, the current text of the conference is very complicated, very ambiguous and very long, with two protocols: but despite its length and complexity, it's also very weak, it doesn't provide the simple answer we need to the simple problem that has plagued us for so long. a proper solution therefore requires a great deal of work. for us, the final outcome of nice will depend to a large extent on the conclusions reached in the qualified majority votes. i am committed to doing whatever is necessary to reach an agreement that provides added value. inevitably the question that will be asked of us the morning after nice will be: are you satisfied with the results? the commission will answer this question frankly and without any rhetoric. at the next partsession in strasbourg, i will tell the house in front of you whether i believe that the enlarged union, which we all want to achieve, will be able to act effectively or not. in fact, it is on this basis that we will ultimately have to judge nice. (applause) important decisions will also be taken in nice to enable the european union to assume its responsibilities in the world. conflict prevention and crisis management are traditional areas of community intervention. it is our task to deliver on our commitments in the light of the new ambitious objectives that the union has set itself. this means that the union must develop an autonomous decision-making capacity and, if nato is not involved, launch and conduct military operations under union command in response to international crises. in this regard, it will be particularly useful to develop fruitful cooperation between the european union, the united nations, the osce and the council of europe. this - and i repeat - does not change the fact that for the member states concerned nato remains the basis of the collective defence of its members and will continue to play an important role in crisis management. crisis management, as we saw in kosovo, is not just about imposing a ceasefire, it is also about keeping opposing factions divided; it means rescuing and evacuating european union citizens, assisting large numbers of refugees, providing food and medicine, and enforcing and maintaining the rule of law. finally, to restore calm after chaos. in general, however, crises do not erupt overnight, but rather are the culmination of a process of escalation of tension in a country or region. one of the main aims of our common foreign and security policy must therefore be to reduce tension and prevent it from developing into armed conflict. the community already has many instruments to do this, and not just today: for example, almost all of our foreign aid programmes are aimed at supporting democracy and stability. what we need to do is to coordinate them better and make them more effective, and the commission is therefore taking the necessary internal measures to that end. the commission is convinced that only an integrated approach to crises will ensure the coherence and efficiency required for the union to play its full part on the international scene. crisis management requires the community to show a better capacity to react, but this must be translated into action which fully respects our institutional framework as defined by the treaties. of course, we will have to cooperate with the other institutions and with the high representative for the cfsp. however, we will have to take decisions on this framework now, because there is no worse time than a crisis to establish powers and responsibilities. the discussion at the conference showed that there were mature issues to be discussed after nice: the incorporation of the charter of fundamental rights into the community legal order, as stated by minister védrine; the reorganisation of the treaties on the basis of existing texts in order to present more clearly to public opinion the objectives and methods of the union's work; a clear distinction between the competences of the union and those of the member states; finally - and this is not a secondary point - if i am not mistaken about the tone of the debate and the prospects for the future of europe, the question is what the balance between the institutions of the european union should be in the spirit of an institutional model which is the community model, which has already successfully passed the test of time. we will of course have a lot to do after nice, but we will have to deal with this later. for now, let us look to the immediate future under the french presidency and concentrate on the priority of bringing a conclusion to nice and paving the way for enlargement. commission. – madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the proposal we are discussing today is intended to extend the existing arrangements concerning the dates and times when the summer time period begins and ends, that is, on the last sunday in march and the last sunday in october at 1 o' clock in the morning greenwich mean time. allow me, first of all, to congratulate your rapporteur, mrs honeyball, for her excellent work and the report she has produced. you will have noted that, compared with the earlier directives the arrangements proposed are of indefinite duration. the study ordered by the commission in 1999, in accordance with the commitment it gave to the council and european parliament when the eighth directive was adopted, concludes that the arrangements are widely accepted both by the public and by the various sectors of activity. however, it has become apparent that adopting the arrangements for a comparatively short period could cause difficulties for certain sectors. for example, the transport sector in particular, but also other sectors of industry, requires stable, long-term planning on account of technical requirements connected with the preparation of transport timetables. there are also the requirements of manufacturers of computers or electronic tachographs and producers of calendars and diaries. last but not least, the time-consuming and expensive repetition of legislative procedures at fairly close intervals at both community and national level should be avoided. while these are all reasons militating in favour of adopting open-ended arrangements, as a precaution the commission has made provision for drawing up, no later than five years after the first year of application of the directive, a report based on information supplied by clinical trials, and i think we can say today: this objective has been achieved. the council has informed us in an informal trilogue last week that it can accept most of the amendments tabled by the committee responsible and that it still wants some editorial changes, which we can bring about tomorrow by compromise amendments from four groups. for a long time, it seemed that an agreement was impossible. the positions were very different here in parliament, but also between the member states and between the various institutions. i would like to thank all those involved, the commission, the parliament's point of view. it is clarified that consent to a clinical trial should normally be given in writing. it is clarified that interference with the human germ line cannot be accepted. it is recognised that non-commercial clinical trials, which industry cannot or will not support, are nonetheless important and that rules need to be created for them. i'm particularly pleased that we've found a very good compromise on clinical trials on people who can't legally consent themselves. this question of research on non-consenting persons has been the subject of very intense controversy in the member states - including here in strasbourg, in the council of europe. we also had different positions among the participants in this legislative process. the council originally did not want to include any rules in the directive and left it to the member states. the european parliament has decided at first reading that such clinical trials are only allowed if a direct benefit for each individual patient can be demonstrated in each clinical trial. we have now reached a compromise, and i believe that this is not a compromise formula, not a compromise formula, but a proposal which is justified by the facts and which can solve the problem well, at least in this area. as regards direct benefit, in clinical trials a distinction must be made between the administration of the medicinal product and the accompanying studies necessary to draw conclusions for future patients. this is an important distinction we make in our report. then we must distinguish between children and other adults who are not able to give their consent. in children, there are also special metabolic characteristics, and therefore medicines given to children must also be tested in clinical trials in children. this is not the case in many areas at present. children are given drugs that have only been studied in adults, which means that children are being treated badly. the aim of the report is to ensure that children in europe are treated better in the future, with fewer side effects and the right dosage. we have very, very strict rules about this. the rules that have been drawn up in the committee and that the council will accept and that parliament will hopefully adopt tomorrow are stricter than what the council of europe has set out in its so-called bioethics convention, but the rules explicitly allow research, and we consider that research, when carried out according to the rules, is extremely important. so i am satisfied with the compromise reached. i 'm unhappy with two things: we had originally called for a shorter deadline for the approval of the clinical trial at first reading and i would have liked to see the 60-day deadline provided for in the common position reduced somewhat, at least for the public authorities. i think that a little more time can be allowed to an ethics committee, which is staffed by people who are not doing this as their main job, but we should put some pressure on the authorities to get to work quickly. unfortunately, this was not possible to reach a compromise in the council, and i therefore prefer to put the compromise reached with the council to the vote rather than have a long conciliation procedure, perhaps without agreement at the end. the same applies to the question of whether a doctor should be the head of the clinical trial or whether other professions should be allowed to participate. parliament also wants clinical trials to be carried out by doctors only in all member states, because we believe that in this sensitive area, nurses or midwives, even if they have additional training, should not be involved, nor should biologists or pharmacists who may have only worked in the laboratory but who have insufficient experience with patients. i must admit, however, that the council was not prepared to make any further compromises. that is why we must accept this compromise with a heavy heart. if we accept this compromise, we will still have a system that ensures therapeutic progress and that protects patients in europe not just as it is, but better, and that is why i am in favour of this compromise.

equality of arms in europe either. there are a number of countries, the classic example being the united kingdom, illustrated and illustrated several times by the example of the london stock exchange, where company law provides for the possibility of excluding acquisitions by virtue of restrictions on voting rights in the statutes of a public limited company. so the consequence of this article 9, as it stands here, would be that some companies from some countries in europe could be taken over much more easily, but other companies in other countries in europe could practically never be taken over if they have such provisions in their statutes. that is why article 9 must be amended. the next problem is the question of the competent supervisory authority. the common position covers this commission. – mr president, the commission realises from previous discussions the great importance of this subject for parliament and i have carefully looked at the numerous amendments to the proposed directive. there are some amendments, in particular those which emphasise the importance of the universal service and of the rural post offices, which i can support. universal service is the cornerstone of community policy in this area and everything we do is designed to create a proper climate for its improvement. with regard to most amendments, however, i must say that very little is left of the original proposal, which the commission presented in may. the commission proposed a step-by-step approach, with a further stage of market opening of 20% overall to be taken in the year 2003. what i see in return is not only a rejection of this degree of market opening but also of the dynamic process of modernisation itself. what exactly do i see? firstly, no 50 grammes, which goes against the need to create actual competition. secondly, no opening of outgoing cross-border mail although this is already a reality in ten member states. thirdly, no definition or special services contrary to the existing directives' objectives and also contrary to the case law of the court of justice. fourthly, no opening of express mail, even though this is a new and separate market. fifthly, no step in the year 2003, which is contrary to article 7 of the current directive, and sixthly, no timetable for further reform, which goes against the conclusions of the lisbon summit and the needs of the operators themselves. this is not a positive way forward. in particular, whereas the heads of state and government at lisbon called for an accelerated market opening, the amendments which i have just now described would result in the opposite, namely a decelerated market opening. the two years' delay in implementing the next step would not be consistent with the current directive. the debate about modernising the postal sector started in 1989 during a telecom council at antibes. look where we are now, more than ten years later. only 3% of the letter market has been liberalised. shifting the next step from 2003 to 2005 would be another delay that, i am afraid, is not acceptable to the commission. the degree of market opening as now proposed by parliament would reduce the 20% of the commission proposals to only 6% from the start of the year 2005, without any prospect of completion of the internal market in the postal sector and that, i am afraid, does not comply with the conclusions of the european council, nor would it meet the needs and expectations of postal clients, both business users and individual households. nor would it meet the interests of the employees in the sector who want to look ahead. in short it would be too little, too late, and would bring to a sudden halt the much needed momentum for further change, gravely harming the incumbent adaptation and threatening long-term employment. in addition, stopping competition in outgoing cross-border mail would be a retrograde step, difficult to enforce by regulation and leading to complaints from competitors. special services are another very important area where innovation and modernisation must be encouraged. under the existing directive the principle is clear. new and distinct services are always outside the reservable area but there is no clear definition of special services in the current directive, and that opens the door to endless debate and market uncertainty. it would be unacceptable to allow continuing litigation to determine what happens here. we need clearer definitions or else we would fail in our duty as legislators to modernise the regulatory framework. i know that modernising the postal services sector is difficult and politically sensitive. the post office is close to people, to consumers and to employees alike. in this process of modernisation, fear should not be our guide but rather the challenge of improving the sector. if we do too little, too late, the postal sector as a whole will be in danger. it will be overtaken by technology and ignored by consumers who do not get service for their money. i am sure that many of you, and in particular the rapporteur, will agree more than politics perhaps allows you to say. i call upon all of you not to shy away from your responsibility as elected legislators to do what is required and to support a dynamic process of change. may i quote three actors in this field. firstly, the chief executive of the uk post office, mr john roberts, has talked about competition leading to improvements in quality and efficiency and lower prices. secondly, the president of la poste, mr claude bourmaud, recently explained how the coming decade will herald the most profound transformation ever for postal operators around the world. he said that between now and the end of the decade the opening to competition of virtually the whole postal market appears to be inevitable. thirdly, french senator, gérard larcher, who is a well-known expert in the field of postal services, called upon all parties to look forward. in 1997 he said, and i quote: “we should not deal with the problems of today by focusing on the notions of yesterday. let us open the debate to solve the problems of la poste in the framework of tomorrow.” all three of these people make important points. the postal service is increasingly having to compete in the wider communications market with modern technology developed by the internet, mobile telephones and the integration of different means of communication. the traditional post offices with their rigid structure of employment and slow adaptation to market requirements will not be able to compete in those markets if they are held back by parliament's amendments. society demands a modern postal sector. may i point to the main european consumer organisations, such as the beuc, which have welcomed the commission's proposal. many consumer organisations would want to move even faster than the commission in opening the postal market because they expect greater competition to lead to higher service quality and lower prices, but the commission has not proposed this fast-track liberalisation as preferred by consumer organisations. our proposal strikes a careful balance, because universal service providers will need time to change the structures further, to become more flexible enterprises so they can adapt to new market conditions. only the introduction of real competition in a controlled and progressive way, according to a fixed timetable, will assist them to do this. if the european legislator fails, those member states progressing rapidly down the road indicated by the lisbon summit will be penalised, as their postal operators will be subject to competition from operators benefiting from an extended monopoly. most of the amendments adopted by parliament's committee on regional policy, transport and tourism would, if accepted, lead to a situation where hardly anything would change. this would mean that postal services would increasingly lose ground to other means of communication. it would be a very short-sighted approach. it would be a rearguard battle. the monopoly of postal services would cause them to ossify and lose volume which would lead to losses of jobs. i am aware of your concern about preserving the universal service and the postal network and i share this concern. i stand for cast-iron guarantees that universal service obligations will always be protected. where we differ is the method to achieve this goal. trying to preserve this status quo and maintaining the structures of the past is not the right way. the market requires flexibility and adaptability to the new communications environments. the commission proposal responds to this requirement in a very reasonable and a gradual way. it recognises that under the existing directive there was already a shift in the balance between the reserved area and other means to ensure a high-quality and enduring universal service. these include licensing requirements, including universal service obligations for new entrants to the market, a compensation fund and setting tariffs at an appropriate level geared to costs. however, without competition, the situation would become unbalanced. in this spirit, i can accept those of your amendments which are non-contentious and others which rightly give emphasis to issues such as universal service as applied in member states, redressing complaints, and the rural network. these concern amendments nos 2, 3, 6, 7, 24, 28, 29, 32, 39, 40 and 41. i can also accept the new amendments tabled yesterday, namely 46, first paragraph, 58 and 59, which clarify certain important points. regarding amendments nos 60 and 61, i can agree with the principle of completing the internal market at a future date to be determined within a reasonable time frame. that is all in line with the commission's proposal and the conclusions of lisbon. however, it will not surprise members of this parliament that the commission cannot accept the remaining proposed amendments. the reason is that they go against the grain of what the commission has proposed – what is necessary to achieve the process of modernisation to the benefit of postal consumers and employees alike. we must maintain the momentum for change and achieve a solid first step, plus a timetable for further change. in conclusion, the european union cannot afford to give uncertain signals in such an important area. that is why i cannot and will not be silent when the future of the sector is threatened by a failure to meet properly the challenges set to us all at lisbon. if the european union, of which the members of this parliament are the elected representatives, wants to have the most competitive, knowledge-based and dynamic economy in ten years time, it needs a modern postal sector. therefore, i would call upon all the members of this parliament to support the european mission and i conclude by saying that the time to act is now.

commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, today marks exactly one year since the sinking of the tanker erika. a shipwreck which contaminated 400 km of french coast, with very serious consequences for the ecological environment, for the citizens who lived and had businesses in that area, whether they were oyster farmers, shellfishers, fishermen or simply citizens connected with the tourist sector. this accident, which followed many others, caused indignation and discouragement among the affected populations and public opinion in general, given the opacity of the maritime sector and the inadequacy of the regulations in force to avoid problems like this one. this feeling, unfortunately, still lives on in the minds of public opinion in europe today. the sinking of the erika had a totally new and surprising effect. never before has there been so much talk about maritime safety in the european union. for the first time there has been a growing awareness of the need to find european solutions to this type of marine pollution issue. it is clear that a single union state cannot have any real influence on world shipping and, moreover, the international maritime organisation today is too slow and lacks effective means to properly monitor the rules it promulgates. european citizens have been pressing for the european institutions to take swift and drastic action to put an end to the convenience boating scandal. one year after the sinking of the erika, we must all ask ourselves whether we have really been able to meet the expectations of the citizens. i sincerely believe that, in view of the rapid progress made in the work of our respective bodies, it is undeniable that all the institutions have fully understood and assumed the importance of the matter. the commission took its responsibilities and adopted a first package of measures just three months after the accident, which was fully endorsed by the european parliament on 30 november. in addition to these first measures, the commission has just adopted on 6 december a second package which, in my view, will respond even more directly to the expectations of the population and which must also profoundly change the rules of the game in maritime transport, to the greater benefit of maritime safety and the protection of our coasts against the risks of pollution. and in that spirit, today i want to present very briefly the contents of this new package called erika ii. firstly, it is a question of setting up a european system of control of maritime traffic. the first measure is a proposal for a directive establishing a european system for monitoring, control and information on maritime traffic. it is clear that port state control, however rigorously it is carried out, only partially protects states against the risks of accidents and pollution, in particular by ships in transit. the commission proposal therefore has three main objectives: first, to improve the monitoring and control of all vessel traffic off our coasts. to this end, vessels must be equipped with devices enabling them to be identified and tracked automatically from shore. the commission is also aware of the importance of black boxes, which are also required by this directive and which must be placed on board ships calling at a european port to facilitate the investigation of the facts in the event of an accident at sea or, where appropriate, to facilitate port state control. this will oblige the captain and the crew to steer the ship more carefully. the second objective is to simplify and speed up the transmission of detailed information on dangerous or polluting cargoes in the event of an accident by requiring ships and authorities to communicate the data electronically. the final objective of this directive is to strengthen the management of emergency situations at sea by means of the obligation to designate port of refuge, the prohibition of going to sea during a severe storm and greater powers of intervention at sea by the coastal state in the event of a serious risk of pollution. secondly, another element of this package is the improvement of the existing rules on liability and compensation for damage in the event of pollution by oil or its by-products. it is enough to recall that the case of the erika oil spill has shown us the inadequacy and slowness of compensation, which is far from having been paid to the victims and those affected by this pollution when a year has already passed since the disaster. and that, in addition, they will not be able to see 100% of the damages they have suffered. the commission's priority is to try to solve these two problems, and the solution we propose is to supplement the existing funds by creating a european fund funded by the oil companies, which offers victims quick compensation of up to 1 000 million euros, instead of the 200 million euros - 180 million dollars - currently granted by international services. we shall also be addressing international bodies to try to review in detail the arrangements laid down by international conventions. if the imo does not take the necessary measures, the commission would submit to parliament and the council a proposal for a community system of liability and compensation in the event of oil pollution. in addition, any person who has contributed by gross negligence to causing pollution will be subject to dissuasive sanctions, which will serve to encourage responsible behaviour by the maritime industry as a whole. the third measure of the erica ii package is the proposal to set up a european maritime safety agency, which will provide the commission and the member states of the union with the technical support necessary to implement the applicable community legislation and serve as a platform between the states and the commission for the development of harmonised practices and procedures, as well as facilitating the flow of information between different ports and between different states and administrations. with more than 15 directives or regulations in force, there is an urgent need to standardise practices and to exercise greater control over the application of community rules, in order to avoid major and unacceptable differences in the field of maritime safety that could occur within the union. the european maritime safety agency is a first step towards increasingly integrating the administrative practices of the member states, which may one day lead to the creation, as has been repeatedly called for by this house, of a genuine european coast guard. mr president, i hope that parliament will take the opportunity of this highly symbolic date - the first anniversary of the sinking of the erika - to recall its determination and to provide the commission with the support it will need throughout the legislative process. this is a matter of crucial importance, since it has asserted the european union's ability to impose its own requirements in the field of maritime safety and pollution prevention in an international environment which is generally unfavourable. i would remind you that the heads of state or government, meeting just three days ago at the european council in nice, gave decisive political impetus to this second package of measures, recognising that it is intended to strengthen maritime safety, improve the european maritime traffic information system and create an agency to fill in the gaps in the existing international regime. the commission has therefore recommended that the member states adopt the appropriate measures a priori and as soon as necessary, without waiting for the parliamentary and council procedures to allow us to adopt the directives to which i have referred.

commission. – mr president, let me first even in her absence congratulate the rapporteur, mrs lienemann for her excellent work, and express my great satisfaction that, thanks to the constructive work of both parliament and the council, we might be in a position to conclude on this important initiative already at first reading. this proposal on sustainable urban development has the potential of having a direct effect on the daily lives as many as 80% of the european population. it will enable and encourage towns and cities throughout europe and beyond to come together and learn from each other's experiences, help them to tackle environmental problems and challenges and to work towards sustainability. the commission is also grateful for the substantial support which the european parliament has provided for this proposal and for the many helpful amendments which have been put forward. the commission recognises the importance of promoting good governance and transparency in its decision-making process. accordingly, we are strongly in favour of the establishment of a platform of dialogue with the key stakeholders to help determine the priority themes to be supported. its innovative approach will involve cooperation with the city networks, member states, eu institutions, ngos and the business community, ensuring that the funds provided from the framework are targeted at those areas of sustainable development most in need of them. i believe that this innovative approach will provide an example for others to follow. the budget for this proposal has been the subject of some debate with a wide range of views expressed about the appropriateness of the eur 12.4 m originally proposed by the commission. many have suggested that the budget is too small. the commission wants to stress however that this framework is not about the implementation of projects at ground level. other community programmes and initiatives are already in place for this. rather, the framework is designed to facilitate the sharing of information and ideas about the best practice of sustainable urban development so that the solutions identified to problems in one city or town can be shared with the other cities and towns throughout europe and beyond. the quality approach of the framework and its multiplier effects are such that despite the relatively small budget it is expected to have a real impact on the promotion of sustainable urban development in europe. the forty-one amendments have been given detailed consideration and the commission is able to accept thirty of them, either completely or in principle. amendment no 33 proposes a revised budget for the proposal of eur 14 m. we must make it clear that the commission's general line on such matters is that no budget increase - the next item is the report (a5-0352/2000) by mrs patrie, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the commission communication on the application of the precautionary principle.
the committee on legal affairs and the internal market adopted a position on the proposal. - the proposal for a regulation (com (89) 0283 - c3-0314/90) by mr de gucht, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the common organization of the market in bananas; the legal affairs committee has identified a number of key points on the precautionary principle, which are also reflected in the excellent report by mrs patrie. we were not concerned with a purely legal assessment. we have taken a political stand. i stress this because the application of the precautionary principle requires more than just flawless legislation. the aim is to ensure that the high level of protection promised in the treaties is actually guaranteed to citizens within the european union. the only way to do that is to take precautions seriously. the aim must not be damage control or compensation, but the ultimate aim must be to prevent damage to people's health or property. we shall achieve this by applying the precautionary principle rigorously, as my colleague has also pointed out. we should always keep this in mind as legislators and we should also encourage the commission to act accordingly in its proposals. the report by mrs patrie is a direct mandate for this. we would have saved ourselves a lot in the past and in the future in relation to bse if we had put in place adequate legal safeguards in good time and also strictly controlled compliance with these laws, which as we know is a matter for the member states. in the defence of american hormone meat to protect the health of our citizens, we have been denied the right to take precautions. it has even been denounced as protectionism! in other contexts too, the interested parties do not tire of pointing out the principle of proportionality and the prohibition of any discrimination. if you look closely, it is not a concern for the rule of law, but rather a concern for money and profit. i am not personally concerned about the excessive protection of the law. the citizens should not be afraid either. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the health of the population is not affected by the disease. i therefore recommend that we follow the line drawn by the rapporteur.
commission. – mr president, i would like to express my appreciation for parliament's initiative in addressing the topic of the precautionary principle and for the excellent work of the rapporteur, mrs patrie. this commission's communication on the precautionary principle was issued in february this year and it proposes guidelines on when and how to use the precautionary principle. the principle and approach is often referred to at national, european and global level when questions related to human health and the environment are discussed. the precautionary principle was also discussed at the nice summit, which took note of a resolution adopted by the general affairs council. the resolution calls on the commission to use the guidelines adopted and to incorporate the precautionary principle whenever necessary in drawing up its legislative proposals and in all its actions. the resolution also highlights the need to work actively for a commitment by international partners to reach an understanding on the application of the principle. we now examine how this resolution should be followed up. the commission communication is not the final word on the issue. i therefore welcome parliament's motion for a resolution on this important issue and would like to comment on some of the points it raises. the commission confirms its intention to make active use of the precautionary principle whenever appropriate. we consider it as a general principle which should be taken into consideration in the fields of environmental protection and human, animal and plant health. regarding its implications at international level, in particular within the world trade organisation, the commission considers that the precautionary principle is becoming a full-fledged rule of customary international law with all the rights attached to it. this entitles the community to prescribe the level of protection notably with regard to the environment and human, animal and plant health which it considers appropriate. it will also raise the capacity of developing countries to ensure protection of the environment and human, animal and plant health. parliament must have noted that the commission is in line with most of the issues raised in your motion for a resolution. however, i would like to clarify some points. concerning the eventual withdrawal of a product on the basis of process or production methods, it is not possible to make any general statement on the legitimacy of such an action prior to a comprehensive risk assessment. the distinction made in the resolution between the precautionary principle and prudence would need to be more precise. the prudential approach is part of risk assessment policy and is an integral part of the scientific opinion delivered by the risk evaluators. on the other hand, application of the precautionary principle is part of risk management. one consequence of this is that initial suspicions or empirical judgments cannot be used alone as regards the application of the precautionary principle. the hazard has to be identified and risk assessment has to be carried out by experts before measures are taken. it is important to stress that it is for the decision-makers to define the level of protection. it is not possible to provide a general de minimis threshold. the commission considers that the motion for a resolution is balanced on this issue and does not support amendment no 3. finally, the burden of proof may be reversed on a case-by-case evaluation. a general rule is not appropriate. to conclude, i would like to thank parliament for its support in addressing this issue. the motion for resolution will help foster a general understanding of the precautionary principle both within the community and internationally.

intimidating environment. many others have to resign themselves to living with police escorts and cannot walk freely with their children in the streets or attend public places without any precautions.
